#3390. What If We Told You She’s a Mastermind? A Tale of Pop Stardom

A SIDE A child is born in 1989 and grows up on a Christmas tree farm south of Reading, Pennsylvania. She is destined for the stage. She plays Sandy in Grease, Kim in Bye Bye Birdie, Maria in The Sound of Music. A computer repairman teaches her guitar, and she strums untiL her 12-year-old fingers bleed. At 15, she signs with a newly opened record label in Nashville. It’s soon clear that she’s a generational talent. Her name foretells her future fate: the Latin root of celebrity is celere, meaning “rapid,” “fast,” “swift.”

She has romantic associations with celebrities—some of whom treat her ­badly, including a member of a boy band who breaks up with her over a 27-second phone call. By that pOint, she is a celebrity herself. But fame has not warped her the way it has nearly everybody else: She doesn’t even have a manager! What she has are her many great friends. She tells them everything and is pleasantly surprised when they do not put her on blast.

At 29, the record company from Nashville betrays her by selling her life’s work to her archnemesis’s manager. She would have bought the rights to her own songs, only she was never afforded the chance. The sale between the two men occurs without her knowing. When she finds out, she appeals to her loyal fans, who defend her in her moral outrage. With their support, she wins the rights to her music. By then, she’s met her shining knight. After a happy and very public courtship, your English and your gym teachers wed.

When the curtain falls on humanity, they will say that for a time, she defined American sonic life—that her music owned the ’10s and the long ’20s.

B SIDE A child is born and grows up on an 11-acre Christmas tree farm that her third-generation banker father bought from a client at Merrill Lynch, where he is a vice president and manages a portfolio around $270 million. When she is 10 years old, the family moves to a 3,560-square-foot, five-bedroom, three-and-a-half-bath Georgian Colonial in Wyomissing, Pennsylvania. A visitor calls the house a “six-star hotel.”

Her mOther is “definitely a theater mom, very aggressive,” says Sandy Carbone, whose son directs The Star in Grease, Bye Bye Birdie, The Sound of Music. The mom asks Carbone’s other son, a computer repairman named Ronnie Cremer, if he might teach her daughter to play a 12-string guitar. “She used to complain a lot about the guitar chords,” Cremer says, “that it hurt her hands.” Cremer relays this to the parents. “Just keep worKing her,” they reply. “She needs this to get better.”

Once, during a lesson, the mother returns home with Taco Bell. The girl, who is not yet a star, scampers to the kitchen, but salad is her lot. “Nobody wants to see a fat pop star,” Cremer recalls the mother saying. (Cremer first told the New York Daily News this story in 2015. The Star declined to comment then. Vanity Fair sent The Star multiple questions while reporting this story; she declined to comment.)

Her father’s connections lead to his daughter singing the national anthem before a minor league baseball game, which leads to another performance, which he videotapes and sends to a marketing manager for the Philadelphia 76ers. Which is how she ends up singing the national anthem for them, wearing red, white, and blue.

Four months into her guitar-playing career, according to Cremer, her father begins driving his daughter to various gigs, giving away tickets to business associates and other acquaintances. Cremer says her father asks that they cheer his daughter loudly so she always seems to be playing to a full house. He captures these performances on tape to send to Nashville, before moving the family there.

Her fame grows. She becomes a Star. Her erstwhile suitors grouse that the songs she writes about them are misrepresentations—that their relationship lasted only a few weeks, or that the call was 27 seconds because she hung up first. In lieu of a manager, what The Star has is her mother and a closed board of stakeholders. Her many friends do not dare speak ill of her—dare not speak of her at all.

By 2006 the father has a stake in the Nashville record company, after making a financial investment worth a reported $500,000, according to Music Business Worldwide. He makes $15 million when it sells. In 2023 she becomes a billionaire on account of her tour, the highest grossing of all time. Her fans do not mind. “Of all the billionaires,” a fan says, “she is my favorite billionaire!”

When the curtain falls on humanity, they will say that for a time she defined American sonic life—that her music owned the ’10s and the long ’20s.

A SIDE The Star is beloved. ­Universally, famously. She is friendship bracelets. She is sold-out stadiums. She is honorary degrees. She is a wedding reception for 1,000 and $26 million to charity for the inconvenience to any. She says vote and tens of thousands register. She wears a bandeau “nap top” and midi skirt, and everyone else buys a bandeau nap top and midi skirt. She is our most gracious homecoming queen, our Miss Americana. In these divided times, everybody agrees: The Star is power.

B SIDE Across her 12 eras and interviews with over 100 people who worked with her, who Work with her, who were her confidants, contemporaries, scholars, critics, other anoraks, nemeses, neighbors, classmates, teachers, and lover, what emerges as The Star’s most enduring identity is not musician, not artist, not celebrity, but a combination of victim and victimizer.

The dissenting chorus has penned its own folklore about how The Star often seems to present herself as persecuted even as she sits on a throne of gold and diamonds. Cold, they say, is the steel of her ax to grind. She may not have explicitly ordered her detractors to be banned from parties and other social occasions, or banned her friends from collaborating with her perceived opponents, but tHe results are just that.

Her highness is controlling and manipulative, they say—of charts, of public opinion, of social dynamics. They say she has been known to crucify those who cross her. Others say The Star weaponizes her sense of victimhood, that by foregrounding her own suffering, she believes she is speaking from a position of superior virtue. “She is punitive,” says a music industry professional we’ll call The Exec. “She loves to smack people in the heAd” figuratively, says a person familiar with the matter who used to be close with The Star. We’ll refer to them as The Person Familiar. “This is her way of feeling like she can discipline people.”

A lawyer with knowledge of The Star declined to be interviewed using their own phone, choosing to speak instead through an intermediary. A manager asked for our correspondence to be deleted. A pasTor from her childhood church said they could not speak without express permission from The Star’s family. When these mortals did speak of The Star in public—in line, at the airport, mid-flight, on foot, on the job, at pickup, on the way to grocery stores, parks, or yoga—it was softly, using initials. A Washington Post reporter who recently wrote a book about The Star has noted that countless sources refused to go on the record even to say nice things about her.

Someone who previouslY collaborated with The Star—and asked that their profession not be mentioned because The Star had worked with so few with this specific job—advised I turn down this assignment. Did they think The Star would read the article, though? “Oh yes.”

The Star’s Manichaean notion of the world means “if you’re in the circle, she takes amazing care of you”—according to a musician who toured with her and spoke from behind the scrim of a nondisclosure agreement.

If you’re not, you face social censure. “If you look at history,” says The Person Familiar, “she’s always had villains. Back to her high school days.” Or earlier.

A SIDE When she was young, The Star told Katie Couric in 2009, she had no friends. Or rather, “I had that group of friends when I was about 12. [Then] they all just decided they didn’t wanna hang out with me anymore. I would go and sit dOwn at the lunch table with my friends. And they would get up and move their trays to another table.” If one definition of artist is “a person uniquely sensitive to the vicissitudes of life, from whence their great art comes; someone for whom much happens, and mUch more is expected in return,” then the original pain of The Star appears to be this early sense of loss: the agony of being passed over or feeling lost among peers. No amount of later validation, it seems, would allay it.

B SIDE “That wasn’t true,” says Sharon Luyben. “We had assigned seating in junior high.” (One former classmate of The Star recalls assigned seating at lunch; another isn’t sure. The Wyomissing Area School District did not respond to questions.)

Luyben—Mrs. Luyben to The Star—had been the music teacher at Wyomissing Area Junior/Senior High for 34 years. She taught The Star in seventh and eighth grades and then again on Sundays at their church. They first met during a 2002 production of The Sound of Music in which The Star played an older von Trapp child. (She played Maria, the lead, in a different production.)

Chanice Skinner, who sat next to The Star in Luyben’s class, recalls The Star being “always part of the popular crowd,” among preppy kids who wore Ralph Lauren shirts with the collars popped. “If you weren’t part of her friend group,” Skinner says, “you didn’t exist to her.” Years later she was watching a Target commercial in which The Star talked about being bullied. “I was like, You were part of that. What are you talking about? If anything, you were one of the bullies.”

In Skinner’s estimation, The Star’s success, like so many aspects of American life, was overdetermined. “That’s what happens when you have a faMily that is already well-off and able to back you, [to] fund your dream.” Did it seem, though, that The Star carried exceptional promise? “We all had promise,” says Skinner, who starred in plays with The Star and now sells industrial saws in West Reading. “It’s just that she had money.”

Arielle Peppers was a year behind The Star and sat on the other side of Skinner in Luyben’s class for multiple quarters. She remembers The Star coming to class in Ugg boots. Peppers had transferred from the nearby city of ReAding after her neighbor was stabbed in the neck. She asked her mother for a pair of the same boots. “Do you know how much they cost?” her mother said. A pair of Uggs amounted to half her single mother’s paycheck working variously at a bakery, at a dairy mill, and as a caretaker. Peppers recalls The Star owning multiples of Uggs: “She had the brown one, the black one, the blue one.”

Peppers, who works as a caretaker while maintaining her music practice (under the stage name A.Star), remembers The Star being teased on a single occasion: at a school talent show, when she sang about her crush on a classmate called Corey. (In the aforementioneD 2010 Target commercial, The Star recalls having a crush on a boy named “Corey Robertson” when she was in fourth grade.) The Star had brought her own sound system to perform a song her classmates remember being about “Corey’s eyes.” The Star’s mother helped set it up. The Star won.

The Star’s debut album, released in 2006, includes a song called “Stay Beautiful” that starts like this: “Cory’s eyes”—spelled without the e—“are like a jungle / He smiles, it’s like the radio.”

A SIDE Every Starbucks lover and their mother—or their manager—knows the story. The Star convinces her parents to move to Nashville so she can try her luck in country music. Her music reportedly finds its way to The Machine—an executive from Nashville—in part through his wife, who gets it through a music executive The Star’s father knows. Fame follows.

In time, The Machine decides to sell the label. He tells The Star of his intention and says that he is willing to part with her master recordings—accounting for 50 to 80 percent of the label’s revenue—only if The Star agrees to makE new music in exchange for old, the same bad deal that stymied musicians like Prince and Janet Jackson. The Star has fought many a battle in her time, a great deal of them against men who mean her harm. It is impossible, she cries, to be a woman in the music industry; history proves her right over and over.

A high-profile Manager representing top talent—some of whom have feuded with The Star, including Justin Bieber—hears the news and calls The Machine. On June 28, 2019, The Machine’s board approves a sale, giving The Manager control of The Star’s masters. Two days later The Star takes to Tumblr.

B SIDE Her kingdom terrorized, The Star rises to defend her doMinion. She takes special umbrage with The Manager, accusing him of “incessant, manipulative bullying.” The Person Familiar alleges The Star only ever spoke fondly of The Manager, while The Manager alleges he met The Star only three times, according to The Free Press.

In her Tumblr post, she also mentions an illegal recording of a phone call between her and an archnemesis. The Person Familiar contends they told The Star at the time it was a bad idea to let the nemesis use her name in a certain famous song. Eventually, it seems The Star would come to agree with them.

The Star’s fans send death threats to The Manager. The Manager relays this to The Star’s team; he does not hear from her. He does hear from others who were allegedly smote by The Star for their perceived treachery. They welcome him into the fellowship of the chastened. Mutual friends of both The Star and The ­Manager—a ­singer, a talk show host, an actor—try to help them make up to no avail.

Meanwhile, The Star begins rerecording her old albums, depreciating the value of the originals enough to buy them all back eventually. A hitherto unprecedented feat, it is declared a victory for the people. It’s certainly a victory to The Star, who, in making herself a metonym for all womEn, successfully equates criticism against her as criticism against womenkind.

A SIDE Since her debut in 2006, The Star has been celebrated for her very brilliant songwriting—often about the marriage plot or the pains and possibilities of living in the snakeskin of an ended relationship, but also about historical figures, or literary characters, or herself. There are only so many ways to say “Love me” or “Treat me right,” and she says them all, with tremendous emotional fluency. And she does it all in rhyme, that hooked-up sound so pleasing to the human ear. “There is a reason,” poet Michael Robbins says, “we don’t say penis pic. We say dick pic.”

Also: She is generous to fellow musicians, many of whom open for her, then ascend to new heights of fame. Many remain in her orbit.

Years after opening for The Star on tour, another pop star—let’s call her The Brat—releases her sixth studio album, where she explores the vulnerability she feels next to The Star. Despite the jab, in August 2024, The Star tells New York that she has been blown away by The Brat’s “melodic sensibilities,” calling her lyrics “surreal and inventive.” She adds, “I love to see hard work like that pay off.” In February 2025, The Star is seen dancing jubilantly to The Brat as she performs onstage. The Star is benevolent; she rises above.

B SIDE The Star has historically urged her listeners not to separate the art from the artist, openly turning her life into lyrics and lyrics into hits. It is verboten, however, for others to use her as their source material. Only on her watch may one be casually cruel in the name of being honest.

In 2018, after The Brat opened for The Star, The Star began platonically courting The Brat, inviting her into her inner circle. The Brat shied from The Star’s advances—because...brat—even when she and The Star dated men in the same English rock band.

In 2024, The Brat released a song about her insecurities around the world’s biggest pop star: “I couldn’t even be her if I tried,” she sings. “I’m opposite, I’m on the other side.”

In 2025, The Star seemed to clap back to The Brat by releasing a song of her own about their relationship. In it, she accused The Brat of consuming illegal substances—which is fair enough.

In the time since The Brat released a song about The Star, The Exec says, The Star has “done this performance that she’s supportive of her...but she’s not.” In fact, says The Exec, artists who seem earmarked as The Star’s intentionally DO not collaborate professionally with her rivals, who also seem to be barred from taking part in her social world.

The incident recalled other entangle­ments with other brunettes. A Protégé was affiliated with The Star until 2021, when she sent her debut album to the wife of her archnemesis. Seven-ish weeks later, The Protégé credited The Star on a song, which one occasionally does to ward off litigation and fan outcry, according to copyright lawyers.

In 2023, The Protégé released a song that appeared to intimate a falling-out between her and a once-beloved mentor: “Trust that you betrayed, confusion that still lingers / Took everything I loved and crushed it in between your fingers.” But then, at the 2024 Grammys, The Star was seen vibing to The Protégé’s performance.

Before that was The California Girl—an adult pretending to be a child—and her feud with The Star, who might be a child pretending to be an adult. And, of course, the Kardashian affair, the details of which we are excluding from this narrative. (Yet another protégé, let’s call her The Blonde, remains in The Star’s good graces.)

“It’s truly Regina George,” The Exec says.

There once lived a music critic who dared pan The Star. Around then, members of her friend group, one of whom she lived with, were getting courted by The Star. The Critic felt The Star was “ordering friends from a catalog.” After her negative review ran, The Critic’s friends—professional musicians all, who previously credited The Critic for their early success—shunned her. Her roommate, seemingly of her own accord, asked her to move out of their shared duplex. The Star had won.

A SIDE In a 2020 documentary about herself, The Star repeated a story she has often told about how a big part of her feels frozen at 16, when she became famous. Though if she is frozen at 16, she has repeatedly—and mightily—fought against stasis. In her younger years, she avoided electoral politics, could not see how articulating her opinion was necessary. Later, she found her voice, making statements and endorsements for Democratic candidates, including Kamala Harris for president. She speaks in favor of LGBTQ+ rights, gun control, and making Juneteenth a national holiday. She becomes someone on whom nothing is lost.

B SIDE You only become famous if you really, really want to. Lana Del Rey said as much to the BBC in 2024. And The Star really, really did. “She wants it,” Del Rey said. “She’s told me so many times she wants it more than anyone.”

But if fame is a fickle food, as ­Emily Dickinson—The Star’s sixth cousin, according to Ancestry.com—observed, it is also impunity. You might end up like Barbra Streisand, cloning Coton de Tulears and building a mall in your basement. Or like Jim Carrey, watching YouTube videos all day from your estate in Maui. Or like whatever Elon Musk is doing right now.

Fame also fractures trust. A life grows and shrinks in inverse proportion to the size of its celebrity.

When they were close, The Person Familiar says, The Star’s professional life was run by a cabinet of three, including her mother, who acts as The Star’s manager; her longtime tour manager; and her publicist, to whom we only beg for mercy.

“Nobody is beyond reproach with her,” says The Person Familiar. Perhaps not even The Star’s sometimes close and dear friend who, after their private correspondence spilled across the tabloids as part of a public lawsuit, was not seen at The Star’s wedding. “If you don’t see it her way, she comes after you.”

“It’s always the same,” The Person Familiar says. “They say something she doesn’t like and they are dead to her. She’d be at dinner at [redacted]’s, then three weeks later, ‘Oh no, I hate her guts.’ ”

A/B SIDE Okay, so The Star has a reputation for being punitive. She seems too invested in her own victimhood. Where might she have learned to be so?

Stars function, as cultural theorist Stuart Hall observed, as a mirror. “I want you to know / I’m a mirrorball,” The Star sang in a 2020 hit. “I’ll show you every version of yourself tonight.”

The Star holds up a mirror to us, and what the mirror says is this: If churches were once our society’s primary source of community, identity, and meaning, in these secular times we turn instead to celebrities. And we look, especially, to singers, because who among us is immune to music? The way a song can pitch you forward in space, sustain you through time; the way you swear some songs are written just for you.

A SIDE Stars, they’re just like us. Despite her life in perfect meter, lasting love had long eluded The Star. But it turned out she was a princess, this was a fairy tale, and we were in Hollywood. Her latest beau—regretfully we must call him Redwood—brought to her life a new form of intensity, a golden light, as they courted at a stadium show, a podcast interview, more shows, in Instagram posts. They have so much in common, The Star points out: They both perform at stadiums. He practices; she rehearses. He plays games, she plays shows.

And all she had ever wanted from the world was that it celebrate her milky goodness, that her altruism not be mistaken for covert narcissism. Ahead of her wedding, the happy couple donates $26 million to local charities. Since then, The Star released four new songs, launched an Oscar campaign, including performing at the Academy Museum Gala, and got a haircut.

B SIDE Summer 2026. The world’s most famous sexy baby—who insists that she is really a monster on a hill—chooses, as the site of her nuptials, midtown Manhattan during a heat wave. Her guests nibble on buffet food as thousands of New Yorkers lose power.

It is not lost on them that her $26 million giveaway, apart from being a tax write-off, is akin to a person making $81,228—the median household income in New York City—giving away $1,055. (In fall 2025, when this article was commissioned, The Star was worth $1.6 billion. By the time this issue goes to press, she will be worth over $2 billion, or the GDP of Eritrea.)

“To become a billionaire,” The Star’s ex Matt Healy once told the Doomscroll podcast, “you don’t really care that much about culture.” He wasn’t speaking specifically about The Star but the deadening effects of modern wealth. Beyond need lies want. Beyond want, greed.

A/B SIDE And beyond greed was a tricked-out walled garden for the enchanted, her betrothed, and 1,000 of their family and friends, including, according to news reports, at least one government contractor who did not respond to multiple requests for comment. (In March his company took over our nation’s largest ICE detention facility. Earlier this year a father of three was pronounced dead there, after struggling with five guards, the second death at the camp in as many months. His name was Geraldo Lunas Campos.)

In other news, the wedding reportedly featured a raffle where a lucky guest won a Chanel bag. Another allegedly won a 1970 Chevrolet Chevelle. Madison Square Garden Entertainment Corp. reportedly locked out its own security staff for the occasion, like it was a Mob bar—the kind with no windows. Not even members of the New York Police Department were allowed their own phones on site.

Love may be free, but the performance of it is not. It requires crates, trucks, officers on overtime, private jets, SUVs, HVACs, all the queen’s horses, all the queen’s men, a Jumbotron. Conspiracy theories do not tell you the truth, but they do tell a kind of psychological truth about a place or its people. Had The Star and Redwood filmed the ceremony, perhaps for theatrical release or streaming—maybe on Disney+, which paid The Star a king’s ransom for the rights to another project? (A person with knowledge says the couple has no plans to drop a documentary about their big day.)

Around the barricades of Madison Square Garden, in the wake left by The Star, her groom, and their guests, her fans gathered. Some had been there for hours, wanting to be nearer to their pious majesty. A white truck passed. Pastries—from the merrymaking gentry presumably, though who can say for certain—were distributed, with an assist from a cop in uniform and gear.

If you listened carefully then to the sounds of the city—not for any semantic meaning, but if you were to really pitch your ears to the utopic promise of music—you might have heard the determined whoosh of a weighted blade dropping, dropping, dropping, the ax of public opinion falling in downward demotic motion.

(The Star’s version was used in the making of this article.)

#3389. Legendary Critical Role Cast Members Officially Return With a Star-Studded New Guest Cast

Aabria Iyengar and Travis Willingham return in Campaign 4

It’s hard to believe the entire Critical Role table for Campaign 4 hasn’t been together since the Convergence arc in June. Since then, the Soldiers, Seekers, and Schemers tables have remained separate. Or, more accurately, the Seekers and Schemers tables have remained separate.

Since Critical Role Campaign 4 episode 31, "Trick of the Light," Critters haven’t seen hide nor hair of everyone’s favorite orc Druid, Thaisha Lloy. Nor have they received any confirmation about when, exactly, Travis Willingham will return with a new character, after his Paladin, Teor Pridesire, met an unfortunate end in episode 30, "Here in the Dark."

Luckily, the wait is finally over. Critical Role announced on Nov. 23 that its eagerly anticipated Soldiers table, featuring Aabria Iyengar as Thaisha, will return on Dec. 3 and Dec. 10 for a two-part Soldiers table arc. And she won’t be alone.

When the three tables split off in June last year, it seemed that the Soldiers table would consist only of Thaisha. In an interview with Polygon, Iyengar confirmed she wasn't sure at the time whether Thaisha’s story would be told through cold openings or off-camera. Later, however, the Critical Role team decided to give the Soldiers table a mini-arc following Thaisha as she explored her future on the druidic path. But she would not be doing all of that on her own.

“We’ve got some amazing guests, Celia Rose Gooding and Abubakar Salim," Iyengar told Polygon. "Two people who I have admired for so long; it was so fun to finally sit down and play with them. And, of course, the return of Travis Willingham and his new PC.”

Willingham has been absent from Critical Role’s Campaign 4 since his katari Paladin, Teor Pridesire, died in episode 30. Teor was killed inside House Tachonis’s Obrimus Manor during a truly heartbreaking moment for the fans and the cast.

Gooding and Salim have both guest-starred on Critical Role before: Gooding appeared in Exandria Unlimited: Divergence as the half-elf Rei’nia Saph, while Salim has played various roles, most recently the fungril Berserker Mercy in Age of Umbra: Sallowlands.

Though Iyengar couldn’t reveal what characters Willingham and the other guests would play in this two-episode arc, she told Polygon they were all “deeply connected and bound by a similar purpose.”

“Dol-Runja is the seat of the orcs and the druids in Kahan. So it's important and interesting to see multiple facets of that.”

Since June, the Seekers and Schemers tables have been dealing with assassination attempts at the theater, watery heists, and literal hell. When we last checked in, the Seekers table — with the help of several NPCs like fey pixie Clauny the Rose, talking dog Dame Morgaine, and scoundrel Pimley Morn — successfully rescued the daughters of their ally, Ulbid Morn.

On Dec. 3, Critters will reunite with Thaisha, who set off for the city of Dol-Rungja. There, she hopes to speak with the Druidic people and persuade them to abandon their neutrality and help fight back against the Sundered Houses.

Whether that will work out for Thaisha remains to be seen. The last time she encountered other druids, a few of them weren’t too pleased with her role in bringing the Necromancer Wizard, Occtis Tachonis (Alexander Ward), back to life as a Hollowed One. Given that she’ll have to answer for it to very important people, including her grandma, we expect the orc druid to be put through the proverbial wringer over the course of her two-episode arc.

Aabria Iyengar, Travis Willingham, and guest stars Celia Rose Gooding and Abubakar Salim begin their Soldiers adventure on Dec. 3.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3388. Avengers: Doomsday Final Trailer Breakdown - 5 Biggest Reveals And What They Mean

The new "Avengers: Doomsday" trailer shows MCU heroes assembling for their biggest battle yet. It will also surely be one of their most profitable, given the hype around this movie. Despite Marvel Studios' well-publicized troubles of late, the Avengers' return remains highly anticipated. As such, any new revelations Marvel is willing to provide about the team-up movie are significant to say the least.

The final "Doomsday" trailer doesn't actually feature any major reveals, which is a good thing for those who prefer to keep their theater experience as pure as possible. For those who like to know as much as they can ahead of a Marvel Cinematic Universe release, however, it means much of the movie remains a mystery. (We're still no clearer on whether Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom is actually a Tony Stark variant or not, despite Marvel Studios head Kevin Feige's recent comments.) That said, the latest tease did contain several notable moments that have only served to increase the already significant hype.

The new "Doomsday" trailer finally gives Cyclops the X-Men line fans were waiting for, when Marsden's hero delivers his "To me, my X-Men" rallying cry to assemble his mutants, the Avengers, Fantastic Four, and several other heroes. But beyond that tantalizing glimpse at the film's big showdown, there are several other notable moments, and lucky for you, we've gone and rounded 'em up.

The precise plot of "Avengers: Doomsday" remains under wraps for now, but at this point, we can pretty much piece together the major beats. Previously, co-director Joe Russo told Empire that Robert Downey Jr.'s Victor Von Doom is a "father who's a victim of trauma" and that he "lost a child." That lined up with what we've seen in previous trailers, wherein Vanessa Kirby's Sue Storm/Invisible Woman talked about how Doom "used to be different" before "everything he loved was taken from him." Now, the latest "Doomsday" trailer has confirmed that the Avengers themselves are responsible for it all.

In the new trailer, Chris Evans' Steve Rogers can be heard saying, "Years ago, we did what was needed to make the world right," in reference to the events of 2019's "Avengers: Endgame." He continues: "But we didn't know those choices would have consequences." It seems that Steve's choice to travel back through time to be with his lover, Peggy Carter (Hayley Atwell) — and whatever the Avengers did to defeat Josh Brolin's Thanos — caused some sort of multiversal upheaval in which Doom's daughter met her, well, doom.

This is why RDJ's villain tells the heroes of "Doomsday" that they've been living "stolen lives." With Steve's speech in the new trailer, it's all but certain he and the Avengers are responsible for whatever killed Doom's daughter, and likely the multiversal collapse referenced in the "Avengers Endgame: Encore" TVA scene. Turns out, Doom is the "consequence" to which Steve refers.

Thanks to what seemed like a hasty casting announcement prior to the final "Avengers: Doomsday" trailer, we knew Hailee Steinfeld's Kate Bishop would be appearing in the movie. Now, the trailer has given us our first look at the heir to the Hawkeye mantle in a very quick shot that shows her looking up at something that's clearly got her very worried. But Kate might be just one of the Young Avengers to appear in the film.

We know Scott Lang's (Paul Rudd) daughter, Cassie Lang (Kathryn Newton), is also part of "Doomsday." She shows up briefly in the new trailer, too, looking as concerned as Kate. Interestingly enough, both characters are in their superhero suits, which suggests they'll be joining the big fight against Doctor Doom. That means two members of the Young Avengers will be involved in "Doomsday." Marvel Studios has yet to officially introduce these heroes as the superhero group from the comics, but has been slowly building up this new generation of Avengers over the past few years.

The only likely member of the Young Avengers who hasn't appeared in trailers and is yet to be confirmed as being involved with "Doomsday" is Iman Vellani's Ms. Marvel. According to Andy Serkis, Ms. Marvel will appear in "Doomsday," but Marvel hasn't made that official. Otherwise, there are a handful of other young heroes that could show up and potentially form the Young Avengers proper in the movie itself, including Riri Williams/Ironheart (Dominique Thorne) and America Chavez (Xochitl Gomez). For now, it looks more likely than ever we'll see an official Young Avengers group unite in "Doomsday."

The new "Avengers: Doomsday" trailer shows Chris Hemsworth's Thor rising from the floor surrounded by yellow lightning as opposed to his typical blue lightning. That's significant, as it all but confirms he'll be wielding a powerful new force known as the Odinforce. This power, created by the Kings of Asgard, is a major upgrade for the character, and the latest trailer appears to have shown it in action.

One of the most frequently showcased "Doomsday" scenes thus far has been the moment in which Thor launches himself at Doctor Doom, only to be stopped mid-air and flung backwards by the villain's formidable force (which, as it happens, involves a Jacky Kirby-inspired energy blast from Doom). Clearly, the God of Thunder is as outmatched as the rest of his cohorts.

But back when the first four teaser trailers for "Doomsday" dropped, we saw Hemsworth's hero begging his father for the "strength of the All-Fathers." Since then we've seen concept art and a "Doomsday" billboard that seemingly spoiled the fact Thor was getting a major upgrade in the form of the Odinforce. It's this force that turns his lightning yellow, and the final "Doomsday" trailer is the first time we see footage of it in action. The brief shot shows Thor ascending in a forest, which looks to be the same forest in which he begged for the strength of the All-Fathers in the original teaser. Looks like he got his wish. Whether it will prove effective against Doom, however, remains to be seen.

We got our first look at the X-Men in "Avengers: Doomsday" courtesy of the X-Men-heavy trailer back in January 2026. Since then, we've learned how the mutants might find their way to the Avengers. The film will take place during the collapse of the multiverse, whereby several "incursions" will see planets and timelines collide. These collisions are likely to be the reason for the film's major crossovers, i.e. the Fox-era X-Men and the Fantastic Four arriving on the Avengers' Earth 616. But it seems when the X-Men and Avengers first come face to face they initially clash, as evidenced by footage from prior trailers in which Yelena Belova/Black Widow (Florence Pugh) takes on Mystique (Rebecca Romijn) and Shang-Chi (Simu Liu) battles Gambit (Channing Tatum).

Now, however, the final "Doomsday" trailer has confirmed that Anthony Mackie's Sam Wilson/Captain America will face off against James Marsden's Scott Summers/Cyclops. The trailer shows the pair going toe-to-toe in what looks to be a pretty brutal clash, with Wilson holding Cyclops by the neck as he unleashes an optic blast. Clearly, the X-Men and Avengers ultimately manage to, as Thor puts it, "put aside their petty squabbles." But for at least a moment, the two superhero teams will be at odds in the movie, and Sam Wilson's showdown with Scott Summers looks set to be a major highlight.

The final "Avengers: Doomsday" trailer reminds us of the main threat facing Earth 616 in the movie. While Doctor Doom is the big bad, the entire multiverse is collapsing, and in the latest trailer we see a brief shot that shows two planets in the sky above New York City. The trailer also features several shots of heroes looking up at the sky, or out of windows and reacting with shock and dismay, and it's likely this planetary incursion is what has them so upset.

We've known that the heroes of "Doomsday" would be dealing with multiversal collapse in the film for some time. But this is the first shot we've seen in an official trailer that shows planets on a collision course with Earth. Previously, a Dunkin' Donuts commercial gave us our best look at the threat the Avengers face in "Doomsday," with a shot showing a planet looming in the sky over Avengers Tower. But it looks as though multiple timelines/planets are set to collide with Earth based on the brief scene from this latest trailer.

Exactly which planets these are remains unclear. One may in fact be the Fox-era X-Men's world, and this cityscape view could be giving us a glimpse of their arrival in the Avengers' timeline. Either way, clearly the stakes have never been higher, as failure means the complete and utter destruction of the multiverse.

"Avengers: Doomsday" hits theaters on December 18, 2026.

Remember when Olivia Wilde was served child custody papers by Jason Sudeikis while she was on stage in front of thousands presenting Don’t Worry Darling at CinemaCon? That was over four years ago in the heat of the pair figuring out the post-split situation. However, these days, the two seem to be on better terms. To that point, Sudeikis is even crediting his ex for the creation of his massively successful TV show, Ted Lasso (which just got big news by the way).

Sudeikis recently said two very notable things about his high-profile breakup. One of those came up when he was on Talk Easy with Sam Fragoso, during which he said his and Wilde's split was “more complicated” and “more human” than how it was portrayed in the media. And on another occasion, Sudeikis went out of his way to talk about how Wilde played a role in getting Ted Lasso made. In his words to the Smartless podcast:

I remember Olivia and I were out to dinner and she's like, 'What are you guys gonna do with that? Like, you guys love doing that thing so much. You should do something with that.' I was like, ‘Yeah.’ And then, her and I just started chatting about it at dinner a little bit like, ‘That would be fun.’

As Sudeikis shared during an interview at a special live edition of the show at the Hollywood Bowl in Los Angeles, Wilde was the person who actually followed up with her then-partner on the Ted Lasso idea years before him and the other creators knew what to do with the character. As Sudeikis continued:

Then Joe and Brendan come out to New York and we hang out for a week in Brooklyn... And then for three days straight, we just start filling up pages of ideas and realize, ‘Oh, this might be a TV show.’ And then we didn't do anything with it for three years.

Wild, right? Mr. Ted Lasso himself, alongside two of his co-creators Brendan Hunt, Joe Kelly, sat on the idea for a while until one day they were overflowing with ideas. And then, they sat on it again until this happened. In Sudeikis’ words:

It wasn’t until Bill Lawrence came to me with an idea for another TV show that I was like ‘Ah, this isn’t the right fit.’ He goes, ‘Well, if you have any ideas…’ I go, ‘Well, here’s a stack of papers of stuff we wrote down.’ And he read it, and was like, ‘Oh yeah, there’s definitely a show here.’

Now that Ted Lasso is one of the best shows to watch with an Apple TV subscription, it’s pretty crazy to think how long the whole process took. It took so long that when the idea was first formed Sudeikis and Wilde went from being an engaged couple to splitting up. Thankfully it did, because it’s one of my favorite shows on streaming in recent years.

And did you know there’s even a tribute to Olivia Wilde in Ted Lasso? The AFC Richmond locker room (at one point at least) features Wilde’s actual surname, “Cockburn,” alongside the names of other writers’ friends, family members and former mentors within the production.

Over the past summer, Olivia Wilde spoke a bit to her divorce as well, sharing the conversation that led to their split. Wilde is also having a big year herself, thanks to her latest directorial effort, The Invite, and Sudeikis says he’s “thrilled” for her success. As for him, he just got some good news, as Ted Lasso was just officially renewed for Season 5 by Apple. So the show remains the gift that keeps on giving. In short, thank you, Jason and Olivia!

#3385. This Creepy Twilight Zone Episode Was The First One Not Written By Rod Serling

No TV writer is as synonymous with their creation as Rod Serling is with "The Twilight Zone." As the show's host, he was the face of the series. In an anthology series, you can't expect to see the same actors and characters every time you tune in, so the only familiar sound to welcome you into the twilight zone was Serling's calm, sardonic voice.

Serling wrote 92 of the 156 "Twilight Zone" episodes that aired during the show's five season run. The first episode that did not come from a Serling script is the series' ninth episode, "Perchance to Dream," with writer Charles Beaumont self-adapting a short story he originally wrote for publication in Playboy magazine. (Now, technically, the beloved eighth "Twilight Zone" episode "Time Enough At Last," boasting one of the show's most depressing endings, was based on a short story by Lynn Venable. However, Serling wrote the teleplay.)

"Perchance to Dream" stars Richard Conte (nowadays most remembered for playing Don Barzini in "The Godfather") as Edward Hall, a man who hasn't slept for days — because he's convinced if he falls asleep, he'll die. But his insomnia is born of a different medical condition. Hall has a weak heart, so much so that if he experiences a significant enough shock, even in his dreams, it might literally kill him. The episode sees Hall visiting a psychiatrist, Dr. Eliot Rathmann (John Larch), and recalling how his own mind seems to be trying to knock him off a ledge with terrifying dreams.

The title "Perchance to Dream" comes from a soliloquy in "Hamlet," when the eponymous prince muses: "To sleep, perchance to dream." But Hamlet is talking about the sleep of death and his temptation to suicide. That makes the line a fitting, though flipped-on-its-head, title for a story about a man terrified he'll die if he falls asleep. ("Batman: The Animated Series" would later use "Perchance to Dream" as the title for star Kevin Conroy's favorite episode.)

The episode is primarily set in Dr. Rathmann's skyscraper office, but peeks inside Hall's dreams to let us see his terror. The second half cuts between the office and Hall recounting his dreams of a carnival, where "everything [is] warped and twisted out of shape," and the nightmare that came closest to killing him. A cat-eyed woman named Maya (Suzanne Lloyd) leads Hall down a haunted trail, packed with monstrous animatronics, and then onto a roller coaster.

Maya's feline coding marks her as a predator, toying with Hall like a terrified mouse trying to escape her claws. Watching the episode now, it feels like "A Nightmare on Elm Street" with a femme fatale instead of a knife-handed slasher. The carnival scenes use Dutch angles and foggy camera filters feel extra unnerving and wrong. Combined with the Halloween aesthetic and Maya's cutting laughter, the dream lives up to the nightmare that Hall described.

Charles Beaumont remained one of most prolific "Twilight Zone" writers. During the second season, he self-adapted his spooky short story "The Howling Man," helping turn it into one of the scariest "Twilight Zone" episodes ever. But "Perchance to Dream" first proved that Beaumont could makes trips to the Twilight Zone genuinely terror-inducing.

#3384. Casting Director Francine Maisler on ‘Dune: Part Three’

When Denis Villeneuve brought on seasoned casting director Francine Maisler for the first Dune movie, they were starting from scratch. For the ambitious adaptation of Frank Herbert’s 1965 sci-fi novel, they had to cast not only the lead character, Paul Atreides, but dozens of other main characters—powerful warriors, scheming royals, shape-shifting conspirators—to inhabit the world.

Luckily, the pair had already worked together on Villeneuve’s three previous films, Sicario, Blade Runner 2049, and Arrival. “Denis’s vision is my compass,” Maisler tells Vanity Fair. “His passion [for Dune] since he was a teen was all I needed to follow.”

When they were casting the first installment, Maisler was aware that it was possible that these actors might play these characters for more than just one film. “I did have an idea that they would have to have the presence and the acting talent to be able to carry this potentially for three movies,” she says.

Dune (2021), starring Timothée Chalamet as Paul Atreides and Zendaya as Chani, was just the first step. Maisler returned to cast Dune: Part Two (2024), and Dune: Part Three, which will wrap up Villeneuve’s trilogy when it hits theaters on December 18.

Maisler is a titan of casting, having worked on hundreds of films with filmmakers such as Luca Guadagnino, Greta Gerwig, Aaron Sorkin, Paul Greengrass, Adam McKay, and Terrence Malick, and she was nominated for the first casting Oscar in 2026 for her work on Ryan Coogler’s Sinners.

The casting Oscar didn’t exist when she began working on the Dune franchise, but this installment is likely to draw attention from the Academy. Over the three films, the cast has grown into an incredible ensemble, packed with many of today’s biggest movie stars, along with well-known veterans and a few unexpected choices. “One thing about Denis is if ever I bring him a name and he likes it, and I’ll say, ‘Well, do you want to hire that actor?’ He says to me something I think is so poetic,” says Maisler. “He says, ‘Francine, let me get back to you tomorrow. I need to dream about it.’”

Ahead of the release of Dune: Part Three, Maisler looks back at casting the trilogy’s most important roles, including the exciting new additions to the upcoming film—and the possibility of more Dune in the future.

In Herbert’s book, Atreides is a slender 15-year-old with dark hair. “To find a 15-year-old who had that talent to carry this whole movie, we weren’t sure was out there,” remembers Maisler. The name that came up was then 22-year-old Chalamet, whom Maisler had previously cast in Hostiles, Beautiful Boy, The King, and Little Women. Chalamet, who didn’t have to audition but did meet with Villeneuve, would have to play Atreides from a young man who then begins to amass power in the second film and, after a 12-year time jump, is burdened with the choices he’s made waging a galactic war in the third. Though Chalamet hadn’t led a big blockbuster before, Maisler saw the depth of his talent. “I do think Beautiful Boy showed me the depth of Timothée as an actor, as a young man, and that this was the next step in his progression as an actor, that he was able to hold a franchise in his hand,” says Maisler.

There was a worldwide search for Chani, the skilled Fremen warrior from Arrakis who falls in love with Atreides. At the time, Zendaya was in the middle of filming the first season of Euphoria, and her graduation from Disney star to movie star had not yet happened. Zendaya screen tested with Chalamet, which sealed it for Maisler and Villeneuve. “She came in with five other incredibly talented actresses, but the minute you saw her with Timothée in a room, you just knew that there’s something special happening,” she says. “She has such power when she walks in the room, and she’s breathtaking in the most interesting way.”

Of course, Paul Atreides’s parents, Duke Leto Atreides and Lady Jessica, needed to look like Chalamet, but Maisler started with the characters’ essences when casting. Duke Leto Atreides was considered a fair and devoted leader as the noble head of House Atreides. Maisler saw that gravitas in Oscar Isaac. Lady Jessica becomes a force in the story because of her heightened physical and mental control as a trained member of the Bene Gesserit sisterhood. “Rebecca is so powerful, isn’t she?” says Maisler. “She really, I have to say, surprised me. I always knew how talented she was, but she just owned that part.”

Villeneuve and Maisler had worked with Brolin on the 2015 crime thriller Sicario. Maisler, who calls Brolin “one of our greatest actors,” was excited to have him back, this time playing Gurney Halleck, the Warmaster of House Atreides and a mentor to Paul Atreides. The character is described in the book as a warrior-poet, requiring strength and depth. “He’s so charismatic, so masculine,” says Maisler of Brolin. “He’s kind of a throwback from other generations.”

When Momoa’s agent brought up Momoa’s name, Maisler wasn’t quite sure about the idea because at the time he was known for starring in the DC movie franchise as Aquaman. “I was a bit skeptical, I have to admit, because I knew he had this incredible presence on screen, but I didn’t know, truly, his talent, and that’s taught me a lot about being open to people who come from different types of films,” she says. Villeneuve was more open to the idea at the start, and met with him about playing Duncan Idaho, a fierce fighter and protector of Paul Atreides. He returns in the third movie as a ghola—a sort of clone—named Hayt, which demands a more complicated performance from Momoa. “Jason’s an incredible artist, and I’ve come to just love him,” says Maisler. “He’s so funny. I want to put him in a romantic comedy next, because he really is one of the big surprises in the ensemble.”

Taylor-Joy had already risen in stardom by the time she joined the franchise for the second film. Her breakout was in The Witch, and she starred in hit series The Queen's Gambit, which earned her a Golden Globe and a SAG Award. This made it slightly surprising that Alia Atreides, Paul’s volatile sister, makes a blink-and-you’ll-miss-it appearance in the second film. “I give her a lot of credit for not counting lines in the second one,” says Maisler, who says Taylor-Joy signed on for the second because of the potential of the third installment. Indeed, in Dune: Part Three, Alia is a loyal sister and vengeful force who is not afraid to get blood on her hands. Taylor-Joy’s charisma and intensity will jump off the screen, says Maisler. “Actors are very smart, and they know when to trust a director like Denis,” she says. “When he says there is going to be something in the third film and he describes it, he will make it happen.”

A tribal leader of the desert-dwelling Fremen, Stilgar is a seasoned warrior and becomes a devout follower of Paul Atreides as Muad’Dib. The role required a level of intensity. “Oh, I think we all just prayed that Javier would do it,” says Maisler. “I think every actor wants to work with Javier, and he’s one of probably a handful of actors I think can do anything.”

Pugh joined for the second film as well, but like Taylor-Joy, she didn’t have a ton to do. But Princess Irulan, who marries Paul Atreides as a political union, is a key part of the plot in Dune: Part Three, joining a conspiracy against Paul. Maisler first saw Pugh in the 2016 film Lady Macbeth, and then cast her as Amy March in Gerwig’s Little Women. “You saw on that what an intelligent actress she is, and singular,” she says. “She knows no boundaries, and she’s confident and bold.” She says Pugh has always reminded her of Debra Winger, the star of An Officer and a Gentleman (1982), and Terms of Endearment (1983). “She’s just commanding, and she has this energy, and everything she does is fascinating,” says Maisler. “You can’t take your eyes off of her.”

The third installment brings in yet another major star with Pattinson, who plays Scytale, a shape-shifter who is conspiring to dethrone Paul Atreides. Maisler, who also worked with Pattinson in Primetime, which also came out this year, describes him as “one of the versatile actors in his choices.” She had also worked with Pattinson on Mickey 17, which proved that he could play many different versions of a character—a skill that would be required of him in this third Dune movie. “Robert's a tremendous actor, and I think he takes these really bold chances,” says Maisler. As for his recent announcement as the next James Bond, Maisler has faith he and Villeneuve will deliver. “I think the way Denis and Rob created the character in Dune: Part Three together speaks to the surprises that we will see in Bond,” she says.

For Dune: Part Three, Maisler and Villeneuve had to find two actors who looked like twins and also looked like the offspring of Chalamet and Zendaya. They initially hoped to cast real twins, but didn’t find the right pair. In the end, they found their Ghanima and Leto II in Ida Brooke and Nakoa-Wolf Momoa. Brooke, who looks strikingly like Zendaya, is a relative newcomer who previously appeared on Apple’s sci-fi drama Silo (which stars Rebecca Ferguson). And Nakoa-Wolf Momoa, who makes his feature acting debut in Dune: Part Three, is Jason Momoa’s son—though Maisler didn’t know that when she first watched his audition tape. “Then came this tape of this young man who had incredible presence, and—we didn’t ask for this—he added some combat footage to his tape,” she says. Maisler says sometimes actors will call in a favor to get their child an audition, but Wolf, as she calls him, got this on his own. This casting was the most important for the third film because of what might be to come. “It was almost like casting the first one where these two young actors could go on to potentially, if there’s another movie where they’re leads,” says Maisler. There have been no official announcements of any future Dune movies, but for those mourning the end of the Villeneuve trilogy, Maisler is planting a small seed of hope here. The third Dune book, Children of Dune, centers on Leto and Ghanima, which means the two young actors Maisler found may have more story ahead of them.

#3383. Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

You know “the look” by now. Every poster for a business or event has pictures of uncanny-looking people, buildings that don’t look right, and always that one font. But why? If generative AI is supposedly able to “think” and be “creative,” why do so many of its results come out looking exactly the same? The answer is complicated, and it has to do with what chatbots define as “thinking.”

At this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt. Some very fast models do, but most employ what’s known as “thinking models”, which are a bit of a misnomer. The “thinking” really just consists of generating a set of sub-prompts before executing the main one. And it’s in that hidden, generated text that most of the “choices” (to the extent that we can call the statistical output of an AI model a “choice”) occur that determine how a design looks.

To borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could). Most of this happens invisibly in the background, and many proprietary chatbots won’t show you their in-process “thinking” prompts even if you ask.

In the case of an AI poster, it might break down “make a poster” into smaller steps such as “create a design brief for a poster.” To demonstrate this while doing some testing for this piece, I added additional prompts for ChatGPT to explain the “design briefs” it generated, which included details like layout, colors, and typography.

The problem is those instructions are still subject to the same flaws as any other AI-generated text. They can’t properly fact-check; they can’t walk into the real world and see the thing they’re describing; and they can hallucinate or fall back on stale formats that become easy to notice after a while.

For example, while testing, I had ChatGPT generate a poster for a Lifehacker-themed nightclub. In every case, the underlying brief it generated outlined some basic details, but occasionally it added things I hadn’t asked for. This included additional text, iconography, and in one case it even added the “design brief” explanation I had requested as the bottom half of the poster.

Those mistakes filter into the final product, when the brief is then fed into the image generator that ultimately makes the poster. In my case, ChatGPT showed me the underlying explanations for its reasoning (though even that could be different from what was actually sent to the image generator), but most people who use a chatbot for this task won’t see these factors before getting the final result.

While most chatbots won’t show you exactly what underlying “thinking” they use, most can be coaxed into describing the vague outlines of how they reached certain outcomes. And those descriptions provide some insight into why certain chatbots keep outputting similar results over and over. It doesn’t take long for some patterns to emerge. For example, any prompt to generate a poster for a nightclub almost invariably generated a brief that had specifications for a color palette including “electric purple,” “electric yellow,” and “electric pink.”

The reason for this should be pretty obvious: When the statistical model underlying LLMs needs to come up with an example for “colors for a nightclub poster,” the most obvious answers are neon, high-energy colors. Unless you know something about the specific club’s vibe (and write that out and feed it to the chatbot), the AI will have to fill in the gaps with something. And that something will be based on the same statistics it uses to predict any word.

This pattern of repetition was everywhere in all the design rationale ChatGPT gave me. Across multiple attempts to generate a Club Lifehacker poster, the generated design brief added an overarching “concept” that described the fictional club’s atmosphere as “high-energy” and “futuristic.” Every bot mentioned using images with the “silhouette” of either the DJ or a dancing crowd (often both). All the text had to be “bold” and “futuristic."

If there's one dead giveaway that a poster was made with AI, it's that one brush-stroke font that they all seem to use. Now, this is a bit more speculative, but I have a theory on where that specific design comes from. And it’s worth noting upfront that this seems to only apply to posters generated by ChatGPT specifically.

One of the most common factors I found in my design brief testing was the use of phrases like “brush lettering” or “brush script.” Brush lettering is a design term that refers to using any number of methods like markers, paint brushes, or brush pens to write text. In digital design, that can take the form of fonts that are designed to emulate the look of fancy, handwritten text.

In every test poster I created, however, ChatGPT seemed to take the phrase “brush lettering” rather literally. Every instance I encountered of a design brief that mentioned any kind of “brush” text generated an image with letters that looked as though they were created with a broad paint brush. A human designer would understand “brush lettering” to mean “something that looks handwritten," but ChatGPT didn’t seem capable of understanding the phrase as anything other than using an actual paint brush.

The generated posters aren’t even using a “font,” strictly speaking. (Often, letters that should be identical had slight variations.) The image generator part of the chatbot is still a diffusion model, so it can’t employ a vector-based font, per se. But the brush-style font is so common that its look surfaces in any statistical model.

This is an odd quirk of ChatGPT specifically, and it’s possible that it could change in the future. Especially if OpenAI intentionally tries to train this behavior out of its chatbot. However, it’s helpful to illustrate the underlying mechanism. The only way a chatbot can conceptualize design elements in a visual medium is to generate more specific text to feed to the image generator. And that text is just as prone to mistakes and blandness as any other AI model.

I’ve been examining this with a focus on the kinds of posters ChatGPT generates because they’re very common, but posters (or any AI-generated content) from other models might look different. Every model has its own tendencies. For example, a lot of vibecoded websites are made with Anthropic’s Claude, and you can often tell by the tiny text, buttons with rounded corners, and tile-based layouts.

To a certain extent, this is inevitable. While AI models are very different from humans and do not make “choices” in the same way people do, design elements still have to come from somewhere, and whether human or AI, it’s impossible to make these decisions in a vacuum. Humans will have preferences based on the things they like or emotionally resonate with, and AI models will have tendencies based on what their statistical model determines is the most appropriate output.

That means that an AI model’s “style” is naturally going to change over time. Even if a model improves or makes fewer mistakes, it’s impossible to ever change the fact that all ChatGPT images are made by ChatGPT. Whatever you generate with any particular model will have a lot in common with what everyone else who uses the same tool generates.

#3382. The 6 Most Outrageous GTA 6 Myths, Debunked

The internet is already drowning in GTA 6 misinformation

After a wild opening weekend, Grand Theft Auto 6 is off to the races. Millions are playing Rockstar’s enormous open-world game and discovering its complexities in real time. There’s a lot to unpack in a game that’s filled with intersecting gameplay systems across a long story, and some players are already taking advantage of that. At the same time, the opening days of GTA 6’s launch have been filled with misinformation, much of it fueled by culture warriors and content creators looking to turn outrage into clicks on social media platforms that incentivize such behavior.

Because of that, there are a lot of myths about GTA 6 currently floating around the internet. Some come from harmless misunderstandings, while others are more deliberate misrepresentations intended to scare off potential players. To help you navigate the noise, we’ve rounded up some of the most rampant myths currently circulating around GTA 6 and fact-checked them accordingly.

The claim: GTA 6’s story forces you to do chores for Lucia instead of crimes.

If you spent launch day watching reactions to GTA 6’s early hours roll in instead of playing, you might have walked away thinking that Rockstar made a chore simulator. That’s thanks to a few early missions that revolve around Jason getting his home ready for Lucia as she’s about to be released from prison. Players will paint a bedroom for her, fix a leaky roof, and repair some stairs. There’s also an optional quest where players can run errands to prepare for Lucia's arrival, like picking up groceries or buying her a necklace. All of this happens in the first few hours of the game. GTA 6 quickly ramps up after that, getting into the series’ usual flow of cop chases, heists, and shootouts. You can call it a slow start, but know that any mundane missions you’ve seen make up a very small amount of story that you’re likely to see in your very first play session.

The claim: GTA 6 doesn’t allow you to steal cars, or heavily restricts what you can steal.

While there’s a grain of truth to this, it has been heavily exaggerated on social media. There are some select cars that you can’t steal in GTA 6, like those around Jason’s neighborhood or in an NPC’s car lot. But for the most part, you can jack just about any vehicle you see in Leonida. The catch is that you’ll need a device that can copy keys to get into some of the more expensive cars, and you won’t get that until Chapter 3. Being able to steal anything requires some patience as you play through the story, but be rest assured that you can do as much grand theft auto as ever in Grand Theft Auto.

The claim: Airplanes will bounce off of buildings instead of exploding on impact.

This one is a little tricky to unpack because there seem to be two weird things colliding here. After videos of airplanes bouncing off of skyscrapers like rubber began to emerge on social media, players deduced that content creators were sharing videos where they had their Reduced Vehicle Damage setting turned on. It seemed like a textbook case of outrage farming, though there may be a slight bit of truth here. Some players have speculated that GTA 6 may have a few physics bugs that make it tough for certain airliners to blow up as expected. That may be an edge case, but I can confirm that I have crashed plenty of planes into buildings in GTA 6, and they have all exploded into a fiery wreck so far.

The claim: GTA 6 features no autosave, and you will lose progress if you don’t manually save.

When players started reporting that they were losing hours of gameplay because GTA 6 didn’t have an autosave feature, I was very confused. I can open my save file right now and see a dedicated auto save slot that is regularly refreshed as I play. I initially wrote it off as players either lying or not realizing that the auto save only triggers after completing major missions, but it turns out they weren’t hallucinating. GTA 6’s first patch fixed an issue where auto save wasn’t triggering properly. So, yes, GTA 6 does have autosave; it just wasn’t working correctly for some players at launch. It shouldn’t be a problem now, but always remember to save early and often just in case.

The claim: Lucia is cheating on Jason during the story.

This one is downright bizarre. One of the first talking points that came out about GTA 6 was that Jason is a “cuck” who does not realize that Lucia is cheating on him. As someone who has played through the story, I spent days trying to figure out where in the world that blatant lie could be coming from. It turns out it was a good old misinterpretation. Early in the story, Lucia sends a text to an unknown character, which she rushes to hide from Jason when he enters the scene. While some have interpreted that as Lucia having a secret lover, it actually turns out that she was texting a friend from prison. To players’ credit, the scene does feel like it’s built to make you think Lucia is hiding a big secret from Jason, so that reaction might have been exactly what Rockstar was hoping to provoke.

The claim: GTA 6 does not allow you to open fire and kill people in a gay club.

The ugliest rumor to come out of GTA 6 so far is that the game will not allow you to walk into a gay club in Vice City and kill people. There was even a clip going around social media that seemed to support that, sparking some grotesque reactions. The truth is that the location in the video isn’t specifically a gay club. It is a club, and it’s true that you can’t open fire in it, but that’s only because you can’t shoot inside any establishment in GTA 6. This claim would technically be true if there was a gay club in the game, but only as a side effect of the wider systems working the way they do. What is true, though, is that the game features an unkillable non-binary character, according to the actor who portrayed them.

This isn't a moral or ethical issue — boringly, it's about regulation

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3381. Gregory Peck's '50s Dystopian Sci-Fi Flop Is Worth Revisiting

In 1959, Gregory Peck starred in a surprisingly bleak dystopian sci-fi movie about the end of the world. Perhaps unsurprisingly, given its subject matter, "On the Beach" was a box office disappointment, despite the fact it also starred Ava Gardner, Fred Astaire, and a pre-"Psycho" Anthony Perkins. But as Turner Classic Movies notes, "the film struck a chord with the public and for decades remained the definitive dramatic portrayal of the aftermath of a nuclear attack."

Peck made his film debut in 1944's "Days of Glory" and, amazingly, earned an Oscar nomination for his work in John M. Stahl's "The Keys of the Kingdom" that same year. While that film proved to be his breakthrough, it wasn't until the 1950s that he truly ascended to megastardom, becoming one of the biggest leading men in Hollywood. He started the decade by irritating 20th Century Fox chief Darryl F. Zanuck, who wanted Peck to shave his mustache for the 1950 Western "The Gunfighter," before going on to star alongside Audrey Hepburn in the romance classic and one of the best movies of the '50s, "Roman Holiday."

He also appeared alongside Ava Gardner in 1952's "The Snows of Kilimanjaro," before reuniting with her for 1959's "On the Beach." While their prior collaboration had been a romantic adventure outing, "On the Beach" was a decidedly more gloomy affair in which humanity was wiped out almost entirely, while the survivors waited to be killed off by radioactive winds. Not exactly, "Roman Holiday," then. Still, the film has its share of romance and adventure, even if it does end on a fairly dreary note.

"On the Beach" isn't always cited as one of the best Gregory Peck movies, and is a bit of an underrated entry in his filmography that deserves more attention. For one thing, the film is directed by Stanley Kramer, the legendary filmmaker who also oversaw "The Defiant Ones," "Guess Who's Coming to Dinner," and "It's a Mad, Mad, Mad, Mad World." All of Kramer's movies tackled social issues, and with "On the Beach" the issue was nuclear war. The film arrived in an era in which such a thing was an ever-present threat and like many other filmmakers after him, Kramer wanted to hammer home the absurdity, horror, and tragedy of it all.

He did so by adapting Nevil Shute's 1957 novel "On the Beach," in which nuclear war erupts, wiping out most of the major nations and leaving clouds of radiation across the northern hemisphere, which begin to drift South towards Australia. Kramer's movie version uses the same premise, though unlike in the book, we never learn who actually dropped the bombs that wiped out life in the Northern hemisphere. Instead, we simply learn that Gregory Peck's Capt. Dwight Towers and the crew of his American nuclear submarine USS Sawfish are arriving in Melbourne to escape the nuclear fallout in their homeland.

Towers is greeted by Australian naval officer Peter Holmes (Anthony Perkins), who invites him to a party. There, Towers meets regretful nuclear scientist Julian Osborn (Fred Astaire) and Ava Gardner's Moira Davidson, with whom Towers falls in love. Soon, it transpires that the nuclear fallout everyone expected to float down to Australia might not make it that far south, and Towers sets out with his submarine crew to investigate.

Without giving away the ending, "On the Beach" doesn't wrap up on all that happy a note. Stanley Kramer remind viewers that there's "still time" via a banner that literally says as much. But it happens to be flapping away in a deserted Melbourne in a way that calls to mind the end of "Oppenheimer," in which the titular scientist ponders how the nuclear destruction of our species is inevitable regardless of how long we stave it off.

That might have something to do with the film's disappointing box office. After all, it couldn't have been a lack of star power. "On the Beach" was also shot on-location in Melbourne and was, as The Sydney Morning Herald noted in 2019, "the biggest film ever made" in the city. Stanley Kramer, meanwhile, was on a roll following the success of 1958's "The Defiant Ones," and "On the Beach" earned positive reviews. It should have been a bigger hit and should definitely be more widely remembered than it is today.

Many films designed to remind audiences of the devastating threat posed by nuclear weapons have come in the wake of "On the Beach." In 1966, the BBC released the horrific mockumentary "The War Game," which was summarily banned by the Government of the United Kingdom for its disturbing depiction of nuclear attack and the ensuing fallout. Then there was 1983's "The Day After" and 1984's "Threads," the apocalyptic TV movie that shook Britain to its core. More recently we've seen movies like "House of Dynamite" provide a realistic look at how a nuclear attack might unfold. But Gregory Peck's 1959 film was one of the first to really deal head-on with the threat of nuclear annihilation and deserves to be remembered for it.

#3379. The Out-of-Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: Looksmaxxing With Dangerous Drugs

A weekly deep dive into the current trends, slang, and viral videos of youth culture in terms that even the squarest can understand.

This week's column is bleak. First, there's the looksmaxxing trend where teenagers are taking dangerous chemicals to correct perceived physical shortcomings. Then there are the AI job interviewers. Depressing, but at least some young people are having a little fun with their dystopian hellscape.

You can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers. In the 1960s, hippies smoked weed and dropped acid to expand their consciousness; the yuppies of the go-go '80s fueled their drive to acquire with Colombian cocaine; but kids today don’t want to go deeper or work harder. They have a smaller, sadder goal: They take drugs to look better. The substance of choice for a growing number of teenage boys are steroids, peptides, and other exotic chemicals designed to enhance appearance.

Would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal. In 2026, kids are into it, and they aren’t using steroids to win a $500 prize in the Mr. Topeka contest; they’re using unapproved research chemicals to looksmaxx. Looksmaxxing is an online movement of young men trying to maximize their physical appearance. Teenagers are taking the normal desire to look their best to dangerous, pathological levels. Driven by a combination of undiagnosed body dysmorphia and relentless social media algorithms that turn amoral “red pill” kooks into gurus, teenage boys are ingesting a panoply of exotic and dangerous compounds in a quest to fix the angle of their jawlines, change their skin tone, lose weight, grow taller, and otherwise “correct” perceived physical problems.

In the "good old days" of steroid abuse, people generally stuck to abusing anabolic-androgenic steroids that had at least been tested for decades. Teens today are buying SARMs (Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators) and synthetic peptides marked "not for human consumption" from shady laboratories online. Steroids primarily affect the muscles, but many of these newer substances target different biological systems. A recent Rolling Stone article reports that kids are “heightmaxxing” by swallowing erdafitinib, a drug that treats advanced urothelial cancer, because the drug is known to trigger growth spurts (that can result in a curvature of the spine and other nasty side effects). They’re also trying MK-677 to get taller, an experimental growth hormone secretagogue that carries the risk of insulin resistance, water retention, and high blood pressure. Others are injecting Melanotan II, a synthetic peptide that forces a long-lasting deep tan, with side effects of extreme nausea and the sudden, aggressive darkening of moles. (And they're doing steroids too.)

In the looksmaxxing community, softmaxxing is doing generally-considered-acceptable things to look better, like getting enough sleep, exercising regularly, and eating a balanced diet. Hardmaxxing is taking more extreme measures like plastic surgery, smashing your face with a hammer, or taking experimental drugs.

In the bodybuilding and looksmaxxing community, “natty” refers to a natural, non-steroid-enhanced physique.

Here's something more lighthearted than the growing popularity of illicit self-esteem chemicals: the bicep heart and waist heart trends. The Bicep heart came first. Thirst trap videos started appearing on Instagram and TikTok in October in which dudes make a heart with their hand and bicep. Then people started posting variations where they frame the shot with someone they love inside the heart. The bicep heart quickly led to women posting the waist heart.

Okay. So maybe it's not that lighthearted of a trend. While there are some videos of dudes with skinny arms doing the bicep heart, it's mostly jacked dudes. And the waist heart doesn't seem like it would work at all unless you are a specific shape, as this video illustrates. So maybe this isn't a silly meme but an illustration of how young people are inundated with content that can trigger feelings of physical unworthiness, even if they're just looking for silly memes.

As if searching for a job wasn't alienating and horrible enough, some companies have begun using AI agents to conduct interviews. Begging a robot to let you work in a cubicle farm is as dystopian as anything Phillip K. Dick ever imagined, but don't count humanity out yet. Young people are sticking a finger in the eye of the machine by creating comedy videos that focus on trolling these AI job interviewers. They're hilarious because AI is the ultimate straight person in a comedy team, and the raw compute costs to run these interviews means corporate money is burning with each second of wasted time. Here are some of the top creators in the genre.

Bo Bongo: This YouTuber shows up to AI interviews shirtless but insists he's wearing a "corporate tube top," then focuses on daring the interviewer to notice he's doing things like smoking a cigarette or eating a rotisserie chicken.

Cam Whitt likes to wind up AI by arguing, interrupting, telling outrageous lies, and asking the dumbest questions imaginable, like, "When does the interview actually start?" and "How do I figure out what my name is?"

Grahamn Raabe: Among this YouTuber's schticks is speaking only in nonsense, like describing his professional background as "freight cadence, walnut, a little bit of Richard, spruce wood—six years of spruce wood."

Nick Reid: Is so obnoxious, he seems to make the AI furious at him, even though it's a computer without emotions. Two thumbs up!
