#3378. Decoding Kate Middleton’s “Tourdrobe” for Her Trip to India

When Kate Middleton stepped out on the green carpet at the Earthshot Awards ceremony in Mumbai this week, it was “an absolute princess moment,” says British designer Amanda Wakeley.

“Catherine has really come into her own. She has found her stride and a new confidence, and you see that in this dazzling but also practical ‘tourdrobe,’’’ Wakeley, who has previously dressed the Princess of Wales and used to dress Princess Diana, tells Vanity Fair.

It has been 10 years since Princess Kate last visited India. Her fashion choices are more sophisticated now than on her visit in 2016, and the speech she delivered at the Earthshot Prize ceremony on November 17 shows a new confidence. With her elevated look, there’s no trace of High Street labels. Kate’s flared floral dresses and the wedge shoes she used to love (but the late Queen Elizabeth apparently disliked) have been replaced by Manolo Blahnik pumps, couture power suits, and clothes by some of her favorite designers, such as Emilia Wickstead.

Prince William and Princess Kate attend The Earthshot Prize Awards Ceremony at the Jio World Convention Centre on November 17, 2026 in Mumbai, India.

Kate’s decision to wear a striking vermilion dress made from handwoven silk by New Delhi–based designer Mahima Mahajan to the Earthshot Prize ceremony spoke volumes. The eye-catching dress, which she paired with a burgundy Prada velvet clutch, was chosen after Kate had selected a special suite of emeralds from the royal gem collection. The green stones on the dress perfectly matched her jewels, which served as an homage to both Queen Elizabeth II and India, as the green of the Indian flag represents growth and prosperity.

The dazzling stones known as the “emerald tassel suite” were worn frequently by the late Queen Elizabeth II, and while Kate has previously worn the earrings, this marked the first time she wore the set. The effect was dramatic.

“Never has Catherine looked more like a queen in waiting,” Wakeley says of the look.

Wearing the suite ensured that Kate, who has free rein of the royal jewels, looked more regal than ever. “What was fascinating was seeing Catherine wear these incredible family heirlooms along with more relaxed collections from some of her favorite modern jewelry designers like Kiki McDonough and Astley Clarke,” remarks Wakeley.

Kate’s carefully curated wardrobe for the trip wasn’t just about power dressing—it was also about showing she can be sustainable as well as on trend.

“It was good to see Catherine making a proper nod to sustainability by rewearing her Roksanda dress,” Wakeley notes. “It’s clear a lot of thought has gone into her outfit choices. Her wardrobe has to be practical, and her clothes have to work harder than most people consider for their clothing; she needs weight in the hem of the floaty dresses. She has learned lessons the hard way. She is often seen bending down, talking to children, so she’s conscious of how low a neckline is, how short a skirt is.”

Princess Kate visits the Nowrosjee Wadia Maternity Hospital, on November 18, 2026 in Mumbai, India.

For her visit to Mumbai’s Nowrosjee Wadia Maternity Hospital on November 18, Catherine chose a striking red tailored Emilia Wickstead skirt suit with Manolo Blahnik pumps. On November 16, she opted for a pistachio blazer by designer Veronica Beard, paired with white Alexander McQueen trousers and pearl-buckled Camilla Elphick flats, a relaxed and accessible look for when she picked up a cricket bat.

Princess Kate plays cricket on November 16, 2026 in Mumbai, India.

As Princess of Wales, Catherine is often compared to Princess Diana. “The main difference is Diana was a fashion icon. Catherine has become a style icon,” Wakeley says. “There’s a big difference. Diana played into the fashion of the day and was finding her style. During the time she resigned from public life, she worked out her style DNA. Catherine has had to do that on the job. Very wisely, she has worked out her style and doesn’t get too impacted by fashion and trends. She goes for what she likes. What works for her rather than trends. She really knows now what works for her.”

#3377. Marshals Season 2 Forces Kayce To Relive One Of His Most Controversial Yellowstone Storylines

"Marshals" Season 2, Episode 7, "Under the Influence," sees Luke Grimes' Kayce Dutton and Arielle Kebbel's Belle Skinner go undercover in an off-grid cult. During their time there, Kayce is confronted by the cult's charismatic leader, who forces him to relive the loss of his infant child — a moment from "Yellowstone" that was both tragic and, in the eyes of many fans, ridiculous.

Kayce Dutton has been haunted by his "Yellowstone" experience since the very beginning of "Marshals." The youngest Dutton scion has seen it all (including the worst things the Dutton family ever did on "Yellowstone") and has been trying to put it all behind him since Taylor Sheridan's neo-Western series wrapped up back in 2024. Unfortunately, as Brett Cullen's Chief Deputy U.S. Marshal Harry Gifford observed in "Marshals" Season 1, "Duttons are born with dysfunction in their blood," and "Under the Influence" forces Kayce to confront one of his most painful memories. That memory just so happens to be linked to one of the most controversial storylines in "Yellowstone" history.

"Under the Influence" sees ATF agent Sam Colby (Adam Joel) go missing after embedding himself in Moonstone Farm, a homesteading cult led by the mysterious and intense Eric Savard. This character is played by Beau Knapp, who delivers a surprisingly compelling performance as the Moonstone figurehead. (The show should bring him back ASAP.) After Kayce and Belle infiltrate the farm, Savard emerges to welcome them at a community meeting that quickly turns sinister when the cult leader forces Kayce to relive the trauma of losing his infant son. It's clearly a rough time for both the Dutton boy and for fans, who have to be reminded of this contentious "Yellowstone" moment.

In "Under the Influence," Eric Savard confronts Kayce Dutton and asks him what he's lost. After a few lies, Savard pushes Kayce, and he's left with no choice but to draw from his real-life experience. "My son," he says. "He was barely an hour old. I wasn't even there." This is a reference to "Yellowstone" Season 5, in which a pregnant Monica Dutton (Kelsey Asbille) decides to drive herself to the hospital during early labor. Why? Well, that remains one of the biggest points of contention, as it seems she and Kayce had no birth plan whatsoever. Meanwhile, Tate Dutton (Brecken Merrill) could have driven her but didn't, and for some reason, calling an ambulance was completely out of the question. All of this led to Monica driving herself, almost hitting a buffalo, swerving, and crashing head-on into an oncoming truck.

The result was the loss of baby Dutton, who was set to be named in honor of Kayce's father, John Dutton (Kevin Costner), who himself suffered a terrible and controversial death in "Yellowstone" Season 5. Baby John passed away roughly an hour after the crash, which is what Kayce references in "Under the Influence."

Baby John remains one of many "Yellowstone" characters who should never have died. His passing not only seemed avoidable but like a quick way to get some drama out of the show's final season and nothing more. Fans have since criticized the whole thing (check out Reddit to get a sense of their distaste), and it stands as one of the show's least effective storylines. Now, "Marshals" has tried to revisit it for some drama of its own. But like most things in this CBS spin-off, there's not really much beyond a surface-level reference.

Earlier in "Marshals" Season 2, we saw a flashback in which a young Kayce Dutton looked in the mirror at a fresh Yellowstone brand on his chest. This is the brand his father, John, used to bring relatives and ranch hands into the "Yellowstone" brotherhood, forever tying them to the ranch. That same brand is shown in "Under the Influence," wherein Kayce is pulled off a man he's fighting only for his shirt to open, revealing the unmistakable Yellowstone mark.

"Marshals" Season 1 had trouble figuring out what it was about, juggling storylines and never seeming to explore any one of them in too much depth. That's mostly remained the case for Season 2, but there does seem to be a bit more of a focus on Kayce reckoning with his past. The second season of "Marshals" began by putting a twist on a "Yellowstone" tradition, namely by using animal imagery to evoke Kayce's inner emotional state. The character would encounter a Buffalo on his property at times when he was trying and failing to mentor Tate Dutton and steer him away from embracing what Tate calls "the Dutton way." Since then, we've seen a small but noticeable increase in scenes showing Kayce reflecting on his family's past.

"Under the Influence" might be the most significant in that respect, as it ends with Tate moving out of East Camp and Kayce drinking again after having abstained for years. What's more, Ash Santos' Andrea Cruz asks Logan Marshall-Green's Pete Calvin about Kayce's story, to which Pete replies it's not his place to tell. At this point, it seems as though the show's writers might actually be interested in going a little deeper into Kayce's Yellowstone trauma, and that's a good thing.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When we think of secrecy surrounding movies, naturally we think MCU, but the amount of secrecy that went into The Odyssey is insane. While I knew everything about it was kept under wraps, I didn’t realize just how much until I heard John Leguizamo’s story about landing the script, and it’s WILD.

The actor portrays Odysseus's blind and devoted servant Eumaeus, a role that has been largely praised by critics. Turns out, Christopher Nolan knew exactly what he was doing when he cast Leguizamo in the part, and he didn’t even need to eat dessert first. The actor has previously gushed about working on the movie and the amazing shooting locations, but now he’s dishing to Kevin McCarthy on his On Film podcast about the Mission Impossible-level secret keeping that went into keeping the script under wraps:

I would go to lunch at Odeon, his favorite restaurant. So we meet. He talks about the character. First of all, he talks about his career and everything. So that was just amazing to sit with him and hear him talk about his career was incredible. And then he says, ‘I have this role for you. It's one of the most loyal characters in Western literature.’ And I was like, ‘Wow, that's a lot to live up to.’ He goes, ‘Yes.’ And I was like, ‘I'd love to do it if you'll have me.’ He offered me the role right there before dessert.

Leguizamo’s performance as Eumaeus has been called “sublime” by critics, and it’s easy to see why Nolan thought he was the right fit. Though the actor understands there’s a certain scene in the movie that earned him some hate for “the rest of cinema history,” and if you’ve seen it, then you know what he’s referring to. The actor didn’t even know the extent of his part until he got the script, which came to him as a top secret mission fit for James Bond:

A week later after we close the deal. I have to be home at 12:00 on a Tuesday to receive the script. Nobody else can receive it. I have to receive it. Sign for it. And it comes in a blood red color that you can only see, you know, during a full solstice. [laughter] I don't know. It's impossible to see, dude. The black ink is shiny, and the red makes it so you can't copy it. But it's hard to read. It's really difficult to read.

Perhaps Marvel needs to take some notes from Nolan. While this seems like an insane level of secrecy for a book to screen adaptation, I admire the commitment to "no spoilers." Though the journalist asked the most important question, who delivered the script? Surely, FedEx wasn’t tasked with such a feat. Turns out one of Nolan’s personal assistants hand delivered it. However, there was still another step for him to be able to keep the confidential script:

That's given to me, and I'm not allowed to share with anybody. My assistant had to sign an NDA.

The cloak and dagger seems to have worked as not even Tom Holland seems to have leaked anything. Additionally, Leguizamo shared that whenever Nolan made tweaks, the actor would have to turn in the old pages. This was definitely a first in his career, but one he feels was completely worth it, and I have to agree as the actor seemed to easily embody the role.

It’s not easy to bring an epic of this scale to life, and it was clear from the get-go that Nolan had a vision. Now that The Odyssey hit the 2026 movie schedule over the summer, the actor can focus on a different role. Though maybe one that doesn’t come with as much secrecy? Leguizamo will reprising his role as Sid the sloth in the upcoming 2027 movie, Ice Age: Boiling Point, which is set for a February 5, 2027 release.

Someone should ask him if he was given the Ice Age 6 script in red. Regardless, I’d love to hear his co-stars take on the spy antics it took to keep the script out of the wrong hands.

#3374. GTA 6 Is So Unstoppable It's Even Made Nickelback Go Viral

Everyone loves Alkistis Protopsalti's cover of 'How You Remind Me'

It's still a debate whether Grand Theft Auto 6 has the best gaming soundtrack of 2026, but it certainly has the most soundtrack of 2026. Rockstar Games' latest open-world crime epic features more than 800 songs, most of which you'll hear on its 26 genre-themed radio stations. Of all this breadth of wild music, you'd figure the most popular song on the soundtrack would be something that had overlap with a Fast and Furious OST. But it turns out the single best song in the GTA 6 soundtrack is something by... Nickelback?

Thanks to GTA 6, Nickelback's 2001 angst ballad "How You Remind Me" has been getting a lot of play — kind of. Technically, this version is a cover. GTA 6's Kaleidoscope FM radio station plays alternate-language versions of popular songs, the indisputable best of which is "Ola Afta Poui Fovamai," by the Greek singer and alternate former tourism minister Alkistis Protopsalti. As far as covers go, this is one for the ages. Seriously, listen:

You might be somewhat surprised to hear "How You Remind Me" making the rounds again, years removed from its days reigning over the Billboard charts. To this day, the most-played radio song of the 2000s has been relegated to background music in the daddest bars from Mississauga to Massapequa. It is arguably the epitome not just of Dad Rock but specifically of Divorced Dad Rock. If "How You Remind Me" was a person, its kitchen would include Slim Jims (assorted flavors), cold pizza (definitely pepperoni), and nothing else. It would drive a 2014 Corvette Stingray (bright red, obviously). It would live on the golf course.

But with "Ola Afta Poui Fovamai," Protopsalti injects a youthful, upbeat verve to Chad Kroeger's genius composition that legendarily emerged, nearly fully formed, from his brain in just 45 minutes following an argument with a partner. It's the sort of track you'd play in a convertible on a sunny day, or in the bathroom while getting ready for a party themed after The Devil Wears Prada (the good one). There is practically zero Divorced Dad energy in "Ola Afta Poui Fovamai." It is transformational.

I am far from the only person to completely lose my shit over the resurfacing of a song that hit number-one on charts in Austria, Canada, Denmark, Ireland, and the United Kingdom, in addition to peaking in the top ten in various other international markets. As of this writing, searches for "Nickelback" on Bluesky are all about "Ola Afta Poui Fovamai." On Facebook, Greek culture accounts are sharing the cover as a point of national pride. When Canadian streamer Dan "Greenskull" Hammill heard it for the first time in-game, he burst into a karaoke rendition that has since gone semi-viral.

Truth told, the Canadian rock quartet legitimately is one of my guilty pleasures. As a teenager, I once suffered a pretty serious concussion in a skiing accident; according to the paramedics, I spent the entire ride to the hospital singing "Photograph" in my unconscious state. Mortifying, but also hard to deny. Such is the allure of GTA 6. In being a mirror of our world, it's also a mirror of our lives, thus revealing truths we may not have otherwise been ready to admit. The boyfriends of the world start doing more chores for their partners. Those of us who've let the gym routine fall by the wayside pick it back up again. Nickelback? A guilty pleasure? I no longer see anything to be guilty about here.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3373. 5 Actresses Who Should Play Moneypenny In Robert Pattinson's James Bond Movies

When I put out a public plea to Amazon and James Bond producers and all but begged them to cast Kristen Stewart as a Bond villain during Robert Pattinson's forthcoming run as the legendary British spy, I admitted that I'm not exactly a Bond superfan. Still, I'm excited that Pattinson is bringing his gifts as an actor — and, hopefully, his predilection for silly little voices — to this storied role. In the wake of this casting announcement, people have been fan-casting 007's standard array of supporting characters.

I do know, from the Daniel Craig run of Bond films, that Moneypenny — portrayed by Naomie Harris in those movies — works as the secretary to M, the head of MI6 and Bond's boss. (That role has been played, most recently, by Dame Judi Dench and Ralph Fiennes.) Harris' modern Moneypenny was sometimes found in the field alongside Bond, and there's a simmer of flirtation between them throughout their interactions ... so ideally, we're looking for a British actress who can flirt and hold her own against Pattinson's 007. Who should play Moneypenny in the Robert Pattinson Bond era? I have some ideas.

Since her breakout role on the sci-fi series "Humans," Gemma Chan has done a little bit of everything. She appeared in one of the most successful romantic comedies ever made, "Crazy Rich Asians," and left an impression as the wealthy but big-hearted Astrid. In "Eternals," she joined the Marvel Cinematic Universe (for the second time) as the deeply empathetic superhuman Sersi, who's in love with her fellow Eternal Ikaris (Richard Madden) despite hiding as a human on Earth and dating a guy named Dane Whitman (Madden's "Game of Thrones" brother Kit Harington). In "Mary Queen of Scots," she starred alongside Margot Robbie and Saoirse Ronan as Elizabeth of Hardwick, a close friend of Queen Elizabeth I (Robbie) who helps her capture the ill-fated Queen of Scots, Mary (Ronan). Chan is versatile; we know that. She's also one of the most beautiful people I've ever seen, and she'd make a great Moneypenny.

Seriously: imagine the feline, stunning Chan flirting up a storm with Robert Pattinson's Bond in one of his (hopefully many) movies in the franchise. The only knock against Chan is that she might be a little too serious — even in comedic projects like "Crazy Rich Asians," "The Afterparty," and "The Five-Star Weekend," she tends to play the straight man — but still, she'd be an excellent pick.

If you don't read the name "Natalie Dormer" and immediately think about how she'd make a great Moneypenny, let me educate you. Dormer, an English actress who's been uniformly excellent for decades now, has played three notably flirtatious roles that have all helped define her career: the original temptress Anne Boleyn in "The Tudors"; Irene Adler (and Jamie Moriarty) in "Elementary"; and Margaery Tyrell on "Game of Thrones." In all three of these projects, Dormer's characters seduce and entrance the guy in charge — Jonathan Rhys-Meyers' King Henry VIII, Jonny Lee Miller's Sherlock Holmes, and brothers Joffrey and Tommen Baratheon, played by Jack Gleeson and Dean Charles Chapman, respectively — and have an ulterior motive simmering just below the surface.

I stand ten toes down behind all of the picks on this list, but the more that I think about Dormer's particular brand of flirting opposite Robert Pattinson, the more I want to see it. Dormer doesn't get enough play for my liking. Not only would she make an unbelievable Moneypenny in future Bond movies, it would put her name back on the map ... and hopefully lead to some other fun projects where she gets to smirk and wink her way through the role. I know I begged for Kristen Stewart to be the villain; now I'm begging for Dormer to play Moneypenny.

On some level, Anya Taylor-Joy is an obvious choice to play Moneypenny opposite Robert Pattinson as James Bond. She's gorgeous, has a British-adjacent accent (she was born in Miami but grew up in London), and she's one of the most popular actors working today. In fact, she's set to appear in the highly anticipated "Dune: Part Three" alongside Pattinson this coming December. Still, sometimes the obvious choice is the right one.

Taylor-Joy, who won a Golden Globe for her turn in the miniseries "The Queen's Gambit" and blew audiences away in movies like "The Witch," "The Menu," and "Furiosa: A Mad Max Saga," is one of the most interesting performers working today. In some ways, playing a "side" character like Moneypenny would be a downgrade for Taylor-Joy, who typically enjoys top billing on her projects. Still, I think she'd be a deeply fun addition to Pattinson's Bond franchise, and I have zero doubt, thanks in part to her work in Autumn de Wilde's stunning 2020 "Emma" adaptation and her turn in the fun but flawed "Last Night in Soho," that Taylor-Joy can flirt and banter with the best of them. Honestly, there's very little Taylor-Joy can't do as an actress, based on her body of work. If she has the time and the energy, I think it would be really lovely to see her pop up in Bond movies as Moneypenny.

Yes, I'm bringing another Westerosi royal into the Moneypenny conversation — but hear me out! Olivia Cooke, like Natalie Dormer, has been a reliable on-screen player for over a decade now. After making a name for herself in the dark indie movie "Thoroughbreds" — where she starred alongside Anya Taylor-Joy — Cooke appeared in "Ready Player One" and Oscar darling "The Sound of Metal" before booking a leading role in the first major "Game of Thrones" spin-off and prequel, "House of the Dragon."

On that series, Cooke plays the conniving and deeply flawed leader of the Green faction, Alicent Hightower, who betrays her childhood best friend Princess Rhaenyra Targaryen (Emma D'arcy) by marrying Rhaenyra's ailing father, becoming the queen, and trying to supplant Rhaenyra with a younger male heir. Then, on the dishy Amazon Prime series "The Girlfriend" that aired in 2025, Cooke starred alongside Robin Wright as the absurdly named Cherry Laine, a flirtatious and openly sex-positive woman who starts dating a man with an overprotective mother (Wright).

Cooke is a versatile actress, and like Dormer, she's able to wield her beauty like a sharp weapon, which would make for an extremely fun performance as Moneypenny. "House of the Dragon" is set to wrap up after its fourth season, so Cooke will be free from that particular commitment. Amazon would be wise to snap her up for their next Bond era.

Michaela Coel is probably the most offbeat choice to play Moneypenny in a future James Bond project, but do me a favor and walk with me here. Ever since her breakout role in "Chewing Gum" and her heartbreaking work as a writer and star on her HBO masterpiece "I May Destroy You," Coel's profile has risen significantly, but I would selfishly like to see it rise further. The actress has popped up in everything from the "U.S.S. Callister" episode of "Black Mirror" to the psychosexual A24 drama "Mother Mary" alongside Anne Hathaway, and she's uniformly excellent in every single one of her performances.

Coel, who also has an Emmy for her guest performance on the Amazon Prime series "Mr. & Mrs. Smith" (and should have several for "I May Destroy You"), is a truly formidable actress who can hold her own against A-listers like Hathaway and Ian McKellen in 2025's "The Christophers," and I think she'd add a serious edge to Moneypenny that would just elevate this role. We don't know what future Bond movies will do with the character after Naomie Harris brought her into modern times, but after Harris, Coel is certainly a worthy actor to pick up the mantle and deliver her own sly, cunning take on Moneypenny. Seriously, if you have any doubt, go watch Coel in "Mother Mary" and tell me you wouldn't love to see her defiantly flirt with Pattinson's James Bond.

Robert Pattinson's James Bond film, as of this writing, will release some time in 2028 with Denis Villeneuve as its director. Hopefully, we'll see one of these five astounding women play Moneypenny.

#3371. You Can Save up to $160 on Headphones From Bose, Sony, and Apple With These Early Black Friday Deals

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Amazon's early Black Friday 2026 sale is already bringing some worthwhile discounts to wireless headphones, with savings of up to $160 across models from Sony, Bose, Apple, Nothing, and other brands. Several of the headphones on sale are relatively new, including Nothing's Headphone (1) Pro and Bose's second-generation QuietComfort Headphones, both of which launched this fall. Better yet, most of the deals below have dropped to their lowest prices yet on Amazon.

There's a good mix to choose from, too, whether you're looking for premium noise-canceling headphones for flights and commutes, a pair with enough battery life to get you through a week of listening, or something inexpensive for everyday use, with prices starting under $50. You can also check out the rest of our Black Friday coverage for more editor-vetted tech deals as the sale continues.

The Nothing Headphone (a) is down to a record-low $109 from $199, making it a solid option for everyday listening, especially for Android users who can take advantage of LDAC for higher-quality wireless audio. For more on it, check out this PCMag review.

Spending another $60 gets you the Nothing Headphone (1), now $169 from $299, which is also a record low. It offers a more premium listening experience with active noise cancellation, automatic playback pausing when you take the headphones off, and the option to listen through either USB-C or a 3.5mm cable, making it a well-rounded choice for everyday use. For more on it, check out this PCMag review.

Nothing's newest and most expensive over-ears, the Headphone (1) Pro, are already $80 off at $319, only a couple of months after launching at $399. This is the pair to get for sound quality, since Nothing moved to a three-driver setup in each earcup, and the result is a fuller, more detailed sound than either the Headphone (1) or Headphone (a). For more on it, check out this PCMag review.

Sony's flagship WH-1000XM6 headphones are down to $378 from $459.99, their lowest price yet. Noise cancellation is still the main reason to buy them, and they remain among the best options for blocking out engine rumble on a flight, traffic during a commute, or chatter in a busy office. For more on these over-ears, you can check out our in-depth review.

Sony's WH-CH730N brings noise cancellation down to a much more approachable price, and at $98, down from $179.99, it's the lowest it's been on Amazon. This 2026 update to Sony's budget noise-canceling line now folds up for travel, which the previous model couldn't do, and battery life has jumped to up to 50 hours with noise cancellation on.

Sony's WH-CH530 is the most affordable pair in this roundup at $38, down from $69.99—that's also the lowest it's been since its release this fall. These are simple on-ear headphones without noise cancellation, but they sound better than you'd expect at this price, and the battery lasts up to 55 hours, so a full week of commuting or classes shouldn't be a problem.

The second-generation Bose QuietComfort Headphones are down to $199 from $359, their lowest price yet. That's a substantial discount for a pair that delivers on two of Bose's biggest strengths: comfort and noise cancellation. You can read PCMag's review for a closer look at how they perform.

Bose's flagship QuietComfort Ultra headphones (2nd gen) are down to $339 from $449, saving you $110. Their noise cancellation is among the best you'll find in consumer headphones, making them particularly appealing for frequent flyers or anyone who spends a lot of time in noisy environments. For more on their features and performance, you can check out PCMag's review.

The 2026 JBL Tune 680NC are down to $49.95 from $109.95, their lowest price to date. That's a pretty good deal for anyone looking for affordable noise-canceling headphones, especially since you get adaptive noise cancellation that adjusts to your surroundings and up to 50 hours of battery life with it enabled.

For the same price, JBL's Tune 730BT trades noise cancellation for a larger over-ear fit and even longer battery life, rated at up to 76 hours. At $49.95, down from $89.95, it's at its lowest price on Amazon, and a sensible choice for anyone who mostly listens at home, at a desk, or on quieter commutes where noise cancellation isn't essential.

The JBL Live 780NC are down to $129.95 from $249.95, making them considerably more appealing than at their original price. Battery life is a major advantage here, with JBL estimating up to 50 hours with noise cancellation enabled and 80 hours without, so frequent charging shouldn't be a concern. They also support LDAC for higher-quality Bluetooth audio with compatible devices. For more on their features and performance, you can check out PCMag's review.

Apple’s AirPods Max 2 are down to $449 from $549, saving you $100 on the second-generation over-ears that Apple released earlier this year. While the design hasn’t changed much from the original, the upgrade to Apple’s H2 chip brings improved noise cancellation, while its sound remains among the best you'll find in wireless headphones. You can read PCMag's review for a closer look at how they perform.

Soundcore's Q20i headphones are down to $42.69 from $69.99, making them one of the more affordable options for anyone looking for noise-canceling over-ears from a recognizable brand. They're particularly worth considering for students, occasional travelers, or anyone who wants a budget-friendly backup pair.

The Beats Solo 4 are down to $129.95 from $199.95, saving you $70. While these lightweight on-ear headphones don't have active noise cancellation, they offer plenty of flexibility for everyday listening, whether you're using an iPhone or an Android phone, with quick pairing on both platforms, notes this PCMag review.

The second-generation Bose QuietComfort Headphones have the largest dollar discount in this roundup, dropping $160 from $359 to $199.

That depends on how much you want to spend and where you'll use them. The Sony WH-1000XM6 and Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones (2nd Gen) are worth considering for frequent travelers who prioritize noise cancellation, while the regular Bose QuietComfort Headphones at $199 offer a more affordable premium option. The JBL Live 780NC at $129 are appealing for their long battery life and extensive audio customization, and the Soundcore Q20i at $42.69 make sense if you're shopping on a tighter budget. For Apple users who value ecosystem integration, the AirPods Max 2 are worth considering.

No. If you find the product you're looking for with a major discount right now, get it. It's not likely to drop any lower, but it could always run out of stock. Take advantage of price matching or guarantees instead of waiting. Remember, you can always return products later if you change your mind. For the majority of products, the deal from Black Friday will be the same one on Cyber Monday.

#3370. One Variant Of Marvel's Doctor Doom Is A Descendant Of A Brutal Historical Villain

In the 2000s, Marvel Comics launched "Ultimate Marvel," a reboot that brought its lead characters into the 21st century. "Ultimate Fantastic Four" pivoted from from the classic "astronauts bathed in cosmic rays" origin (which is so 1960s). Instead, the "Ultimate" FF were teen geniuses transformed in a teleportation experiment.

"Ultimate Fantastic Four" also reimagined the FF's nemesis, Doctor Doom. Renamed Victor Van Damme, this Doom was part of the Baxter Building think tank and was also transformed in the Four's accident. This Doom has no armor, but literal metal skin. (You can see that both the 2005 and 2015 "Fantastic Four" films took from "Ultimate Fantastic Four" for their Dooms, to their detriment.)

"Ultimate Fantastic Four" #7 (by Warren Ellis and Stuart Immonen) depicts Victor's childhood. On his tenth birthday, Victor's father revealed to him that they are descendants of Vlad Țepeș, or Vlad the Impaler/Vlad Dracula, the infamous 15th century king of Wallachia. Van Damme Sr. explains to his boy:

"Vlad Dracula understood that truth is inborn. That men of greatness must bend an ignorant world to their truth by any means necessary. And so he bent Wallachia to his will. He was cruel, but cruelty is no vice. It is a tool of necessity."

From that moment, Victor was told he must be a man who bends the world to his will. His father instructs him to memorize his family line from Vlad down, beating him whenever he fails. Doom being the descendant of royalty, coming from money, and being imparted from childhood with lessons that a great leader is a ruthless one are all big changes to his character. Victor von Doom acts like an aristocrat, but unlike Victor Van Damme, he came from nothing.

Doctor Doom is an Eastern European king, beloved by his own people but seen as monstrous by outsiders. He's a monarch in Vlad the Impaler's image, so making Doom a literal descendant of Vlad fits. But "Ultimate" Doom does not live up to his family legacy.

His first "kingdom" is a camp of squatters in Copenhagen. Clad in green rags (instead of a regal cloak), Doom compares his new skin to "Wallachian armor," but he didn't forge it himself. His metal body can form sharp spikes, like the kind on which Vlad impaled his enemies. Reed Richards, much pettier and hotheaded than his classic self, scratches Victor with one of those spikes and leaves a scar: "Impaled on your own sword, Victor."

Vlad is associated with dragons; his father, Vlad II, was a member of the Order of the Dragon knighthood, and known as Vlad Dracul, or "Vlad the Dragon." (Vlad III's infamous moniker can mean "son of the dragon.") "Ultimate" Doom brands his followers with dragon tattoos made up of mind-controlling microfibers.

Dracula can also mean "son of the Devil." Doom's metallic body has cloven hoof legs, echoing goatlike depictions of Satan. But "Dracula" or not, Doom doesn't drink blood — and neither did the real Vlad the Impaler. Pop culture has reforged Vlad into the historical basis for Bram Stoker's "Dracula" and its vampiric villain. Later "Dracula" adaptations like Francis Ford Coppola's 1992 "Dracula" film or the action-horror manga "Hellsing" explicitly depict Dracula as the same person as the historical Vlad.

"Ultimate Fantastic Four" indulges this, too. Victor's father tells his son that Vlad let his enemies believe he drank blood. As Doom, Victor brands his subjects on their necks, and controls them like vampires do familiars.

Dotor Doom echoes both the historical Vlad and the literary Dracula; his fictional nation, Latveria, is a pastiche of the gothic Transylvania seen in "Dracula" movies. (Many "Fantastic Four" adaptations also insert Doom having an infatuation with Sue Storm that he never has had in the comics, like how many "Dracula" films make the Count and Mina Harker lovers, not monster and victim.)

"Dracula" is often paired with Mary Shelley's "Frankenstein," especially thanks to Universal and Hammer's films of both. Doom melds "Dracula" with "Frankenstein." He shares Dr. Frankenstein's name, Victor, and both men's lives are defined by the death of their respective mothers. Victor Frankenstein tried to create life in grief over his mother's death, while the machine that blew up in Doom's face was an attempt to contact the "nether world" and his mother's soul.

As the classic Doom stands in the shadow of these villains, historical and literary, Victor Van Damme in "Ultimate Fantastic Four" stands in Doom's. "Ultimate Doom" almost feels like a purposefully-inverted villain, taking Doom down a peg yet only highlighting the strengths of the original.

Classic Doom was born into a poor Roma tribe. The world told him he was lesser and he made himself into a king to prove it wrong. "Ultimate" Doom was taught from childhood that the world was his birthright, but he isn't strong enough to carry it — like Kendall Roy if he was a Eurotrash super-villain. Classic Doom created an armored second skin to hide himself and his supposedly scarred face from the world. "Ultimate" Doom's flesh hardened like a chrysalis, turned brittle, and cracked off, leaving only metal — as if a heartless tin man with the features of the Devil is all he ever was.

Modern Family may have ended, but Julie Bowen has never stopped being a "mom" to her on-screen kiddos. For instance, Bowen was present when TV daughter Sarah Hyland got married in 2022, and both were part of that epic cast reunion at her wedding. Of course, Bowen also has love for her other faux kids, Ariel Winter and Nolan Gould. In fact, Bowen gave them a shout out during a recent event, and she trolled them in a seriously mom-coded way that's hard not to love.

Bowen recently attended the 2026 Baby2Baby gala at the Pacific Design Center in West Hollywood, California, a non-profit she has been involved with for over 15 years. While there to raise money for children in poverty, Bowen was asked by Entertainment Tonight for her thoughts on Winter and Gould living together “almost like real-life brother and sister.” On that note, the Claire Dunphy actress didn't hold back her hilarious response:

Screw them. Screw the two of you. They live so close to me, and I never see them. I run into them. I’m like, ‘What’s going on?!’

This is sitcom-level irony, but this kind of fun tends to happen amongst the cast. For instance, Winter has playfully called out on-screen big sis Hyland for having a mini reunion without sending an invite to her and Gould. However, Bowen's comments are particularly funny, because they speak to the jokey but somewhat maternal relationship she has with her young co-stars.

I can't see Hyland losing her “best fake daughter” title anytime soon due to Winter not sending an invite to her and Gould's new abode. However, in all seriousness, Bowen’s comment is all in good fun, and she went on to gush about Gould and Winter -- who played Luke and Alex Dunphy, respectively -- as well as their firm friendship:

I love them so much. I love that they live together. I love that they’re best friends. Everybody's like, ‘Are they together?’ I'm like, ‘No.’... They are roommates and best friends. They’re the best. I love them so much.

Not only are they NOT together, but it turns out that the best friend of your best friend makes for a good boyfriend. Winter is currently dating Gould’s best friend, after being introduced to him by her TV bro. Given she keeps her private life mostly out of public eye, she hasn’t revealed many details about the relationship. I'd imagine her former co-stars are update to date, though, as Bowen previously shared that their close bond is why the cast has remained on such friendly terms.

Given Bowen literally watched the younger cast members grow up, it’s understandable that she would have a motherly relationship with them… right down to the A+ mom jokes. As for possibly hanging out with them, Bowen also shared this quip:

Hit me up, Ariel and Nolan. Come on. Mommy needs you.

It's a moment like this that makes me wish a Modern Family revival of sorts would happen at some point. The cast's chemistry was just too perfect, and they clearly continue to have that bond off camera. I'm not sure whether ABC would be interested in such a production, but I'll keep my fingers crossed that it happens.

For now, though, it’s lovely to know that Julie Bowen is thinking about her on-screen kids… and (playfully) calling them out. It's a moment that feels like it's almost straight out of Modern Family, and If you don’t believe me, you can watch every zany family moment from all 11 seasons using a Disney+ subscription.

Also, let’s hope Winter and Gould get the message and hit up Bowen for lunch pronto!

#3368. Prince William Reportedly Wants to Strip Prince Harry of His Titles

Prince William is reportedly actively considering a plan for a “far-reaching restructuring” of the British monarchy, which he would implement once he ascends to the throne. His brother, Prince Harry, would be at the forefront of these changes: The future monarch reportedly wants only active members of the royal family who carry out duties on his behalf to retain their royal titles and the style of “Royal Highness.” These titles would therefore no longer be an “automatic privilege of birth” but would instead be equivalent to a “job title.”

The plan was detailed by Tom Sykes, a journalist and writer specializing in the royals, in his book Dukes of Hazard, to be published next February, excerpts of which were published by the Mail on Sunday on Saturday, November 21. The author, “a royal authority with impeccable society contacts” as the newspaper puts it, is said to have obtained confessions from friends of Prince William.

“If you are a working royal—going out, touring the country, doing diplomatic work, doing government work, having a public role, pressing the flesh, getting out of bed on a wet Wednesday to go to Sheffield—then you will be an HRH and you will have a prince or princess title. You will also get an allowance, a salary, and a place to live. One place to live,” the associate of the prince explained to Sykes. “If you are not doing those things and you are not a working royal, you will not get to be an HRH, you will not get a free or subsidized place to live, and you will not get any special favors. You will, however, be a private citizen free to get on with your life and make money any way you choose.”

By implementing this measure, Prince William hopes to prevent potential media scandals regarding the legitimacy of certain individuals’ right to retain their titles if they are not prominent members of the Firm (Prince Harry) or if they are under legal scrutiny (Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor). But also, and above all, the Prince of Wales hopes to offer an option to his children, Princess Charlotte, 11, and Prince Louis, eight, who could easily renounce their titles to pursue independent careers. The question does not arise for the eldest child of the Prince and Princess of Wales, Prince George, 13, whose future as heir to the throne is “guaranteed.” In fact, none of the three use their royal titles, preferring simply to be called by their first names and the surname Wales.

Under the rules established by King George V in 1917, the title of prince or princess, along with the predicate, is granted at birth to the sovereign’s children and to the children of the sovereign’s sons, as well as to all the children of the Prince of Wales’s eldest son. Prince William’s children, therefore, received these titles at birth, while Prince Harry’s children, Archie and Lilibet (ages seven and five), did not become prince and princess until King Charles III ascended the throne.

They may have to give them up if Prince William carries out his plan. “Under William’s current plan, the prince and princess titles of Harry and Meghan’s children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, would be legally removed, along with the royal styles and princely titles of Harry and Meghan themselves,” writes Tom Sykes in his book. To do so, according to Sykes’s book, constitutional advisers have told William that he could issue letters patent, an official document authorized by the king. Such a decision could strain the relationship between the two brothers.

Sykes is convinced that Prince William would garner the approval of his subjects and “enormous public support in a country increasingly impatient with the cost and perceived excess of a sprawling royal household,” according to those close to him.

In October 2025, Prince William confided to actor Eugene Levy—whom he was hosting at Windsor Castle for the taping of Levy’s show The Reluctant Traveler—that “there are points when you look at tradition and go, Is that still fit for purpose today? Is that still the right thing to do? Are we still doing and having the most impact we could be having?”

Kensington Palace, however, declined to comment on the rumor. “As a matter of policy, we don’t comment on books or claims made within them.”

Originally published in Vanity Fair France.

#3367. How To Watch Fjord At Home

Cristian Mungiu's Palme d'Or-winning, Sebastian Stan-starring film "Fjord" will be available to rent on digital platforms beginning November 24, 2026. Given that this is a few days before Thanksgiving, "Fjord" will be the perfect film to watch with the extended family, and won't inspire any kind of snippy, angry political discussions whatsoever.

That, of course, is sarcasm. "Fjord" is, in fact, very, very political. According to /Film's review, "Fjord" is a clumsy, one-sided, and very ideologically weighted drama that is presented as unbiased through its efficient visuals and realistic style, but which is very biased indeed. Even in a room of people who are politically aligned, either to the left or the right, "Fjord" will inspire discussion. Or an argument. Watch it with your politically opposed family members, and let the sparks fly.

"Fjord" tells the story of the Gheorghiu family, which consists of stern Romanian father Mihai (not listed as one of Stan's best roles on /Film's countdown of them) and Norwegian mother Lisbet (Renate Reinsve), along with their two teens, two elementary-school-age kids, and an infant, who move from their long-term Romanian home to the small Norwegian town where Lisbet grew up. The Gheorghius are conservative Christians, which is very different from the local community, mostly made up of non-adherents.

When the Gheorghiu parents are unexpectedly accused of physically abusing their children, Norwegian Child Protective Services immediately takes the kids away (like, in an afternoon), leaving the Gheorghius having to find any kind of legal recourse to get them back. They will eventually have to explain themselves in court. The Gheorghius aren't wholly innocent, confessing to spanking their kids from time to time.

The progressive government of Norway is presented as being full of harridans and busybodies who are hellbent on removing children from their well-meaning parents. "Fjord" presents a political conflict between conservative and liberal ideologies. The Gheorghius attempt to gin up support for their cause by calling in conservative protestors and staging their legal struggle as a bias against Christians. By Romanian social norms, a light spanking is seen as socially appropriate, but the Norwegian government is determined to keep the Gheorghiu kids away from Mihai and Lisbet. The movie sides with the conservative characters, making the entire film feel like light social propaganda.

"Fjord," however, won the Palme d'Or at Cannes, as well as the François Chalais Prize, the FIPRESCI Prize, the Prize of the Ecumenical Jury, and the Prix de la Citoyenneté. It is also beloved by most critics, racking up a 91% approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes, based on 165 reviews. Justin Chang's review in The New Yorker noted that some of the villains in "Fjord" are unrealistically larger-than-life, but that it was ultimately subtle. He wrote:

"Is 'Fjord' guilty, as some have charged, of stacking the moral decks in the Gheorghius' favor? We are presented with a few potentially hissable villains ... Yet Mungiu has an uncommon ability to temper bluntness with nuance."

As soon as it's easily available to rent online, one can watch "Fjord" for themselves and see if it's politically charged, naturally neutral, or morally complex. Cristian Mungiu tends to handle politically difficult issues with frankness and directness; he reminded us of the necessity of abortion with his 2007 drama "4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days." You, however, are the one can must decide if "Fjord" is as powerful.

#3366. 25 Years Later, GTA 3 Is Still the Most Fascinating Open-World Experiment

It’s October 2001, and you’re standing in a dimly lit game store, where rows upon rows of boxes sit in anticipation as you glance across their titles, unsure exactly which among them you'll end up taking home. Unfortunately, you can only pick one. Your eyes are already darting between Devil May Cry, Silent Hill 2, and Ico, which all feel eerily attuned to those pre-Halloween vibes. Noticing your indecisiveness (and the look of impatience on your mother’s face), the store clerk strides over with an assist, placing in your hands a game you had never heard of until that very moment.

The artwork’s nothing to write home about, just a collage of pictures in red, blue, and green hues, featuring obscure faces, a police chopper, and a car up in flames. Your instinct is to just go with your gut; Silent Hill 2 is what you came here for, after all. But something’s telling you otherwise. Maybe it’s the store clerk going on about its open-world premise, or the name itself that strikes a chord within you. Whatever reason incites it, you make the ultimate decision. Little did you know, you’d be walking home with one of the greatest achievements in video game history.

Grand Theft Auto 3 was a jolt of raw adrenaline. It was a paradigm shift that made the possibilities of 3D open-world design feel almost limitless. The game thrust players into what Rockstar co-founder Dan Houser described as “an old, post-industrial American city,” a mash-up of Chicago, Pittsburgh, Detroit, Philly, and mostly New York teeming with grim alleyways, pedestrian-filled streets, and sky-slicing buildings that eclipsed many of the incredible worlds that came before it, from The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time to Driver. It was called Liberty City. No game had molded such immense verticality into a 3D world that felt like a living ecosystem where the inhabitants and environments reacted to you directly. It was a feat many at the time considered impossible on existing hardware — and Rockstar did it with virtually no load times to boot.

Like nearly every title the studio would develop for the system, GTA 3 pushed the PlayStation 2 to its absolute limits. Developers DMA Design (now known as Rockstar North) had to cleverly stream around 130MB of data, including 3D animations, textures, models, and audio, through the PS2’s 32MB of system RAM. For perspective, just one Liberty City island amounted to roughly 50MB of static geometry. To make it all work, the team engineered a dynamic streaming system that fetched sectors of the map ahead of the player, while purging the city behind them. It’s why you’d often see the city pop in and populate right in front of you if you were driving at top speeds and quickly looked behind the character. When code couldn't bridge the gap, Rockstar cleverly designed curved roads to slow down sports cars, added subtle aerodynamic drag to prevent vehicles from outrunning the laser reader, and capped active traffic to eight models. What technical leads Adam Fowler, Obbe Vermeij, and their colleagues accomplished with GTA 3 was nothing short of magic.

Technical limitations weren’t the only roadblocks for Rockstar. Following the release of GTA 2, which he felt suffered from a lack of narrative thrust due to its non-linear design, Houser set out to give GTA 3 a far more complex story. With the help of co-writer James Worrall, they devised localized character "hubs" that served as contacts for missions, like Joey Leone, Toni Cipriani, and Salvatore Leone. Rather than treating open-world freedom and story progression as opposing forces, Houser used these dynamic webs to bridge the gap, tying mission arcs directly to specific territories and turf wars. That allowed GTA 3’s story to organically teach players the city's layouts and mechanics, moving through the industrial side of Portland with Toni Cipriani, navigating the Leone family's criminal empire with Salvatore, and eventually venturing into Staunton Island's political corruption and corporate underbelly. Each new contact pulled Claude deeper into Liberty City's criminal ecosystem, gradually opening up new territories while revealing another layer of the city's interconnected underworld. Coupled with the decision to keep Claude a silent protagonist, the hub structure allowed players to chart their own path without sacrificing the momentum of a cohesive crime saga.

The radio stations of GTA 3 also gave it that extra level of immersion, but before Rockstar could throw cash at some of the biggest names in the industry, the developers had to improvise with completely original music. Led by audio directors Craig Conner and Stuart Ross, the team wrote and recorded genre-specific tracks under aliases, like “Lucy,” “The Mudds,” “Marydances,” “Da Shootaz,” and more. Ross and Conner were also responsible for the GTA 3 Main Theme, a moody, “dark jazz” track inspired by The Sopranos and Goodfellas, which is still one of the best in the series. Combining underground hip-hop, drum & bass, and licensed classics from Giorgio Moroder’s Scarface score, the team was able to capture a gritty realism in the sounds of Liberty City. It’s a testament to Rockstar’s sonic ingenuity, one that finds a kind of spiritual successor in GTA 6, which features original scoring by French electronic duo Justice. The tools have changed, but the underlying idea remains the same: original music can give a fictional city an identity all its own.

What elevated these stations even further was GTA’s name-brand comedy, still in its infancy but just as hilarious, brought to life in Chatterbox FM. Scripted by Houser and hosted by Lazlow Jones, the talk-radio station's absurd caller rants and SNL-like commercial parodies gave Liberty City a lived-in texture long before you ever stepped out of your (likely stolen) vehicle. An especially on-the-nose example is a first-time-caller mother who rants about parenting in the age of video games: “I let my kid play video games, and now he runs around the house looking for gold coins. This is teaching our children to go chase money!” One of my personal favorites involves a suitably redneck-sounding character raving about how “guns don’t kill people, death kills people.” They go on to add: “You can’t die from a bullet, you can die from a cardiac arrest or organ failure or major hemorrhage. Small piece of metal ain’t the problem.” It’s no wonder Chatterbox is still widely considered some of the funniest and most satirical writing in the entire GTA series, though GTA 6 is shaping up to give GTA 3 a run for its comedy gold.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

On the heels of 9/11, released just 41 days after those fatal terrorist attacks, GTA 3 also remains a strange time capsule. Rockstar delayed the game by a few weeks to surgically scrub dialogue and a mission referencing terrorism, and changed the city’s squad cars from blue-and-white NYPD knockoffs to generic black-and-whites. Even the original box art was scrapped in North America, giving birth to the now-iconic grid layout that emblazons the cover of every series follow-up. Yet beyond those surface-level tweaks, the game took on a surreal weight in the wake of the tragedy. Having grown up just across the river in New Jersey, the attacks were an inextricable part of my life, even if much of the chaos of that era remains a blur. But I’ll never forget the long nights spent driving through Liberty City in the shadow of such devastation. Steering through those dark and rainy streets felt hauntingly poignant; a digital New York pulsing with life at a moment when the real world had suddenly ground to a painful halt.

GTA 3 was a baseball bat to the face of the gaming industry at a time when it was flourishing. It landed in the same year as Ico, Silent Hill 2, Halo: Combat Evolved, Final Fantasy 10, and Metal Gear Solid 2. Even in the face of such greatness, Grand Theft Auto 3 is unparalleled in its scope, bridging some of the most sophisticated world design ever attempted with a bespoke narrative engine that forever changed gaming. No one said it better than Sam Houser, who told IGN in 2001: “It has its own personality in a way I've never seen before in a game, to the point where it actually becomes part of the gameplay experience.”

Personality. That's what has always made Grand Theft Auto one of the most compelling entertainment properties on the planet, and GTA 3 was where that personality truly came into its own. 25 years later, with Rockstar's dominant open-world adventure being the latest example, Liberty City remains a testament to how ambition and clever design can fundamentally reshape an entire medium.

The internet is already drowning in GTA 6 misinformation

Does this mean Constantine could be coming back soon?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

With James Gunn and Peter Safran’s exiting DC, it's unknown if the DCU will continue or if we can expect yet another reboot. However, with one chapter closing for the studio, the start of a new might mean some long-gestating projects could get a second chance. Amid the corporate change, people have been asking about Keanu Reeves' long-discussed Constantine sequel again, and honestly, I don’t hate the possibility of seeing the 2005 movie finally get a follow-up.

A Constantine sequel has technically been "in the works" since 2022, and at the time, it was reported that writer Akiva Goldsman was working on the script. Director Francis Lawrence has been committed making another flick centered on Reeves' DC character, and he previously confirmed the leading man was "excited" about the idea. While there was a positive update in 2025, news has been scarce since then. Yet, when the director spoke with Collider about Sunrise on the Reaping, he gave John Constantine fans some hope:

Well, I’ll tell you this. Not that I want anybody to lose their jobs, so this is not like a schadenfreude kind of thing, but I will say that we’ve been trying to make Constantine 2 for 20-something years, and we have an idea, and we have a script, and we’ve been wanting to make it, and the people that were at DC were an impediment to us making it. So, we are now more hopeful as of yesterday’s news that maybe now there will be another opportunity.

This is sure to be music to some fans' ears amid the major corporate shift. Jeremy Latcham, a Marvel Studios alum who worked with Gunn on Guardians of the Galaxy, is stepping into the role of DC Studios CEO. As a result, Gunn’s DC universe might be over, and Lawrence -- who's sympathetic to the exiting CEOs -- seems to be confident that this could open the door for a Constantine sequel.

Of course, Lawrence is also upfront about having no idea what the studio has planned. For all he knows, they could want a different John Constantine for a shared universe. With that in mind, he’s also perfectly fine if the studio want to do a new take and allows him to make a sequel to HIS version with Reeves. In Lawrence's mind, two iterations can co-exist.

At this point, Francis Lawrence has made it clear that the project is further along than fans think, as they have a script ready to go. The only obstacle in his way is a thumbs up from the powers that be:

But again, we’ve been trying to make this for 20-something years, and there’s always been obstacles in the road to making it, and it’s not me, it’s not Keanu, it’s not Akiva. J.J. [Abrams] is on it, as well. We all want to do it. So, it’s really going to be people at Paramount, Warner, whoever’s running DC now, getting everybody on board to say, like, 'Hey, we can do a sequel of our version of Constantine.'

2005's Constantine has earned quite the cult following. Believe it or not, Reeves wasn’t fans' first pick for the role, and that's because of how much of a departure from the comics his take on John is. The character has lived on in the live-action space since then, with Matt Ryan taking on the trench coat in 2014 for a short-lived NBC show. Ryan continued to portray Constantine in The CW’s Arrowverse and voiced the DC antihero in various animated works through 2024.

However, a portion of fans still seem hopeful that Keanu Reeves will get another chance to play the character, and I’d love to see him back in the role. Considering Reeves' skills as an actor and his love for John, I have no doubt he can slide right back into the role. We'll have to play the waiting game on that front, though, as DC Studios has yet to reveal any new plans that will follow James Gunn and Peter Safran's departures.

In the meantime, stream Francis Lawrence's Constantine using an HBO Max subscription.

#3363. Tom Hardy And Gary Oldman Had A Batman Reunion In This Forgotten Western Gangster Movie

When you think of Tom Hardy and Gary Oldman working together, chances are you think of 2012's "The Dark Knight Rises," in which they played Bane and Commissioner James Gordon, respectively. But this generation-spanning British duo have crossed paths on screen multiple times throughout the years, including in a movie that debuted the same year as their Batman team-up. Yes, "The Dark Knight Rises" was one of two films in 2012 to give us a Hardy/Oldman collab (as well as a weird Tom Hardy accent). The other was "Lawless," a Southern Gothic gangster outing that's been mostly forgotten, but was a fairly big deal at the time.

Today, Hardy and Oldman happen to be on two of the best shows on TV. The former plays the perpetually embattled mob fixer Harry Da Souza on "MobLand," and the latter plays the perpetually disheveled Jackson Lamb on "Slow Horses." But the duo have worked together on four separate projects throughout their careers, beginning with one of the greatest spy movies ever made: 2011's "Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy." Asked by Digital Spy about working with Oldman on the John le Carré adaptation, Hardy had nothing but praise for the man. "Gary Oldman is my hero, that's it," he said. "He's right up there." The actor went on to say he's "stolen everything" from Oldman, with whom he'd re-team a year later on "Lawless."

Unfortunately, the pair don't actually share any scenes in the film, but their respective presences help elevate the whole affair, which is well worth a watch for the quietly intense performance from Hardy and the signature flourish of a performance from Oldman.

"Lawless" is directed by John Hillcoat, who made his breakthrough by overseeing one of the best dark Westerns ever made: "The Proposition." That 2005 effort was written by Nick Cave, who also penned the script for "Lawless," based on Matt Bondurant's historical novel "The Wettest County in the World." It's a lot less brutal than Hillcoat's 2005 effort, and boasts a typically compelling score from Cave himself.

Similarly compelling are the performances. A month prior to the film's release, in August 2012, Tom Hardy had simultaneously terrified and bewildered moviegoers as Bane in "The Dark Knight Rises," famously delivering his best known weird accent through a face covering worn by the ruthless brawler. But he didn't disappoint in the accent department as Virginian bootlegger Forrest Bondurant, either.

"Lawless" follows Forrest and his two brothers, Jason Clarke's Howard Bondurant and Shia LaBeouf's Jack Bondurant, as they run a bootlegging operation in 1931 Virginia. When U.S. Marshal Charley Rakes (Guy Pearce) arrives from Chicago, he decides to be far less lenient with the brothers than local law enforcement, forcing the trio to defend their livelihoods. Throughout it all, Hardy emanates a quiet intensity as Forrest, rolling a toothpick over his tongue and delivering lines that are quite often incomprehensible. But his screen presence is undeniable — which makes it even more of a shame that he has no scenes with Gary Oldman's gangster character, Floyd Banner.

Gary Oldman is only in "Lawless" very briefly, though he does get one of the best scenes, pumping a car full of lead while casually chewing on a cigar. We don't get to see Tom Hardy appear alongside the man from whom he claims to have "stolen everything," but luckily the two "Dark Knight Rises" stars reunited one more time for crime drama "Child 44" in 2015 and shared several scenes (though they ultimately failed to save the movie as a whole).

"Lawless," meanwhile, debuted at the 2012 Cannes Film Festival ahead of its theatrical release in August of that year. I remember the film being somewhat of a big deal due to Hardy's "Dark Knight Rises" role, and the fact "Lawless" was his first big film post-Bane. When I say "big deal," I mean relative to the movie being a small-town Southern Gothic drama and period piece; it was never going to draw in the crowds the way Christopher Nolan capping off his Batman trilogy did.

That said, the film did make $54.6 million on a $26 million budget and earned solid reviews. Today, "Lawless" sits at 67% on Rotten Tomatoes, though some critics seemed baffled by Hardy's accent. Still, "Lawless" is arguably one of Tom Hardy's best movies, giving the actor plenty of screen time to showcase his trademark combination of sheer aggression and insouciance (which has been on full display in "MobLand" of late). A scene in which Hardy's bootlegger sits lazily on his porch, barely paying attention while his brother roughs up two police officers, is just a lot of fun to watch. Had Oldman and Hardy had any screen time together, it might have been a true must-see.

#3362. Jane Fonda on Documentary ‘Gaslit,’ Trump, and What the Democrats’ Midterm Victory Means for Climate Change

In “Gaslit,” a new documentary about climate change activists, Jane Fonda stands outside one of Formosa Petrochemical’s Texas facilities and looks through a thermal camera. The Oscar-winning actress is brought to tears by what she sees: a tremendous expulsion of methane gas into the air.

“Methane is 80 percent more destructive to the climate, in terms of global warming, than carbon dioxide,” Fonda explained during a recent Zoom interview. “It’s the most destructive chemical that we’re using, and it’s extremely dangerous for people. And yet here it is billowing into the air, and nobody even knows it.”

For years, Fonda has been sounding the alarm about the looming environmental catastrophe that will take place if the world doesn’t wean itself off fossil fuels. She launched a series of climate change protests dubbed “Fire Drill Fridays” in 2019 — a reference to activist Greta Thunberg’s charge that people should “act as if your house is on fire” — and has been arrested multiple times for civil disobedience. Fonda is embracing the cause with the same passion that has led her to speak out on everything from the Vietnam War to feminism to LGBTQ+ rights. But she worries her efforts may not be enough. Related Stories Paul Thomas Anderson’s ‘Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall’ Getting Nationwide Release in January Rian Johnson Leaves the Door Open to Star Wars Return: ‘It’s a World I Deeply Love’

“Our emission of global warming chemicals has gone way up since Donald Trump has become president,” Fonda said. “And of course the concern is always: Have we passed too many tipping points or a tipping point? Many climate scientists say if we act fast now, it won’t be too late. But it’s very hard to act fast when Trump is president.”

The political winds are changing. The midterms were a blue wave election that saw Democrats take back the House and the Senate in commanding fashion. They not only performed well in liberal bastions, but also captured the governor’s mansion in Texas and elected James Talarico to a U.S. Senate seat that has been in Republican hands for decades. Much of “Gaslit” focuses on the environmental damage wrought by the oil fields in West Texas’ Permian Basin. Will the change in leadership make a difference?

“It won’t hurt,” Fonda said. “I don’t know how strong Talarico is on these issues. We can’t do too much until our members are seated, and we actually have the majority in the House in January.”

“Renewables are ready,” she added. “They’re cheap. They’re safe. They’re job-intensive. It’s the perfect solution. It’s right there. It makes all the sense in the world. The only thing we lack is political will, and hopefully, with this swath of new people that have been elected to the House and the Senate, we will have the political will when we take power to turn this around.”

Fonda believes average citizens concerned about climate change can’t afford to be passive.

“One of the most important things that people can do is to demand that their elected officials pass legislation that makes these polluters pay for what they’re doing,” Fonda said. “Right now, it’s consumers, it’s us taxpayers that have to pay for the damage. They should pay, and we have to stop the $21 billion annual subsidies that we pay them. They make trillions of dollars of profit. If we cancel those subsidies, it would spell the beginning of the end for fossil fuels.”

Fonda is blunt in her warnings that the chaos and damage that global warming has caused will only accelerate unless the world switches to renewable sources of energy. Her assessment is sober, even terrifying, but one thing that gives her hope is the work that the activists highlighted in “Gaslit” are doing. “Gaslit” was financed and produced by the environmental group Greenpeace USA, and it focuses on people in the Gulf Coast and Texas who are trying to change things across the political spectrum. They range from a Republican cattle rancher, who has seen what the oil and gas business has done to his family’s land, to cancer survivors and community organizers who are hoping to change hearts and minds about fossil fuels.

“What is so moving to me about the film is we’re showing these people who do not give up; they will not,” Fonda said. “All of these activists are so brave and so incredible. They inspire me.”

“Gaslit” was directed by Katie Camosy. It is now available to rent or buy on Amazon Prime and Documentary+. As of November 19, the film can be streamed on the Greenpeace USA YouTube channel, with additional platforms rolling out.

#3361. There's Actually a Simple Explanation for All These Widespread Outages

It feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another company is having an outage. Last week, there was Microsoft, whose outage took down services from Outlook to Teams. Then, the FAA grounded all flights across the U.S. following "communication issues." This week, a number of banks experienced outages, as did Apple. Even the NSA's internal communications network went dark. Some of the biggest corporations and organizations in the world can't seem to keep their services running, leading to widespread disruptions and confusion. When it's a one-off, it's an annoyance; when it's outage after outage, it starts to feel like a pattern.

That pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public. What could possibly be causing Apple, Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase, and the NSA alike to go dark at roughly the same time? Is it a coordinated cyberattack? An AI revolt? Is the end finally nigh? To an outside observer, it certainly appears like something coordinated and nefarious is happening here. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is insistent that there is "zero evidence" that hackers or bad actors caused any of these outages, and President Trump is particularly unconcerned by the whole ordeal, saying, "It's life," and "Things like that happen."

But to skeptics of the U.S. government, these trickles of information aren't necessarily reassuring. While I agree with calls for someone from the government (perhaps the president himself) to make an official announcement explaining the situation, the root cause does appear to be clear at this time: The short answer? AI is at fault here, but not in the way you think.

Love it or hate it, AI is a force to be reckoned with. While you might know that AI can generate hyper-realistic videos and manage your emails on your behalf, certain models are adept at discovering new security vulnerabilities in software. These models aren't just helpful tools; they far surpass the abilities of human researchers. You might remember Anthropic initially pulled the brakes on its breakthrough model, Claude Mythos, when it found that the model could root out security vulnerabilities in just about anything.

Mythos, and models like it, are a double-edged sword. On the one hand, they can be major assets for developers and researchers to find new security vulnerabilities that humans otherwise wouldn't have discovered, and patch them accordingly. Unfortunately, the same can be said for bad actors, who can use these models to learn about new security flaws and attempt to exploit them before researchers have a chance to find them. As such, software developers across the spectrum, from small-time devs to major corporations, have been racing to patch as many security vulnerabilities as they can find—and they're finding a lot.

You might notice your PC's security updates, for example, are shipping with more patches than usual—historic levels, even. Microsoft keeps breaking its own records with its Patch Tuesday updates, including over 1,400 fixes with its October update. The company's October 2025 Patch Tuesday update, by comparison, included fewer than 180 fixes.

It's important to understand that just about every company that develops software is furiously working to patch its systems before hackers or AI agents exploit vulnerabilities first. And while there are successes (Microsoft is now protecting its customers from thousands of flaws each month), this speed is also inadvertently breaking things along the way. That's not just speculation: According to The Washington Sun, both Wall Street executives and the NSA explained to members of Congress that patching security flaws discovered by AI models caused this week's widespread outages.

Barring some campaign to cover up a coordinated attack on systems and services, it does seem like these outages are simply the result of companies breaking their own products in an attempt to stop AI-assisted hackers from exploiting undiscovered flaws. But that's not all that reassuring, either. AI models are only going to keep getting better at finding vulnerabilities; likewise, AI agents are only improving at hacking into systems autonomously. Companies will need to ramp up their efforts to patch their software before both hackers and AI agents discover those flaws first, and so the cycle will continue. Unless something changes, we may see routine outages as companies try to fix things as quickly as possible.

The implications aren't specific to any one company, either. Our world increasingly relies on fewer companies to keep us all connected. We saw that last year, when cloud hosting providers like AWS and Cloudflare each experienced outages. When these services go down, so do all of the networks that rely on them. If AWS or Cloudflare break something while trying to patch their systems, whole parts of the internet go dark.

Of course, it'll only be more difficult for the general public—if not the developers themselves—to recognize when outages are the result of maintenance or a cyberattack. Just because recent outages don't appear to be nefarious in nature, that doesn't mean future outages will be so innocent. For the time being, however, it seems we can worry less about an active cybersecurity incident, and more about how AI is disrupting modern life in ways few of us saw coming.
