The Voice newbie Riley Green is having a killer first season on NBC’s long-running singing competition, which is currently airing on the 2026 TV schedule. He easily won over the majority of the country music hopefuls during the Blind Auditions and has given the competitors excellent advice that they can continue to carry with them. But no competition is smooth sailing, and the “Don’t Mind If I Do” singer is revealing the toughest part of coaching.

With the Live Shows in full swing, the country hit maker has two of Season 30’s strongest contenders, Joe Henley and Ferryn & Brinkley, still on his team. As we move ever closer to the unveiling of the winning coach and star, Green, who can currently claim the title of being one of 2026’s Sexiest Men Alive, has struggled with having to send so many talented singers home. He told People why he’s having fun during the live performances:

I’m really excited that I’m not having to send people home. That was the toughest thing about what’s gone on so far. It was tough in the auditions because you hear these amazing stories that people have... and they’re taking off to come try to chase their dreams, and maybe they don’t get picked.

Nobody is ever really an overnight sensation, so The Voice’s superstar coaches absolutely understand what it’s like to chase your dreams and have setbacks along the way. I can’t imagine how agonizing it must be to know you have to send home some really talented singers. Whether you’re rookie Queen Latifah or veteran coach Adam Levine, cutting someone’s dream short never gets any easier. So, I get why Green is relieved to just sit back and enjoy the performances, and leave it up to the audience to decide who continues on and who gets cut.

In an interesting twist for Season 30, the Live Shows have replaced the Knockouts, which happen to be Levine’s least favorite part of the competition for a very similar reason. No The Voice coach wants to have to send home talented singers, and leaving it all in America’s hands takes the pressure off the coaches. The Marshals guest star also said this about his experienceon the show:

Worse than that is once you’ve worked with them and they are on your team and then having to send them home after that, I’m so sick of having to make those decisions. So I’m glad America can do it, and I’ll just try to help them along the way.

One of the best parts of the reality competition show is watching how the coaches really become fans of their own team members. Kelly Clarkson has expressed her commitment to continue collaborating with Team Kelly, and I’m sure other coaches feel just as dedicated to creating such a supportive atmosphere.

I wouldn’t be surprised to see Green touring or doing special performances with his Team Riley singers, especially considering how connected he sounds like he feels with all of them. Also, it would probably go a long way toward making him feel better for those departing contestants.

The Voice Season 30 continues to air on Mondays until December 14th, when a two-hour finale will reveal who is crowned the winner. You can also watch the next day with a Peacock subscription. And Season 31’s The Voice: Celebrity is already waiting in the wings with new host Keke Palmer.

#3359. Star Trek's Brent Spiner Voiced A Heroic Version Of A Classic Batman Villain

Actor Brent Spiner is most famous for playing Data, the emotionless android who wants to learn humanity, on "Star Trek: The Next Generation." If an actor is part of a "Star Trek" main cast, they're essentially geek royalty for life. Spiner has parlayed that into, among other things, occasional guest roles on a handful of superhero cartoons. Spiner played the Joker in two episodes of the "Young Justice" cartoon series and that's not even the only Batman villain on his voiceover resume.

Spiner appeared as the Riddler/Edward Nigma in an episode of "Justice League Action," except in the episode, the Riddler had reformed. "Justice League Action," which aired 52 episodes from 2016 to 2018, was essentially a more kid-friendly "Justice League Unlimited." Episodes were 11 minutes long, and would feature three or four DC heroes from a larger rotating cast starring in adventures.

"Justice League Action" is not part of the DC Animated Universe that began with "Batman: The Animated Series" and concluded with "Justice League Unlimited," but its style is adjacent due to creative team overlap: Alan Burnett was one of the producers on "Justice League Action" and Paul Dini wrote several episodes. It also reused some DCAU voice actors, like the late Kevin Conroy as Batman and Mark Hamill as the Joker.

In the show's Riddler episode, the Joker has kidnapped Batman and left clues to his location all over Gotham. Wonder Woman (Rachel Kimsey) and Green Arrow (Chris Diamantopoulos) are hopeless at solving riddles, so the Riddler offers his services. Declared sane and recently freed from Arkham Asylum, the Riddler has reinvented himself from a super-villain to a private detective, using his riddle-solving skills to fight crime instead of to cause it. The episode is, accordingly, titled "E. Nigma, Consulting Detective."

There are two dominant interpretations of the Riddler; a cool, collected trickster who condescends to everyone less intelligent than him, or a short-fused, hyperactive showman. You can divide different Riddler actors across those lines fairly neatly: John Glover in "Batman: The Animated Series" is the former, Frank Gorshin in the 1960s "Batman" show and Jim Carrey in "Batman Forever" are the latter.

In fact, many Bat-historians would argue the violently murderous modern Joker owes more to Gorshin's Riddler, who flies off the handle and often loses control of himself to sadistic laughter. How amusing, then, that in "E. Nigma, Consulting Detective," the Riddler joins the case to save Batman because he's angry at the Joker for stealing his act of leaving clues at crime scenes.

Spiner's Riddler is cool and smug — definitely closer to Glover than Gorshin. His costume, a green suit and bowler hat with a question mark cane, is the one that Glover's Riddler wore in "Batman: The Animated Series" as well. It's the classic "refined" Riddler look, being more respectable than his original jumpsuit costume, and one that fits a Nigma who is trying to rebrand himself a respected professional. But the Riddler's design otherwise still has classical villainous features: triangular eyes with big black eyebrows, pointed nose and chin, etc.

Even as Nigma helps Wonder Woman and Green Arrow, he talks down to them. He may be working on the side of good, but he's still only solving mysteries to prove how smart he is.

Overall, "Justice League Action" is a pretty light and comedy-heavy series. The riddles that Nigma decodes in the episode are logic leaps in line with the '60s "Batman" TV show. There's also the episode's last twist that the Joker actually orchestrated this scheme to get revenge on the Riddler, not on Batman. Why? Because the Riddler once stole his donut in the Arkham Asylum cafeteria.

In the climax of "E. Nigma, Consulting Detective," the Joker traps Riddler. He asks him a riddle ("What has four eyes but doesn't see?") and, if the Riddler answers it, that will activate the death trap that holds Batman hostage. The Riddler tries to stop himself but he compulsively answers the riddle ("Mississippi"), leaving Wonder Woman to save Batman.

The Riddler rarely appeared on "Batman: The Animated Series" because his riddle gimmick made plots too complicated for a half-hour, action-driven cartoon. But that show still planted the seed for "E. Nigma, Consulting Detective." In his third and last appearance as the main villain, "Riddler's Reform," Nigma tries and fails to go straight. When Paul Dini wrote "Detective Comics" in the 2000s, he revisited that idea by making the Riddler a private detective who reluctantly partners with Batman.

"E. Nigma, Consulting Detective" in "Justice League Action" takes its title from Dini's "Detective Comics" #822, even though Dini didn't write the episode (Jonathan Callan did). The Riddler endangering Batman with his compulsion is the same conclusion the status quo-bound comics eventually reached: Edward Nigma is too selfish to ever fully reform.

#3358. GTA 6's Best Easter Egg Is a Classic Tom Cruise Crime-Thriller You Can Stream For Free

A random taxi ride in Vice Beach takes a detour into Michael Mann’s Collateral

One of Grand Theft Auto 6’s strangest random encounters occurs when you’re offering taxi services, and a man with a beard wearing a dark suit and sunglasses climbs into the backseat with a gun. This can happen if you’re playing as either Jason or Lucia, but both scenes play out the same way: The man wants you to run a red light, ignore phone calls, and drive him to Harborside Park in Vice Beach. He also sounds an awful lot like Tom Cruise, with a calm but forceful demeanor that seems almost sociopathic. Several clips of the sequence have already hit the internet, and to many people, it’s an obvious nod to Collateral, Michael Mann’s 2004 thriller about a hitman who takes a cab driver hostage.

Jason or Lucia gets a better deal than Mann’s cabbie in this Easter egg. If you take the stranger to his destination and follow him inside after he takes out some of the criminals there, you can find a ton of valuable loot. Most players seem keen on eliminating the stranger rather than keep driving him around. In Collateral, Jamie Foxx’s character, Max, has to spend the whole night driving Cruise’s Vincent around Los Angeles. If you’ve never seen how that goes for him, Collateral is streaming for free on Pluto TV — and it’s a must-watch, especially if you want a movie that has a vibe as wild and crime-filled as GTA 6’s.

Max is a cab driver who’s been telling himself for years that the job is temporary. He wants to start his own limo company someday, so when a well-dressed passenger named Vincent (Cruise) offers him $600 to drive him around for the night, it seems like the kind of opportunity that could get him a little closer to quitting. Then a body lands on his cab at their first destination. Vincent has five people to kill before the night is over. Max has just agreed to drive him to all five stops — and he’s already an accomplice.

Vincent is one of Cruise’s best roles because so much of what makes him convincing as an action hero makes him downright scary here. The same certainty that lets Ethan Hunt talk somebody into jumping out of a plane makes it seem perfectly reasonable, for about half a second, when Vincent asks Max to help him stuff a body in the trunk. He’s also an obnoxious backseat driver. The longer he spends in the cab, the more interested he becomes in why Max has seemingly wasted so much of his life. Some of his advice is irritatingly solid, yet he’s also a man who could end the conversation with a single gunshot whenever he wanted to.

Despite the plot focusing entirely on Vincent’s assassinations, Foxx emerges as the real heart of Collateral. Early on, he picks up a prosecutor named Annie (Jada Pinkett Smith), and their conversation has the easy rhythm of two strangers who realize they’d like the ride to last a little longer. You get to see how good Max is at putting people at ease as he flirts a little. Then, Vincent hops in the back, and the nightmare begins. Once the hitman is in the car, even the smallest decisions Max makes​​​​​​​ — like when to look in the rear-view mirror and when to keep his eyes on the road — feel like consequential choices Max must make carefully​​​​​​​.

For a movie about a man on a deadline, Collateral is remarkably willing to pull over and look around. Vincent himself comments early on about how much​​​​​​​ he despises the city’s sprawling, depersonalized atmosphere. Mann often dwells on that atmosphere​​​​​​​ to build up tension. In the movie's best quiet moment, a coyote crosses the road in front of the cab, and both men stop talking to watch it. Los Angeles feels eerie and sinister, lit by flickering streetlights and bland storefronts. As their night continues, even mundane locations feel like the most dangerous places in Los Angeles.

The story’s arc is also immensely satisfying. We see what this pressure cooker does to Max, forcing him to evolve from a passive bystander in his own life to someone who takes an active role​​​​​​​. The evolution is subtle at first as Max resists Vincent’s demands, eventually mustering up the courage to become openly defiant​​​​​​​. Vincent spends the night needling Max about all the chances he’s too scared to take — putting a down payment on a limo, calling Annie since she left him her card, etc. — and by the time they inevitably face off, Max is finally willing to take one.

GTA 6 so often positions your character as the Vincent of its story, stealing cars and killing people for the next big score. But forcing you to become something closer to Max, at least for a little while, is nothing short of brilliant. The Grand Theft Auto franchise at large owes a great deal of its overall vibe to Mann’s filmography. GTA 5, in particular, is largely inspired by Mann’s 1995 crime film Heat. So it's only fitting that its direct sequel pays homage to another Michael Mann classic — with a little bit of Miami Vice thrown in too, for good measure.

Collateral is available to stream for free on Pluto TV and with a subscription on Paramount Plus.

Warning! The following contains spoilers for the 90 Day: Hunt For Love episode "The Boy Who Left His Mark." Stream the episode with an HBO Max subscription, and read at your own risk!

After their confrontation was shown in the previous episode, 90 Day: Hunt For Love finally showed Razvan Ciocoi's removal from the spinoff. I have mixed feelings about how it was handled, and questioning whether it was the best way for this to be shown to viewers.

For those unaware, Razvan was removed from 90 Day: Hunt For Love after he allegedly used a racial slur to refer to Jamal Menzies during their argument. Rather than show the incident, the 90 Day Fiancé show decided instead to flash the following text onscreen before moving on to the next day:

Razvan was asked to leave the retreat due to a code of conduct violation.

The scene then switched to Iris meeting up with the other 90 Day: Hunt For Love singles and explaining that he left. There was no discussion about what happened, and it was more to state that Iris was "back on the market" with her match gone. Had someone watching only learned of the incident from the 2026 TV schedule, they wouldn't have known what happened.

90 Day: Hunt For Love Has Me Wondering If Brittany Intentionally Sabotaged Michael's Love Life

I don't know all the context that went into this decision, but I can already see some problems with it. To start, I don't think avoiding what happened with Razvan is going to dissuade viewers out of the loop from looking up what happened. He was a prominent part of 90 Day: Hunt For Love up to this point, and I think his absence will be felt.

On the same token, there's a discrepancy on whether or not the event in question happened. Razvan has denied it was ever uttered, and if there was evidence to the contrary, TLC opted not to show it. Additionally, no one spoke about the incident beyond Razvan being gone, so it's still up in the air beyond TLC's statement.

I also would be willing to cut the franchise some slack, had it not just based an entire storyline in a previous spinoff on a racially insensitive remark by Shekinah Güven. 90 Day: The Last Resort dove deeply into her telling Thaís Ramone to "go back to her country," and even addressed it again at the tell-all special without her being present. So, I doubt the incident was a bridge too far by the show's standards, which makes me all the more curious why it was sidestepped.

The questions and drama will continue on 90 Day: Hunt For Love on TLC on Mondays at 8:00 p.m. ET. Despite this unfortunate moment, I'm still enjoying this season and wondering which couples will link up at the end of it all.

Well, let’s do a quick comparison between two cultural phenomenons that I’m definitely not just lumping together in a desperate — some might say “heroic” — attempt to write an involving review lede for a movie that never makes even the slightest effort to earn your attention. Ahem: On the one hand, it took 13 years for Rockstar Games to produce another numbered installment of their marquee franchise, during which time they leveraged cutting-edge technology and unprecedented financial resources in order to radically iterate upon a proven formula so that the company’s Baudrillardian allegory of American pathos would map onto an era that has become too shattered for more coherent sense-making. On the other hand, it took 16 years for the combined power of Universal and Paramount (a Skydance Company) to will another “Focker” movie into existence, during which time someone realized that it might be kinda funny if Robert De Niro said the words “Jamba Juice.”

And in fairness, they weren’t wrong. A Robert De Niro character shouldn’t know what Jamba Juice is, let alone want to drink there! Not only that, but he correctly emphasizes the “JAM” of it all, the formal precision of which suggests that Jack — a red-blooded Boomer who’s recently become an exercise-obsessed vegan health nut — has developed a sincere degree of respect for the smoothie chain and its various blended offerings, even if it’s taken him 16 years to do so.

Given that John Hamburg’s “Focker In-Law” brings back so much of the franchise’s original cast almost three decades since they first played these roles, the film benefits from a Linklater-esque sense of temporal continuity that invites us to imagine the time between movies as a living space. Don’t be fooled by the gruel-thin story, the parade of self-amused callbacks, or the painfully contrived jokes that substitute for real emotion, this isn’t an opportunistic cash-grab meant to capitalize on our collective appetite for big screen comedies — it’s a family reunion.

the expectations for a legacy sequel are much lower than they might be for the most expensive video game in history, especially in the context of a franchise that’s sustained by the idea that the surname “Focker” sounds almost indistinguishable from the word “fucker.” (Don’t be embarrassed if you hadn’t put that together before — it’s subtle, and film critics are professionally trained to identify such things). “GTA VI” had to revolutionize interactive entertainment in order to be considered a success. “Focker In-Law” just has to deliver more of the same. It does that over and over and over again; I don’t know about Jack’s nipples, but Greg (Ben Stiller) can certainly milk an old joke until it turns to dust in his hand.

The cinematic equivalent of half-rotten Thanksgiving leftovers that you’d only eat in lieu of having any other food in the house, “Focker In-Law” might be an increasingly rare big-screen comedy, but it’s endowed with the “whatever”-level apathy of the worst straight-to-streaming junk. Depressingly, that feels like a systemic failure more than a creative one, as Hamburg is a very funny guy who directed several of the better comedies of this century’s pre-Netflix era (e.g. “Along Came Polly”), and he’s far from the only proven talent who gets wasted here.

The basic story — for which Hamburg shares credit with Austen Earl and, curiously, Ilana Glazer — offers a natural riff on the franchise’s initial premise: Greg might wear Radiohead t-shirts and sport facial skin tighter than any scene in the movie around him, but he’s now older than Jack was during the first movie, which means he and his wife Pam (Teri Polo, making the easiest money of her life) have aged into the “Parents” who are due to be “Meet”-ed when their son Henry (an overqualified Skyler Gisondo) brings his big-eyed new girlfriend Olivia (Ariana Grande) to Jack’s 80th birthday celebration.

The joke, and it’s not a bad one, is that Greg — a beta male bozo who’s desperate to make his children and their partners feel welcome — immediately bumps against his probable daughter-in-law, while Jack — a dominant and unyielding patriarch whose “Circle of Trust” is harder to crack than a captured enemy spy — cottons to her from the moment she gets to his house. It helps, of course, that Olivia is an ultra-rigid life coach and former hostage negotiator who shares Jack’s taste for military discipline, as well as his knowledge of different polygraph technologies. Why she’s drawn to a softboi like Greg’s son remains unclear, but the “Wicked”-like theatricality of Grande’s performance is farcical enough for such open questions to be their own reward (it makes sense that her character would be so emotive and intentional), and at the end of the day what matters is just that Greg has a reason to feel rejected all over again.

He doesn’t take it well! In fact, he acts like a massive asshole about it to a degree that steers the movie away from cringe comedy comfort food and closer towards a character study about a malignant narcissist instead. Stiller is a maestro of self-involved unpleasantness (his work in “Greenberg” and “The Meyerowitz Stories” has never gotten the recognition it deserves), but that kind of toxicity is far more unpleasant in the context of a film that thinks it’s cute and/or easily redeemable.

In “Meet the Parents,” Greg got into all sorts of wacky trouble because he meant well and cared so much about seeming worthy of Jack’s daughter. In “Focker In-Law,” the hijinks stem from the fact that he’s a scheming monster who’s trying to sabotage his son’s relationship so that Henry might stay closer to home. The clean and simple fun of watching good intentions curdle into misunderstood chaos has been replaced by the dull ache of watching someone try to pass off diagnosable psychosis as the stuff of routine parental anxiety.

Alarm bells start ringing from the very first comic setpiece, in which a classic setup — Greg tries to cut the airplane bathroom line by sneaking from coach into first class — is almost completely undone by the logic gaps that have come to define the character. Why does he impulsively steal Olivia’s birth control out of her bag before he even knows who she is, and how is it possible that such an overbearing dad hasn’t even seen a picture of his son’s very serious new girlfriend? Such questions aren’t really worth answering, and Hamburg at least has the courtesy to distract us from them with a fly-by cameo by Cole Escola, but the vibe is all the way off by the time we even touch down in New Jersey for the main event, and nothing that happens there is remotely inspired enough to redeem the pervasive sense that no one can remember why “Meet the Parents” became a franchise in the first place.

Was it Owen Wilson’s amusingly oblivious performance as Pam’s charmed ex-fiancé, Kevin? There’s only one way to find out! Was it Jack’s penchant for lie-detector tests or his affinity for unlovable pets? Let’s give them both a shot and see what sticks. (I was amused by the German shepherd he trains in this film, who sets up a very good joke accusation that I don’t want to spoil here). Maybe it became a phenomenon because people crave manic setpieces that end in a plume of human ashes — we should run that back just in case. Anything to avoid the obvious and enduring coziness of a “home for the holidays” movie, which “Focker In-Law” inexplicably forfeits by setting its story at the height of summer.

The ballad of Gaylord Focker certainly didn’t become a thing because of Greg’s daughter and her long-term boyfriend, whose presence this movie struggles to accommodate despite the fact that Beanie Feldstein and Eduardo Franco are both eager to help liven things up. In fairness, why open the floor to potentially amusing new characters when you can spend half the film’s runtime agonizing over Greg’s uncomfortably demented attempts to steal the engagement ring that Henry wants to give to Olivia? Some opportunities are just too good to pass up, I suppose.

That “Focker In-Law” maintains any of its series’ long-faded charm can be attributed to De Niro, who sleepwalked through the previous two sequels but feels revived by Jack’s newfound looseness in this one. The actor delights in playing off Grande’s type-A eagerness, just as his character takes a muted pleasure in how much Olivia causes Greg to crash out. In a comedy as flat, stilted, and generic as this one, De Niro’s still-inimitable star power is almost enough to save the movie from its own reheated cynicism. “JAM-ba Juice.” They actually just go by “Jamba” now. The franchise’s juice is long, long gone.

Universal Pictures will release “Focker In-Law” in theaters on Wednesday, November 25.

#3354. Margot Robbie Appeared In A Time Travel Movie The Same Year As Her Big Break

You probably know who Margot Robbie is, right? She's a pretty big star. From "Barbie" to "Babylon," Robbie is one of the most popular and profitable stars working today, and you probably know her from her big break in 2013 when she starred alongside Leonardo DiCaprio in Martin Scorsese's delightfully nasty "The Wolf of Wall Street." You should also know, though, that Robbie appeared in a gorgeous, sweet, and absolutely lovely romantic comedy in 2013 — and it's called "About Time."

Written and directed by Richard Curtis, "About Time" employs a genuinely bonkers premise. After a New Year's Eve where he completely screws up his chance to kiss a girl at midnight, Tim Lake (Domhnall Gleeson) learns from his father James (the always-perfect Bill Nighy) that Lake men can travel through time within their own experiences and memories. Across one summer, Tim attempts to use this bizarre and largely unexplained power to woo Charlotte, a friend of his sister Katherine (Lydia Wilson), who spends a summer at the Lake house in Cornwall and is played by (you guessed it!) Robbie. During one do-over, Charlotte tells Tim that if he'd asked her out before the last day of the vacation, things might have gone differently; when he does his trick and rewinds to the beginning of said summer, she says they should wait and see how things go.

Years later, while Tim is living in London and dating a publishing executive named Mary (Rachel McAdams), he crosses paths with Charlotte and they share a dinner ... but when she invites him to go back to her place, he goes home to Mary instead and proposes to her. Robbie's role is small but pivotal, and it's a stark contrast to her breakout performance.

Margot Robbie rather infamously slapped her future co-star and on-screen husband Leonardo DiCaprio during her audition for "The Wolf of Wall Street," but clearly, Martin Scorsese and his long-time collaborator liked her cojones ... because she got the job. In this film, which also released in 2013, Robbie showed off a completely different side of herself as Naomi Lapaglia, a lingerie designer who woos DiCaprio's Wall Street crook Jordan Belfort away from his first wife and who's known as the "Duchess of Bay Ridge."

The role of Naomi requires a lot from Robbie. Not only does she have to speak in a perfect Brooklyn accent — Robbie is Australian — she has to absolutely dominate an actor as powerful as DiCaprio, toe the line between being absurdly hot and being legitimately terrifying, and she has to essentially live a whole lifetime on-screen as she has children with DiCaprio's Jordan and watches him succumb to his excesses. Robbie manages to pull all of that off; think of the scene where her Naomi torments Jordan in their children's playroom, where she splashes water on his face during an argument, or when she tearfully runs towards her young child strapped into Jordan's expensive car.

Robbie didn't earn an Oscar nomination for her work in "The Wolf of Wall Street" — those nominations would start rolling in a bit later — but for my money, she should have. Thankfully, after showing off her insane duality in "About Time" and "The Wolf of Wall Street," the best was yet to come. It's genuinely incredible that she was able to deliver both of these performances in the same year, but in retrospect, I guess it's not that surprising.

Like I said earlier, Margot Robbie is one of the most well-regarded and famous performers of her generation, and "The Wolf of Wall Street" was just the beginning for her. After "Focus" in 2015 with Will Smith and her first turn as Harley Quinn in the 2016 version of "Suicide Squad" — a role she'd reprise in "Birds of Prey" and James Gunn's 2021 reinvention "The Suicide Squad" — Robbie scored her first Oscar nomination for "I, Tonya," Craig Gillespie's bombastic account of Tonya Harding's scandalous rise and fall as a figure skater.

In 2018, she lent her skills to the deliberately anachronistic "Mary Queen of Scots," which cast her as Elizabeth I facing off against her royal rival Mary (Saoirse Ronan), and in 2019, she earned her second Oscar nod for playing a fictional Fox News reporter in "Bombshell" and also portrayed a non-doomed Sharon Tate in Quentin Tarantino's "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood."

"Barbie," though, is arguably Robbie's most enormous outing to date. This 2023 release that led to an actual cultural event alongside Oppenheimer also grossed over a billion dollars in a matter of days and scored a nomination for best picture, earning Robbie a nod as a producer. Speaking of that, Robbie has produced movies like "Promising Young Woman" and TV shows like "Sterling Point," paving the way for more female writers, directors, and actors through LuckyChap Productions. None of this would be possible without "The Wolf of Wall Street," but also, I think "About Time" helped launch Robbie into the stratosphere too. You can stream "About Time" on Netflix.

#3352. James Cameron’s Sci-Fi Sequel Masterpiece Is Officially Being Removed from Netflix

With one of the great final film battles of all time

In an action movie, there’s nothing worse than an underwhelming final battle. While Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings was one of the best post-Avengers: Endgame movies of the Marvel Cinematic Universe, its final battle became a disconnected CGI fest that was hard to follow. For Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: The Secret of the Ooze, the sequel’s fun energy was undermined when a mutated Shredder died after collapsing a dock onto himself without a fight ever even starting.

It can be hard to stick the landing with that final boss fight, especially after a movie has been good up until that point, and a lame final battle can undermine everything that came before it. Fortunately, James Cameron’s 1986 action thriller Aliens — leaving Netflix on Dec. 1 — does not suffer from this issue, even after setting an impossibly high bar for itself.

After Ellen Ripley (Sigourney Weaver) defeated one Xenomorph alien aboard a spaceship in Ridley Scott’s 1979 horror thriller Alien, Cameron blew up the franchise by having Ripley visit a planet full of those same creatures and fend off dozens of them with the help of a platoon of Colonial Marines.

Towards the end of Aliens, after Ripley rescues the young girl named Newt (Carrie Henn) from an alien nest filled with eggs, Ripley encounters the Xenomorph queen, a massive creature far larger and more frightening than any of the aliens she’d encountered thus far. After a momentary hesitation, Ripley proceeds to turn her blowtorch on the eggs and blow up the egg sack attached to the queen, while the creature writhes in pain. After Ripley escapes with Newt, the queen tears herself free from the egg sac​​​​​​​ and pursues the duo, who narrowly escape.

What follows is one of the great fake-outs in cinema history. Bishop (Lance Henriksen), the loyal android, retrieves Ripley and Newt in a dropship, and they escape as the alien-infested planet below is nuked.​​​​​​​ They return to the main ship and all seems well until​​​​​​​ the queen, who had stowed away on the scout ship, tears Bishop in half and comes after Ripley and Newt. Newt hides under the floor panels and the queen nearly gets her​​​​​​​ until Ripley reappears with an exosuit cargo loader and the two have an epic brawl for the ages.

Discussing the queen in a 1987 interview, Cameron explained,​​​​​​​ “The queen was an opportunity to take a design stance that was beyond the first film — create a new organism, basically.”

She was a creature that Cameron designed himself, building upon the work of artist HR Giger, who designed the Xenomorph alien for the first film.

“I had an image of what I wanted this thing to look like, which was, obviously, inspired by Giger's approach,” said Cameron. “I wanted to continue with that design philosophy, but I wanted to give it certain other characteristics in terms of size and speed and grace and certain feminine characteristics that the alien warrior didn't have. So I just sat down and drew a few different versions of it. And, actually, the first full sketch that I did of it is pretty remarkably close to what we finally wound up with.”

Special effects wizard Stan Winston​​​​​​​ then led the team of effects artists that created the most complex animatronic monster made up to that point​​​​​​​. It took up to 16 puppeteers to control the queen, with some parts moved by hydraulics and others by rods and cables​​​​​​​. And, because this was 1986, none of that operating equipment could end up in the shot to be removed later digitally. What we see in the movie is precisely what was filmed during production.

Perhaps the most impressive thing about the Xenomorph queen, though, was just how perfectly it built upon everything else in the film. When compared to the single alien in Ridley Scott’s original film, Aliens was already full of surprises just by the sheer volume of creatures, but the queen managed to perfectly pay off the entire film with a terrifying design and an incredibly tense battle with Ripley. Four decades later​​​​​​​, it’s still one of the best final fights in cinema history, and certainly worth revisiting before the film leaves Netflix.

Aliens is available to stream on Netflix until Dec. 1. It's also on Hulu and Disney Plus.

#3351. The Naruto Movie Sounds Like It Could Be Better Than We Ever Imagined

Fresh off making the best "Spider-Man" movie in about a decade with "Brand New Day," director Destin Daniel Cretton is plunging into the Land of Fire and ninjas, adapting Masashi Kishimoto's manga/worldwide phenomenon "Naruto" into a live-action film, two years after it was first announced. Translating a battle shonen manga/anime into live-action carries negative associations of past, failed attempts. Why bother moving a story designed to stretch reality's limits to a medium that's inherently more confining than a hand-drawn one? Will "Naruto" break this curse? It has a huge stage to do so, and the early steps look promising.

Deadline has reported that actor Hiroyuki Sanada ("Shogun," "John Wick: Chapter 4") is in negotiations to star in "Naruto" as Hiruzen Sarutobi, the Third Hokage and leader of Naruto's ninja village, Konohagakure. Sanada is the second major actor rumored to be joining "Naruto," after reports in August that Charles Melton had been approached to play Kakashi Hatake, Naruto's masked sensei.

This alone suggests "Naruto" is serious about getting impressive talent: one of the coolest actors alive in Sanada, and a major young actor in Melton, who's won acclaim for his performances in "May December" and "Beef" Season 2. Not for nothing, Sanada and Melton are Japanese and Korean American, respectively — no whitewashing here, so far, contrary to "Naruto" fans' long-standing jokes about Tom Holland or Timothée Chalamet starring as Naruto.

"Naruto" has launched a "global" search/audition process for the movie's three young leads: Naruto and his teammates Sasuke Uchiha and Sakura Haruno. That suggests the film's creators are looking for young actors — possibly, even plausibly, unknowns — who can embody those characters first without prioritizing pre-existing star power.

Casting Hiroyuki Sanada as the Third Hokage suggests the "Naruto" team is already looking to the horizon and seeing sequels. Hiruzen is only a background part of the first "Naruto" arc, "The Land of Waves" (which is the ideal starting place for a movie series). But he takes center stage in the second and third arcs, where one of his former students, the snake-like Orochimaru, serves as the main villain. Hiruzen gets a major action sequence confronting Orochimaru, and casting Sanada — a martial artist who holds a black belt in karate, just as Charles Melton has one in taekwondo — seems like casting with that scene in mind.

If the goal is adapting the "Naruto" manga as a whole, then forward thinking will be key. The manga runs 700 chapters, divided into several story arcs; you'd likely need somewhere between seven and 10 movies to complete it. The live-action "Naruto" is being produced by studio Lionsgate in partnership with Sony. Lionsgate recently proved once more that "The Hunger Games" is a reliable hit for them with the success of "Sunrise on the Reaping." But it's never smart to put all your eggs in one basket. "Naruto" hits overlapping demographic appeal and even some similar story beats as "The Hunger Games" (like children becoming killers and the tragic horrors of war).

Moreover, comic books have become the prime IP of Hollywood these past two decades, and yet manga outsells American comics many times over. Manga/anime is in the cultural mainstream for anyone younger than a young millennial, and the first studio to crack that could be sitting on a cultural gold mine. So, yeah, Lionsgate has a strong incentive to get "Naruto" right, and the talent it's recruiting suggests they understand that.

Even if Destin Daniel Cretton doesn't stick around for any of those potential "Naruto" sequels (I have to imagine Sony and Marvel Studios want him back for more "Spider-Man" movies), getting him as director for the first is another sign that Lionsgate is taking this seriously. Look at what he's directed, and consider how he's intent on casting actors with genuine martial arts bona fides for "Naruto," and it's clear why he's the man for the job.

An essential part of "Naruto" is its fight choreography, which is more choreographed around hand-to-hand martial arts than most other battle shonen. Yes, the ninjas in "Naruto" use "jutsus," or magical/superpowered attacks powered by spiritual energy, or chakra. But the core of the series' fight scenes is mano-a-mano fights that lay on the brutality and raw emotion; that's especially true in Naruto and Sasuke's various duels.

The combat in "Naruto" likewise employs parkour acrobatics in the vein of wuxia. (In-universe, ninja learn to channel their chakra to balance on, climb, and run through trees.) Cretton directing "Shang-Chi," a wuxia-flavored Marvel movie, and Spider-Man, who webslings through New York City like how Naruto and his ilk dash through forests, gives him the perfect experience to deliver the heightened-but-not-completely intensity of the action from the early "Naruto" arcs.

Cretton also has the perfect sensei to consult with in Masashi Kishimoto, who has endorsed Cretton as the perfect director for the project, the same way that "One Piece" creator Eiichiro Oda personally approved elements of Netflix's "One Piece" series. "One Piece" proved live-action shonen manga/anime can work in the TV format, and "Naruto" might be the project that proves it can be a blockbuster movie.

#3350. Steven Spielberg Directing His First Western with Paul Thomas Anderson Writing the Script

Steven Spielberg has directed musicals, sci-fi epics, adventure films, and biopics, but one genre has eluded him over the course of his decades-long career. He has never directed a Western, despite having openly longed to put his spin on the type of movies that turned one of his idols, John Ford, into a legend.

Well, the wait is over. Spielberg is developing an untitled film for Focus Features about two fugitives charting a course across the American West, and he’s assembled a crack team to help him. The ensemble will include Jessie Buckley, fresh off her Oscar win for “Hamnet,” Cillian Murphy, the Oscar-winning star of “Oppenheimer,” and Mark Rylance, a frequent Spielberg collaborator who won, you guessed it, an Oscar for “Bridge of Spies.” Related Stories ‘Focker In-Law’ Review: An Eager Ariana Grande Isn’t Enough to Save a Comedy Sequel That Can’t Remember What People Liked About This Franchise Jane Fonda on Documentary ‘Gaslit,’ Trump, and What the Democrats’ Midterm Victory Means for Climate Change

But there’s more to get cinephiles’ hearts racing! Paul Thomas Anderson, the Oscar-winning filmmaker behind “Boogie Nights,” “There Will Be Blood,” and “One Battle After Another,” is writing the script. It’s based on Kevin Barry’s novel, “The Heart in Winter.” Though Anderson usually directs his screenplays, he’s done script doctoring for Ridley Scott (“Napoleon”) and Martin Scorsese (“Killers of the Flower Moon” and the upcoming “What Happens at Night”). He also did some work on “Corky Romano” — hey, they can’t all be winners! So why not join Spielberg’s merry band?

Spielberg is still one of the all-time greats, but he could use a hit. “Disclosure Day,” which marked his return to summer movies, was a box office disappointment, and his most recent films, like “The Fabelmans” and “West Side Story,” struggled to connect with audiences despite earning excellent reviews. Maybe saddling up will be just what the movie gods ordered.

Kristie Macosko Krieger, Sara Murphy, Anderson, and Spielberg will produce the film, which is expected to hit theaters in 2028. Tim Headington, Neil Shah, Ryan Zacarias, and Ana Leocha will executive produce it.

#3349. These Noise-Canceling Skullcandy Headphones Are 50% Off Ahead of Black Friday

Black Friday is an excellent time to score a new pair of headphones that would otherwise be a splurge, with retailers like Amazon and Walmart already offering massive discounts on tech essentials from top brands a week ahead of the holiday. One of the early Black Friday deals that should be on your radar is the Skullcandy Crusher ANC 2 headphones, a mid-range noise-canceling option that’s perfect for bass lovers and is currently 50% off, dropping to $119.99 (originally $239.99).

PCMag says they deliver “brain-rattling levels of bass” and have a comfortable fit, with generous memory foam cushioning and minimal clamping pressure that lends itself well to long listening sessions. The aesthetic is nothing to scoff at either, with a refined and modern style. It’s worth noting they also come in a hardshell zip-up case with a fabric-lined exterior.

Powered by 40mm dynamic drivers, they offer reliable noise cancellation with the ANC slider set to max on the companion app, which lets users adjust a range of controls and listening modes, including the intensity of bass. The bass boost feature is ideal for those seeking bass-heavy headphones, but may be overwhelming for those who prefer a more balanced sound.

Battery life lasts around 50 to 60 hours per charge, with Skullcandy claiming that you get four hours of listening time from around 10 minutes of charging. While brands like Bose will outperform in ANC quality, if you’re looking for noise-canceling audio gear that checks most boxes at a reasonable price point, the Skullcandy Crusher ANC 2 headphones are a smart choice, especially at over $100 off.

This film deal comes after Levy and 21 Laps as recently as September signed a new overall TV deal with Disney’s 20th Television, with him exiting his Netflix deal. That pact doesn’t begin until October 2027.

Levy is reuniting with Sony’s leadership Tom Rothman and Sanford Panitch after he previously directed the “Night at the Museum” movies, “Cheaper by the Dozen,” and “Date Night” for them while they were all at Fox.

“I go ALL the way back with Shawn. We made a pile of hits together before he went on to far greater successes, none of which surprised me in the slightest,” Sony Pictures Motion Picture Group Chairman and CEO Tom Rothman said in a statement. “His talent as a producer, director and head of the coolest creative company around, is rivaled only by his unmatched enthusiasm. I feel lucky as hell to reunite, and excited for everyone at Sony to discover what I have long known — Shawn Levy is the real deal.”

“Tom, Sanford and I have a long history together, and some of the most formative and rewarding experiences of my career came during the years we worked together at Fox,” Levy said in a statement. “Tom saw the future of my career before I did, and he bet on me early and with a bighearted (and loud!) conviction that is one of his trademarks, and for which I’ll be forever grateful. 21 Laps was built on empowering fellow filmmakers and helping them tell stories imbued with their unique voices and visions. Along with my entire 21 Laps team, I’m thrilled to begin this next chapter with the team at Sony, and am excited about the wide-open breadth of opportunity across Sony’s many labels. I deeply value their commitment to theatrical filmmaking.”

While just about everyone else in Hollywood has taken a victory lap with the success of “Backrooms,” you may have forgotten that Levy and 21 Laps were producers on the A24 horror movie, and he of course directed and produced Netflix’s “Stranger Things,” which concluded at the end of last year. Up next for Levy is “Star Wars: Starfighter,” which is a “Star Wars” spinoff starring Ryan Gosling and which opens May 28, 2027. And he’s also teaming with Gosling and Disney yet again on Marvel’s “Ghost Rider,” which opens July 28, 2028. His last feature he directed was “Deadpool & Wolverine,” which made $1.3 billion worldwide.

On the 21 Laps side, the banner is producing a rom-com with Emma Stone and Chris Pine set at Universal called “The Catch;” Netflix’s drama series “The Sticks,” starring Michelle Monaghan; Amazon MGM Studios’ supernatural horror film “Seasons;” Netflix’s feature comedy “One Attempt Remaining,” starring Jennifer Garner and John Cena; and an untitled Netflix spy feature starring Kevin Hart and Henry Cavill.

Shawn Levy and 21 Laps Entertainment are represented by WME and Wendy Kirk at JSSK.

But all hope is not lost: Costco recently started its own early sale, so you're still in time to find something you want at a low price. #3346. Matt Damon’s 144-Minute Sci-Fi Survival Masterpiece Officially Arrives on Hulu

Matt Damon is riding high on the success of The Odyssey this year. After multiple collaborations with Christopher Nolan, Damon finally plays the leading man in his latest movie. The highly anticipated feature was not only technically perfect but also had compelling performances, yielding a billion-dollar gross at the box office, with fans rewatching the brilliant piece of cinema in theatres.

Damon has a versatile filmography; in the same year, he appeared in a streaming-only feature like The Rip and shouldered the big-budget R-rated feature. His filmography is full of brilliant titles, like playing the titular role in The Talented Mr. Ripley and in Steven Spielberg’s Saving Private Ryan. Playing real-life characters in Air, where he plays Nike executive Sonny Vaccaro, Carroll Shelby in Ford v Ferrari and Leslie Groves in Oppenheimer. But The Bourne franchise has a separate fan base and is probably the crown jewel of his filmography.

Among the long list of titles, there’s a feature which is thematically close to The Odyssey. He plays a resourceful hero stranded far from home and yearns to return. The feature in question is Ridley Scott’s The Martian. It casts Damon as an astronaut, Mark Watney, who strives to survive on Mars when a space mission goes wrong. While he undergoes different challenges attempting to stay alive on Mars, his colleagues at NASA exhaust all options to bring him home. The Martian is very close to The Odyssey with its “stranded hero” archetype, who fights overwhelming odds to return home. Like Odysseus, Watney too relies on his cleverness and strategy to combat an unforgiving environment. Perhaps the biggest similarity is the “Bring Matt Damon home” trope that fans have noted across many of his films. Now, after watching The Odyssey, fans are returning to movies that follow the trope.

For fans who want to see The Martian, they're in luck, as the movie just got more accessible. The Martian is coming to Hulu on December 1, as per ComicBook. The 91% Rotten Tomatoes-rated sci-fi survival depicts an astronaut's struggle to survive on Mars after being left behind and NASA's efforts to return him to Earth. Along with Damon, the feature also stars Jessica Chastain, Jeff Daniels, Kristen Wiig, Chiwetel Ejiofor, Sean Bean, Michael Peña, Kate Mara, Sebastian Stan, and Mackenzie Davis. With compelling performances and a gripping narrative, the film earned $653.6 million worldwide on a $108 million budget and is often considered one of Ridley Scott’s best movies.

Check it out on Hulu on December 1 and stay tuned to Collider for more such updates.

#3345. ‘Cliff Booth’ Star Elizabeth Debicki on Slapping Brad Pitt, ‘The Movie Critic,’ and the Rom-Com Question

Don’t let the title fool you: “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” might offer up a breezy, very fun-to-watch new entry into the life and times of titular (and fictitious) Hollywood stuntman, but co-star Elizabeth Debicki steals the show in David Fincher’s film (in addition to stealing the heart of Brad Pitt’s Cliff). Is it time to greenlight “The New Adventures of Karen Crosby”? We think so.

The much-anticipated sequel to Quentin Tarantino’s “Once Upon in Hollywood” picks up nearly a decade after the Oscar-winning antics of the previous film, finding Cliff pursuing new professional endeavors (film projecting! bartending! contract killing, kind of!). Stunt work? Eh, only when he feels like, and he certainly feels like after taking an unexpected meeting with Hollywood agent Karen Crosby (Debicki), whose grace and good humor instantly delight both Cliff and the audience. Related Stories Shawn Levy and 21 Laps Set Overall Film Deal at Sony Pictures Steven Spielberg Directing His First Western with Paul Thomas Anderson Writing the Script

Tossed together by the wacky demands of Karen’s marquee client, actor Charlie Nelson (Scott Caan), the shaggy, Tarantino-penned “Cliff Booth” meanders its way through every corner of Hollywood, finding real emotional ballast and crackling chemistry every time Pitt and Debicki share the screen. Characteristically wordy and dense, we learn plenty about Karen along the way (including her early forays into film criticism and her current feelings about movies), and she wins Cliff’s heart by, well, literally and physically slapping the crap out of him.

Ahead, IndieWire catches up with the Aussie star (who gets to use her real accent this time) about Fincher’s film, from slapping her co-star to some serious ruminations on the instantly iconic “pig monologue speech.” No wonder Cliff went so crazy for Karen; she’s a delight.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

IndieWire: What was your relationship with “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” when the film came out in 2019?

Elizabeth Debicki: I went to see it in the cinema. I think I went by myself, which makes me think I must have been on a job. I was definitely in the States, maybe I was in L.A., and I went one afternoon. I went and sat in the cinema, and I loved it. It’s really vivid in my memory.

I didn’t watch it again before we made this for performance reasons. In a way, I realized I didn’t really need to because, [there’s] something about Quentin’s movies, they just kind of wedge themselves in your brain. I can literally see the Playboy Mansion scene. I can see the Manson kids driving up to the house. I can see Margaret Qualley’s feet on the dashboard. I can see everything.

So it sounds like you came into this as a Tarantino fan.

And to get Tarantino and Fincher is this incredible two-for-one.

It’s funny, because obviously in the making of this, I had to sort of normalize that. And they helped me do that because they were, from the second I got onto set — which was a two-week rehearsal period where we really worked through the script — we had Quentin for that whole period. [It was] very, very collaborative.

A part of me wonders whether it was that thing where they have sat with the material for so long and had their full body relationship to it, and then I was fresh. I had my own thoughts and feelings. My memories of those rehearsal periods were really all three of them [Fincher, Tarantino, and Pitt] just turning to me and saying, “What do you think? What do you think?” The first time it happened, I was like, “Oh my God, what do I think?” After a little while, I started to actually say what I thought, which was great.

I didn’t audition for this. David emailed me and asked me if I would be interested in playing a part. I remember he phrased it in an email as he hoped that I would consider playing a very tricky part in a film he was hoping to make in July. It was a very David-ism kind of email. I think it said something like, “I hope you understand the seriousness of this conundrum,” or something. And I called him up and yeah, I was obviously ready to say, “I’ll do it.”

He was very, very insistent. He was like, “Wait, wait, wait. I really want to tell you everything about it.” Because at that point he and Quentin were doing a massive edit of the script. He couldn’t send it to me there and then.

Karen is so singular, but she is in a familiar position if you’re working in Hollywood. Did you base any part of your performance on any agents or managers or publicists that you know or have encountered?

When I first read the script, there were things that just rang so true to me, and might seem outrageous for anyone or slightly absurd maybe for anyone who doesn’t work in this industry. The incredible pig scene where Cliff talks about killing a pig, and then the scene in the car where Karen says, “Now because of you, I now have to spend my entire morning finding a pig. That is not a joke, that is literally what I have to get up and do. And you know what? I had a lot of things I had to do, and it wasn’t find a pig. And now I have to drive your ass all the way to Marina del Rey because I have to just deliver you because that’s what my client needed.”

It’s kind of this absurd ask, but it’s folded into “that’s what I need for my process.” Quentin and David, they’re so fascinating because they are Hollywood. They are Hollywood, and also they sit outside it, and they observe it from these very, very unique vantage points. Quentin, in particular, his love affair with L.A. is so profound, and with Hollywood. Part of the thing I loved about her too is that she’s sort of accidentally an agent, which is not frequently do you come across that. One of the things too that feels very human about her is that she sort of had this other dream, but she took one really bad knock, and it broke her heart, and she just buried it deep inside and then made decisions based off that.

When we get to that scene with Karen and Cliff when you’re talking about how Karen had this other career as a film critic, I how much of that was lifted from what would’ve been Quentin’s movie, “The Movie Critic”?

I don’t know. I don’t actually know the answer to that question in terms of the parallel there. But I do love that in the middle of this film about 1977 in Hollywood, that there’s a really important moment where we think about Pauline Kael, and we think about her and she lives in this film. I’m so glad that there’s this moment where my character gets to say, “Pauline Kael is my god,” because she was. She was incredible.

As Karen, you have this great monologue explaining to Cliff who you used to be, what had happened with that career path, how wonderful it was that Pauline supported you, and then it didn’t work out. And then you have another monologue about seeing movies as hamburgers. It’s a really funny tension for Karen, because the audience likely assumes she loves movies and does see them as art.

That’s right, there is a tension there. I feel like one of the things that Quentin can do so well, and kind of totally unique to his own brain, is that he sort of plucks an idea out of the zeitgeist, something that we’re all thinking about, and he feeds it through his characters in a way that feels very organic. This is a big conversation that people are having as the industry shifts and changes. It also was a huge conversation that was happening in 1977. There was this big question of, “Is that art still if it’s commercial, if its box office success equates to this?” I think that the dichotomy of what she believes in her heart and wants to be true and what she spouts in front of people, I sort of think both things are true at once, and I think that’s just the kind of human element.

But I also think that it’s important to remember in that monologue that Charlie really pulls it out of her. She really doesn’t want to do the dance, the dancing monkey, or what did she say? “There’s a dancing bear aspect to your request,” I think is such a great line. But yeah, I think both things are true for her.

You have the sense she’s said this speech before, and again, maybe she doesn’t totally believe it, but Charlie just loves it and so she has to do it.

David and I spoke about it a lot, and we sort of landed on we feel like she did it once off the cuff, like at a table at the Emmys or the Globes, and everyone went, “Gee, Karen, that’s genius.” And Charlie heard it and went, “Yeah, that’s genius. She’s my agent, look how smart she is. She’s so great.” Then she’s done it one other time at a dinner. So, by the time we get to the pool, she’s like, “Oh, my God.” It’s becoming a routine against her will, which was also a really fun element to play with in terms of how much she does or doesn’t enjoy it, and finding that balance.

Do you personally read reviews of your work?

Has it always been the case? [Smiles] I’m sure anyone who doesn’t read a review once read a bad review.

It doesn’t even have to be a bad one. What I learned is, you can read a review that is seemingly positive, but it might not be what you were trying to do, and then you feel heartbroken about that too. So yes, I really avoid it. Yeah.

You get to slap Brad Pitt a lot in this film. Was that hard to do?

It’s a very beautiful face, and we had to do it. We had to do it. And Brad is a very good sport and a very good stuntman. I think that Brad was very, very comfortable, and I was very nervous. We shot the dialogue for two days, that we were just in almost this sort of trance of the two of them, and of the very unusual power dynamic that [they have]. One of the best things about that scene to me, which I didn’t analyze at the time, it’s so intricate the way that Quentin wrote it. It’s this moment where, in revealing what he wants, he becomes so vulnerable that the power dynamic kind of very subtly shifts in this kind of core foundational way between these two characters.

So, we shot that for two days and then all of a sudden it was like, “Oh, my God, it ends, and I need to figure out how to do this.” We had an amazing stunt coordinator on that job.

We had to do extremely complex things with people, but with me, I was like, “Hey Dave, could we just pop out the back there and have a little chat about the slap…?”

Everyone knows that David likes to do a lot of takes. How many takes was the actual slapping?

Not so many! It was probably the least amount of takes we did. We probably did a couple, five, maybe six. And then I do remember that Brad sort of went, “OK, I think we got it. I think we’re good now,” and we moved on. But we did the inside [slap] first. It was such a joy to do. It’s such a happy memory. We filmed it, and then we all ran around to the monitor, and we watched it in playback, and we’re like, “Oh, my God, it’s so good.” And then we filmed it again. We were so pleased with ourselves. [Laughs]

What scenes did David ask for the most takes?

The thing about the takes is, it’s coverage-dependent. So, if you have four actors in a scene, like the hamburger monologue, let’s say there’s four setups on each actor, you do 10 takes per setup. So, that becomes a lot.

I will say that in the pig speech monologue, I don’t have a lot of lines, but we did just as much coverage on me as we did on Brad and Scott. That was one of my first days on set, and I remember thinking, “This is so, so unusual. Why is he doing this?” And then a couple weeks later, he showed me a kind of rough edit, and I thought, “Oh, my God, that’s why he did it.” He is using Karen as the kind of go-between. As David would always say, at least there’s one grown-up in the room, and it’s Karen.

So I do have this really funny memory too of doing that during the pig monologue scene. I was off-camera, or we were catching just the side of me; I was very much out of focus, and I took a drag of the cigarette, and I remember he gave me a note for that, something about the speed of it or the intention of it. And I remember thinking …

Exactly! I was like, “You saw that?” And he was right, he was absolutely right, but I thought, “OK, this is not a set where we get away with anything.”

Especially in that scene, you have these facial expressions where you are having the appropriate reaction to what we’re hearing, but in such a beautiful way. I think that’s when we all fall in love with Karen. We’re like, “She gets it. She knows how ridiculous this is,” but she is part of this world.

I’m particularly proud of the Tic Tac crunch; that was my prop idea, and I just thought we should end with her crunching down on something, because she’s so pissed about having to then go and spend her entire morning looking for a hog in Malibu Colony or something. Where is she even going to find that pig?

She did it. I mean, David and I would talk about that too. I’m like, “Do you think she did it or she sent Mallory, her assistant, to go do it?” Either way, someone did it, someone paid for it.

Speaking of falling in love with Karen, there’s been this sentiment circulating as people see the film that there is a real rom-com built into it with Cliff and Karen. Do you see it that way?

I don’t think it’s a rom-com, but I think it’s romantic, and I think they’re funny. Don’t get me wrong, rom-coms are my religion. Yesterday I was walking through New York, and I literally felt like I was in “You’ve Got Mail.” I was like, “This fall day, I need a bunch of sharpened pencils.” But I don’t think that this necessarily falls into that category. It’s sort of undefinable, indefinable, but I do think it’s really romantic. I felt that when we were playing it, and we really enjoyed that together.

The romance of it is kind of surprising, because it surprises her. It’s sort of best case scenario romance, that you think you have it all together, and this person walks in that you absolutely dismiss in terms of that, and then little by little they just sort of reveal this thing. More beautifully, they pull something out of you. I didn’t necessarily intellectualize any of this while we were shooting it, it’s just that I can see that now retrospectively. Not that I read anything, but I am curious what people will make of them.

Netflix will release “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” in IMAX theaters on Wednesday, November 25. It will be available to stream on Netflix starting Wednesday, December 23.

#3343. Terry Pratchett's 18-Year-Old Fantasy Series Has A Near-Perfect Magic System

In 2008, one of the best TV shows based on Terry Pratchett's work was released. After watching The Color of Magic, it's impossible not to be impressed with the story's magic system, which might be the best fantasy fans have encountered in a long time.

Whether they're soft or hard, a magic system is one of the most critical pieces of any work of speculative fiction, and Pratchett understood this when writing his iconic novel series, Discworld. The top-tier Terry Pratchett TV adaptations successfully translate the balance Pratchett strikes between witty tone and love of fantasy that he brings to every aspect of his writing. With an all-star cast including Sean Astin, David Jason, and Tim Curry, The Color of Magic proves that Pratchett's work can be brought to life onscreen.

Terry's Pratchett's Discworld encompasses 41 mainline novels, which can be a daunting undertaking for readers looking to get into the series. However, there's no wrong place to start when diving into Pratchett's hilarious, vividly imagined world. After watching 2008's The Color of Magic, you'll want to start with the first two installments, The Color of Magic and The Light Fantastic, as an introduction to the wildly entertaining universe of Discworld.

The magic system in The Color of Magic strikes the perfect balance between offbeat and compelling in the TV series. The primary user of magic in the show, the wizard Rincewind (Jason), is initially unable to learn any new spells at Unseen University, causing him to be kicked out because he knows one of the spells from the extremely powerful spellbook Octavo. The other spells he might learn didn't want to be in the same head as the Octavo spell, which also makes it impossible for Rincewind to die. This inability to die also ties in with one of Pratchett's best Discworld characters, Death himself.

Each of the Terry Pratchett TV adaptations have their own strengths and weaknesses, which makes ranking them difficult but

Rincewind gets into plenty of sticky situations throughout The Color of Magic alongside his companion, Twoflower (Astin). The fact that Rincewind only has knowledge of a single spell and that his misadventures as a wizard are played for laughs throughout The Color of Magic, but the ways in which the Octavo spell helps him and demonstrates its power still scratch the itch of a transportive, high fantasy magic system.

Pratchett has consistently proved that a fantasy world doesn't need to be dark or lack humor in order to be poignant and gripping. It's because Pratchett is unafraid to include humor and challenge the traditional expectations of speculative fiction that his moving quotes stay with readers and audiences for years to come. Readers will find themselves learning a lot more in the pages of Pratchett's Discworld than they ever expected.

Pratchett's Discworld universe is proof that a magic system doesn't need to have strict rules and boundaries in order to make sense; it just needs to match the tone of the story. For a world like The Color of Magic to have a magic system that is closer to a scientific process than the whims and delights of the off-kilter narrative, this would be bewildering. Readers and audiences come to Pratchett's Discworld because it's less concerned with logic than it is with thematic purpose.

It's no surprise that the 2008 The Color of Magic was so warmly received by fans and critics. Discworld isn't afraid to make the viewer think deeply about the story and reflect on their own lives. However, it does so in an entertaining and richly imagined way that encourages the audience to expand their imagination. Magic is ephemeral and changeable in Discworld, and the beloved series wouldn't be half as good if this wasn't the case.

Recently, Netflix released a film based on a popular fairy tale, but from a different character's perspective, and it has become a streaming hit. The fairy tale in question is Cinderella, a story about a young girl forced into servitude by her evil stepmother and stepsisters; with the help of her Fairy Godmother, she goes to the ball and dances with the prince, but must leave before midnight. After leaving her glass slipper behind, the prince searches the kingdom for his true love and eventually reunites with Cinderella.

​​​​​​​This fairy tale has been adapted many times, including Disney, so much so that the character made her way to the Descendants franchise, revealing that Cinderella and the Prince have children. Recently, Netflix released an animated children's fantasy film called Steps, a retelling of Cinderella from the perspective of one of Cinderella's stepsisters, Lilith, voiced by Ali Wong. Steps was released on Netflix on November 20, 2026, and has since become a streaming hit, reaching #2 on Netflix's Top 10 Movie Charts Worldwide, between Guarding Stars and Heartland. Alongside its streaming success, Steps was well-received by fans and critics alike, earning a 78% critics score and a 71% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes.

Steps follows Lilith, one of Cinderella's stepsisters, whose family is treated as outsiders while Cinderella (Amanda Seyfried) earns the kingdom's sympathy following her father's death. The movie puts a twist on the classic fairy tale when Lilith steals the Fairy Godmother's (Bette Midler) wand and crashes the royal ball with her sister, Margot. However, things take another turn when Cinderella's rival, Priscilla (Nikki Glaser), steals the wand and uses its magic to make the prince fall in love with her and seize control of the kingdom. Now, Lilith and Cinderella must put aside their differences and work together to restore order.

Four Netflix characters, four completely different ways of showing up for somebody. This is the one who fits how you actually do friendship, and what having them in your life would be like.

You do not do friendship at half volume, and neither does he. What you want is somebody who says yes to the plan before you have finished describing the plan.

You are the friend who makes things happen, and so is she. Together you would be mildly exhausting to everyone around you and completely delighted with yourselves.

You have no patience for pleasant lies, and she has no ability to tell them. What looks like coldness from the outside is the most reliable friendship on this list.

You look after whoever is having the worst day. So does he. It is the least strategic way to move through the world and the best possible quality in a friend.

Steps isn't the only Cinderella retelling that puts the stepsisters in the spotlight. Back in 2007, Disney released Cinderella III: A Twist in Time. Like Steps, the movie features Cinderella's stepsister, Anastasia (Tress MacNeille), stealing the Fairy Godmother's (Russi Taylor) wand, and Lady Tremaine (Susanne Blakeslee), Cinderella's evil stepmother, using its magic to travel back in time and change the original movie's events, ensuring Anastasia marries the prince instead and leaving Cinderella (Jennifer Hale) to set things right.

While both movies feature a stepsister stealing a magic wand, Steps follows Lilith and Cinderella as they reconcile their differences and rebuild their relationship. Meanwhile, the Disney version has Anastasia learning that she wants to find her own true love rather than force someone to love her through magic. She eventually reconciles with Cinderella, while Drizella and Lady Tremaine face punishment for their actions.

#3335. How Sound Design Helps ‘Minotaur’ Get Away with Murder

Editor’s Note: This article contains spoilers for “Minotaur.”

Director Andrey Zvyagintsev has worked with supervising re-recording mixer Andrey Dergachev for 20 years, since the director’s second film, “Banishment.” On each project, including their most recent portrait of a rotten marriage in a rotten world, “Minotaur,” they’ve tried to improve the sound design—using it as a hook that makes the film’s world feel more vital and alive for the audience.

Seriously, spoilers. This is never more true than in the absurdly sad and funny, then suddenly murderous confrontation between cuckolded husband Gleb (Dmitriy Mazurov) and his wife’s lover Anton (Yuriy Zavalnyouk) at the hinge point of “Minotaur.” Related Stories Super Bowl LXI to Play Live on IMAX Screens ‘Cliff Booth’ Star Elizabeth Debicki on Slapping Brad Pitt, ‘The Movie Critic,’ and the Rom-Com Question

Zvyagintsev and Dergachev generally strive to preserve as much authentic production sound from performances as possible. “On my third movie, ‘Elena,’ we recorded the live sound from shooting, and it’s maybe two or three phrases we had to rerecord, but otherwise the whole sound that you hear is fully recorded during the shooting,” Zvyagintsev told IndieWire on an upcoming episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit podcast. “Our main purpose is to keep as much sound from the shooting as possible and not to add anything extra, and it was the same for ‘Minotaur.’”

But for the moment that Gleb attacks Anton, and its aftermath, it was important to Zvyagintsev that the world beyond the apartment start intruding on Gleb — that even though he wants desperately to cover up what he’s done and make sure no one sees or learns about it, we hear dozens of ways in which he isn’t alone. That required a lot of work outside of the studio to record the background noises Zvyagintsev and Dergachev could then layer into the scene.

“We were creating [background] sounds of the kids playing football in the backyard. We would spend the whole day recording the kids, how they’re speaking, the way they’re playing, people passing by on the street,” Zvyagintsev said. They also recorded different sound layers from Gleb’s luxury SUV, which they could deploy to create maximum panic in both Gleb and the audience.

“The car signals, the leaves on the street, the birds — they all pronounced, and [emphasized] something. So we were modulating all those layers that we recorded, and then we combined them to create the atmosphere and to put it all in one place for the scene,” Zvyagintsev said.

There’s atmosphere from outside and from inside, as Zvyagintsev and Dergachev refused to let Gleb have a moment of peace on the soundtrack — until, as with all the cruel jokes of “Minotaur’s” filmmaking, he gets it in the worst way, at the worst possible moment. There’s a terrible silence once he’s struck Anton on the head with his own camera. And then the world comes rushing back in, even louder than before.

“We were trying to create this volume of sounds right after the hit. And then, when Anton is falling, there is this complete silence. And then somewhere far away we hear the car alarm and even more sounds that create this volume. This is what we were looking for,” Zvyagintsev said.

It was important to finesse the sound design of the sequence so as not to overplay it. Zvyagintsev initially wanted to add music to the moment, but had to hold himself back. “It was really tempting,” Zvyagintsev said. “My composer Evgueni Galperine even wrote the music, which we added. But when we saw the result, we realized, and I understood that no, no, it has to be completely silent.”

Silent as the grave, one might say. But it’s the sound design, the modulation between loudness and silence, that makes the moment so horrifying. Zvyagintsev and Dergachev did it by hand, just to make sure of it.

“Minotaur” is now playing in select theaters.
