#3333. 6 Mutant Family Trees That Make Absolutely Zero Sense

X-Men has introduced countless new heroes and villains with intriguing, complex lore, and some have expanded on fan-favorite characters through familial relationships. However, there are times that these relationships become tangled, whether it's through secret parentage, genetic experiments, cloning, time travel, multiversal variants, or even retcons. With so many unexpected twists at play, some mutants’ backgrounds are incredibly difficult to follow.

While these particular family trees are rather convoluted, they also add an interesting layer of backstory and history to each character, no matter whether the family connection holds or not. Even with different continuities, retcons, and the like, these mutant families are just as intriguing as the characters themselves, often delivering a thrillingly fascinating, albeit tangled, legacy.

Professor Charles Xavier is best known as the founder of the X-Men, but his own family history also stands out as a very complicated affair. Among his relatives are a psychic parasite who masquerades as his twin sister, Cassandra Nova; a stepbrother who inherits power through a mystical entity, Cain Marko, who is better known as Juggernaut; and several direct offspring, including David Haller, also known as Legion, Charles Xavier II, Xandra Neramani, and more outside the main continuity.

Xavier’s complicated romantic history adds to the confusion regarding his family tree, especially his relationship with alien royalty, the Shi’ar Empress Lilandra, resulting in their daughter, Xandra, who was created through genetic engineering long after their marriage ended. Beyond that, his connections to Mystique produced a son, Charles II, while his relationship with Gabrielle Haller led to the birth of his other son, David, who stands out as one of the most powerful mutants introduced in the X-Men universe.

Without counting his family tree outside of the main continuity, Xavier’s family history is full of unusual family ties and unconventional circumstances. While it’s far from the most confusing among X-Men families, Professor X does deserve a spot among the mutants with the most complex and intriguing family trees.

Wolverine’s family history is nearly as complicated as his own personal history across the comics. Decades of secret relationships, forgotten offspring, and revelations about his own parentage have made his lineage rather difficult and confusing to follow. Wolverine was born as James Howlett, initially believing he was the son of a wealthy landowner named John Howlett, only to later find that his biological father was the estate’s groundskeeper, Thomas Logan.

Wolverine's replacement makes their official debut, thrown into battle against the original Logan and his teammates by a terrifying X-Men villain.

That revelation also made Dog Logan, his childhood bully, his half-brother, making a rather unconventional immediate family. Beyond that, Logan also fathered numerous biological children and genetic clones whose connections to him vary between different continuities, with the films produced by Fox further complicating his backstory and family history.

Among his best-known children are Daken, his biological son with Itsu, and Laura Kinney, a genetically engineered clone, also known as X-23, who eventually becomes his daughter. If one clone wasn’t convoluted enough, Laura also has a clone of her own, Gabby Kinney. Among Wolverine’s other children in main continuity are the Mongrels, a group of illegitimate children who are manipulated into seeking revenge against him, resulting in Logan unknowingly killing some of his own children.

Shatterstar and Longshot arguably have the strangest family relationship in Marvel history due to their connection standing as something far more complex than a simple father-son dynamic. Longshot is Shatterstar’s biological father with Dazzler, but due to extenuating circumstances involving time travel and genetic cloning and experimentation, it’s much more complicated.

Shatterstar is sent back in time to the Mojoworld, where scientist Arize uses his DNA as a template to create Longshot, who later goes on to meet Dazzler and have a child who turns out to be Shatterstar himself. What this means is that Shatterstar is both Longshot’s biological son as well as his genetic father, effectively making Shatterstar his own grandfather. In short, their relationship is a closed genetic loop where neither character’s origins can be separated from one another.

To make matters even more odd, Shatterstar helps deliver his infant self and then arranges for the child to be sent forward in time in order to keep the timeline intact. While Longshot and Dazzler’s memories are wiped, the resulting family tree, history, and paradox loop is exactly as bizarre as it sounds.

Quicksilver and Scarlet Witch’s family history has been heavily rewritten across X-Men comics, with their biological parents changing several times throughout their publication history. While Pietro and Wanda Maximoff always remain twin siblings, their supposed parents have shifted from various Marvel characters, with each one carrying its own ramifications that completely alter the twins’ place within the Marvel universe.

Instead, they were revealed to not be natural mutants and were instead ordinary children who were experimented on by the High Evolutionary.

The two were originally associated with the Romani couple Django and Marya Maximoff, but were then later identified as the biological children of the Golden Age heroes the Whizzer and Miss America. However, this too was later changed when the revelation that Magneto and Magda were their parents made them biological siblings of Polaris. Yet, a 2014 retcon severed their biological connection to Magneto entirely.

Instead, they were revealed to not be natural mutants and were instead ordinary children who were experimented on by the High Evolutionary. Beyond their origins, their children’s origins are just as complex. Wanda’s sons, Speed and Wiccan, were born of reality-warping magic and fragments of Mephisto’s soul who eventually return through reincarnation. Pietro also has a daughter, Luna, with the Inhuman royal Crystal, which was unheard of at the time.

Nightcrawler’s origins have undergone several significant revisions, making Kurt Wagner’s biological family tree incredibly complicated. For decades, Mystique was established as his mother, while his father was identified as Baron Christian Wagner and the demonic mutant Azazel. However, a later revelation fundamentally changed the explanation behind his birth.

In 2023, X-Men Blue: Origins restored writer Chris Claremont’s original intentions for the character by revealing that Destiny was Kurt’s biological mother and Mystique his biological father. When Mystique used her shapeshifting abilities to take the form of a man, it also altered her genetic makeup, allowing her to impregnate Destiny using genetic material from both Azazel and Baron Wagner.

Professor Charles Xavier himself played a role in concealing the truth for decades by manipulating Mystique’s memories. Yet, beyond his parentage, Kurt’s extended family is just as tangled. His half-siblings include Graydon Creed, the son of Mystique and Sabertooth, and Raze Darkholme, Mystique’s son with Wolverine in an alternate future. Rogue also stands as his adoptive sister, having been raised by Mystique and Destiny, while Kurt himself grew up with an entirely separate foster family.

Scott Summers and Jean Grey have a particularly difficult family tree to follow because their partnership has produced several children across different timelines. Paired with clones and genetically engineered descendants, the two have a family tree that is far from ordinary, despite standing as the central couple in the franchise.

To start, Scott’s marriage to Madelyne Pryor, a clone of Jean created by Mister Sinister, resulted in the birth of Nathan Christopher Summers, better known as Cable. Nathan was ultimately sent to the future to survive a techno-organic virus and was later cloned himself, producing Stryfe, who would later go on to become his enemy. Cable also goes on to later adopt Hope Summers, adding another branch to the family tree.

There is also Rachel Summers, originating from the Days of Future Past timeline, who stands as the biological daughter of Scott and Jean, making her the biological sister of Nathan. Scott has also fathered other children, such as Ruby Summers, without Jean Grey, adding half-siblings to the already complex lineage and making their family history difficult to keep track of.

#3332. The 13 Best Christmas Movies of the Last 5 Years, Ranked

Christmas and the holiday season have proven to be a time-honored tradition and a great setting for several beloved and cheerful films that perfectly use the festivities to create timeless classics. It's become a staple of many households to put on some of the most iconic and beloved holiday films for the season, with a great number of highly memorable Christmas films to choose from. However, while it always works to put on a classic like Home Alone, National Lampoon's Christmas Vacation, and Elf, there are still a great number of holiday films being created during the modern era.

While it may seem like a Herculean task to create a modern Christmas film that can live up to the undeniable stature of the many classics, a few successfully create similar cozy feelings perfect for the season. While no Christmas film can attain the legacy and strengths of its predecessors, the best and most iconic Christmas films of the modern era act as a great addition to the zeitgeist of the holiday season on film.

Animated family Christmas films have been a long-lasting trend in holiday filmmaking for decades, with a wide array of different filmmakers utilizing the medium to bring to life feel-good stories of holiday cheer and whimsy. While That Christmas doesn't break the mold or stray too far from the traditional values of animated Christmas films past, its inherent earnestness, combined with an array of lovable vocal performances, makes it one of the most underrated animated holiday films of recent memory.

The film follows an array of different storylines that intertwine with one another, almost acting like an animated equivalent to Love Actually, another film written by acclaimed screenwriter Richard Curtis. Animation proves to work with this style of storytelling tremendously, especially when the connecting link that brings all of these stories together is a disastrous snowstorm that vastly alters everyone's individual holiday plans. While it may not be as iconic as Curtis's other holiday films, it certainly has the potential to be a hidden holiday gem of the modern era.

A goofy, musical comedy adaptation of the holiday classic A Christmas Carol, Spirited provides just the right amount of comic absurdism and charm to make for a compelling, modern rendition of the Dickens classic. The inherent chemistry and dynamic between Ryan Reynolds as a Scrooge-styled media consultant and Will Ferrell as the Ghost of Christmas Present is enough to make for a joyously fun comedic time. The musical aspects of the film also work surprisingly well, with the entire supporting cast able to bring the holiday spirit required to make its musical numbers so cheery and infectious.

While the film has been largely overlooked and overshadowed due to being an Apple TV original, it has slowly amassed a reputation as one of the more entertaining and approachable Christmas Carol adaptations of the modern era. Its inherent concept of the Scrooge-archetype character flipping the script of A Christmas Carol back onto the ghosts immediately distinguishes the film from other adaptations, giving it a niche that will help it considerably as time goes on.

One of many prominent comedies from director Michael Showalter, Oh. What. Fun. sets itself up as a Christmas movie playing to the appeals and struggles of mothers, specifically mothers who are not thanked or appreciated for the work they put into the family. Michelle Pfeiffer in the leading role plays this perfectly, as she plays a family matriarch who is fed up with her family after being left home alone, deciding to set off on her own adventure and leaving her family scrambling to find her.

While Pfeiffer herself is the major draw and strength of the film, it's the comedic chemistry and dynamic of the entire supporting cast that makes Oh. What. Fun. such an engaging modern Christmas film. The likes of Denis Leary, Felicity Jones, Dominic Sessa, Jason Schwarzman, and Chloë Grace Moretz each add their own signature charms and strengths to make this one of the most memorable Christmas movies of the streaming era.

One of several successful parody slashers from writer Michael Kennedy, best known for his work writing Freaky and Heart Eyes, It's a Wonderful Knife brings the energy and scares of a horror slasher to the base premise of the all-time Christmas classic It's a Wonderful Life. The film sees a young teen (Jane Widdop) still reeling from the pain and trauma of having saved her town from a psychotic killer on Christmas Eve. However, when she wishes that she were never born, she ends up transported to a parallel world where the killings never stopped and have gone on non-stop for a full year.

While a lot of the film hinges on the ingenuity and intrigue of its wild parody premise, there are a lot of inherent strengths that help give the film its own identity beyond simply being a cheesy parody. Most notably is the hilariously over-the-top villain performance from Justin Long, who, complete with a goofy high-pitched Southern accent, steals the show. The film also doesn't shy away from brazen and openly LGBTQ+ themes and characters, being much more accepting than the average slasher or Christmas film.

Even just describing the plot of the film simply doesn't do justice to Hot Frosty's chaotic and absurdist nature, as it's the type of wild, nonsensical experience that simply needs to be seen to be believed. The film follows a young widow living painfully alone during the holiday season before unexpectedly bringing an attractive, male model snowman to life with a magic scarf. She finds herself doing her best not just to make sure the snowman doesn't get into trouble, but also keeping her feelings in check as he slowly but surely begins to warm her heart.

Taking the mythos and fantasy concepts of the holiday season and creating a massive blockbuster experience with a $250 million budget out of it, Red One is arguably the first film that comes to mind for general audiences when considering memorable holiday films of the past few years. This Dwayne Johnson and Chris Evans-led blockbuster made waves by initially releasing in theaters in early November before having a massive streaming release right in time for the holiday season.

It certainly does a good job of replicating the feel and energy of a modern blockbuster, seamlessly implementing classic Christmas elements and transforming them for modern, digital-technology times. The action comedy strives for mass appeal above all else, playing to the strengths of its leading stars and certainly having fun in its execution as they deal with the goofiness of Christmas magic on a massive blockbuster scale.

Not for the faint of heart, even for die-hard horror fans, Terrifier 3 brings the same level of shockingly gruesome gore and violence that the previous films provided, yet with the added texture and energy of the holiday season. The film fully commits to the iconography and energy of the holiday season, whether it be through Art dressing up as Santa for a large chunk of his kills or using holiday-themed weaponry to create maximum carnage. It builds upon the chaos and energy of previous entries to make for a gruesomely good time, although it's definitely the type of Christmas film not meant to be watched by the whole family.

Terrifier 3 is easily at its best when it allows Art to play into the madness and absurdity of holiday slashers as a whole, even when many of his antics are absolutely sickening and abhorrent to watch unfold. While many simply won't be able to handle the overwhelming gore and sadistic pain that the film presents, it's a shockingly good time for those who are accustomed to this style of gruesome slasher. As far as modern holiday horror films are concerned, Terrifier 3 easily stands above the rest as the most entertaining and sickening of them all.

Four Netflix characters, four completely different ways of showing up for somebody. This is the one who fits how you actually do friendship, and what having them in your life would be like.

You do not do friendship at half volume, and neither does he. What you want is somebody who says yes to the plan before you have finished describing the plan.

You are the friend who makes things happen, and so is she. Together you would be mildly exhausting to everyone around you and completely delighted with yourselves.

You have no patience for pleasant lies, and she has no ability to tell them. What looks like coldness from the outside is the most reliable friendship on this list.

You look after whoever is having the worst day. So does he. It is the least strategic way to move through the world and the best possible quality in a friend.

A short yet sweet side story in the MCU, The Guardians of the Galaxy Holiday Special sees Drax and Mantis setting out on a mission to make this Christmas unforgettable for Quill. The team heads off to Earth in search of the perfect present, but Earth proves to be a challenge to the hapless duo, leading to a great deal of chaotic Christmas mischief.

Despite its short runtime of less than an hour, The Guardians of the Galaxy Holiday Special makes use of every available moment, filled with all the classic comedic greatness that the trilogy is so beloved for. It's a testament to the chemistry and dynamic between the Guardians as a whole and just how well they can adapt comedically to any situation, as they make a surprisingly perfect fit for holiday festivities. Its short runtime also makes it incredibly rewatchable, an easy and cozy film to have to put on and let loose for a while.

Violent Night sees a team of mercenaries break into a wealthy family's compound on Christmas Eve and take everyone inside hostage. However, the unthinkable happens, as Santa Claus finds himself on the premises in the middle of delivering presents. After the young child of the family calls out for Santa's help, he makes it his duty to go from nice to naughty and show the mercenaries a taste of their own medicine.

Action movies and Christmas go surprisingly hand in hand more often than not, especially for those who consider Die Hard a Christmas film. Violent Night fully commits to the comedic premise of "John Wick but with Santa Claus," with the perfect balance of silly hijinks and exhilarating action to make the film a cheerful blast to watch. Especially for those who are tired of the safer and wholesome energy that overwhelms the season, Violent Night provides enough high-octane brutality and action to bring joy to any Grinch's heart.

There really isn't an experience quite like a holiday get-together with extended family, as this charming gathering of beloved family members over sweets, games, and presents is all sorts of comforting, but has a hint of isolation in the most unlikely of places. It's this unique feeling and energy that Christmas Eve in Miller's Point seamlessly recaptures in its execution, showing both the beauty and the difficulties of the holiday with family in its own melancholy way.

The indie dramedy film certainly isn't as approachable as a traditional Christmas comedy, as it doesn't strive to have a major overarching plot, instead showing a scatterplot of moments and characters interacting with one another during the holiday season. However, in a way, this adds to the beauty of the film, because family get-togethers are never about linear stories, but are instead embraced and remembered for the feelings that they conjure up in us, and in that way, this film succeeds with flying colors.

#3330. From ‘Disclosure Day’ to ‘Devil Wears Prada’: Emily Blunt Breaks Down 10 of Her Greatest Movie Moments

Jimmy Stewart once said that with movies, it’s key moments that people remember.

Emily Blunt, who’s on the circuit these days talking about her standout role as a language-spouting meteorologist in Steven Spielberg’s “Disclosure Day,” gave me some memorable scenes that she will never forget from her wide-ranging filmography. (We spoke on Zoom.)

Clearly, Blunt can deliver in any genre: romance, comedy, musical, sci-fi, action, thriller, drama. So far, Blunt has notched one Oscar nomination, for Supporting Actress in Christopher Nolan’s bio-drama “Oppenheimer.” Sci-fi thriller “Disclosure Day” could score Blunt’s first Best Actress nod. (More below.) Related Stories How Sound Design Helps ‘Minotaur’ Get Away with Murder Super Bowl LXI to Play Live on IMAX Screens

1. “My Summer of Love” (2005, Pawel Pawlikowski) was Blunt’s first movie role. “I remember the wildness of that Edith Piaf dance [‘La Foule’], where I have the cigarette dangling out of my mouth, and she’s trying to romanticize this girl from the wrong side of town and sophisticate her. I remember the scene with Paddy Considine where she tries to seduce him and then she laughs at him. I will never forget the energy in that room and how Paddy was in that scene. I have taken what Pawel taught me about ambiguity and reality on camera, and I have used it throughout my career. I am an untrained actor. I don’t have anything technical to fall back on, but the aliveness that he created on ‘My Summer of Love’ was informative for how I moved forward: what lies beneath the character. You know what the front foot is, and what is the shadow of that person? What’s really going on?”

2. “The Devil Wears Prada“ (2006, David Frankel) marked Blunt’s Hollywood breakout as Miranda Priestley’s beleaguered first assistant Emily Charlton. After she gets hit by a taxi, second assistant Andy Sachs (Anne Hathaway) visits her hospital room. Charlton is angry and tearful at everything she is missing. “The hospital scene makes me laugh because that’s really who she is: this completely broken down, vulnerable, insecure person.”

3. “The Young Victoria” (2010, Jean-Marc Vallée) gave Blunt a queen to embody. “I remember the scene where she asks [Prince] Albert to marry her, because he was not allowed to ask her. She is the monarch, and had to be the one to ask. That scene was so vulnerable and beautifully twinkly, how Jean-Marc shot that.”

4. “The Adjustment Bureau,” a romantic sci-fi thriller, co-starred Matt Damon. “I remember never being able to get through a scene with Matt Damon without laughing. But I did love the scene in the bathroom where they meet. That scene had to sparkle because otherwise you don’t care about them, and you don’t care about them using their magical fedoras to get back to each other. Matt Damon doesn’t know how to be bad. That’s the truth. He doesn’t know how to play a false note. There is something about what Matt does, and he’s so dexterous in his humanity, but I don’t feel it’s technical with Matt. He’s like a laser beam of truth, and I feel myself, anyone who watches him, they ease back and they go, ‘Oh, thank God, Matt Damon’s here.’ He just leads with the truth. He’s like Josh Brolin. They only know how to be honest, and so they have such humanity to them. That’s why you can’t take your eyes off them. John [Krasinski] and I were so proud of what Matt did [with “The Odyssey”]. It’s obviously the most Herculean undertaking, but he grounded everything with that performance.”

5. “Edge of Tomorrow” (2014, Doug Liman) co-starred Tom Cruise and thrust Blunt into action mode for the first time. Her moment was a war scene set on a beach. “It was the beach set, and we started calling it ‘the bitch’ because it was such a nightmare. That set was always flooded. You were always exposed to terrible elements of the weather, freezing, and we shot that beach scene for a month. Tom Cruise gave me a lot of flowers on that one. He was so good to me, and he revealed halfway through the shoot that this was the deep end of action for him— this was the most challenging action movie that he had ever done, and it was my first action movie, so I was flung in at the deep end of action. But we held each other through that. I loved athletics when I was a kid, and then couldn’t be bothered to work out, and then thought I knew what working out was, and then I realized I didn’t know what working out was until I started training for ‘Edge of Tomorrow,’ and that was a transformational thing to my body. She needed to look lethal, absolutely lethal. And so it helped me a lot, doing all of that physicality.”

6. “Into the Woods” (2014, Rob Marshall), adapted from Stephen Sondheim’s stage musical, boasted a huge ensemble cast; Blunt played the baker’s wife opposite James Corden. “‘Moments in the Woods,’ that big song she has right before she gets squished by the giant. She’s weighing up the duality of life, whether she goes for this poetic interlude in her prosaic life or if she goes back to the prosaic life. That kind of agony that she’s going through in the song was cool. I had I’d never sung in front of anyone before, really, other than one small TV thing years ago. I didn’t even want to audition for it, and Rob Marshall said, ‘Look, I’m not looking for singers who can kind of act. I’m looking for actors who can kind of sing,’ and that was great advice. I said it to my 12-year-old this morning as she went off to her musical audition at school. I said, ‘Don’t worry about the notes; just tell us a story. That’s it. That’s what the song should be, and that’s what will make it sound amazing.'”

7. “Sicario” (2015, Denis Villeneuve) plops Blunt’s straight-arrow FBI agent into a violent Mexican border scenario. “The scene that stands out for me is a spellbinding one, when Benicio del Toro comes to my apartment, and he puts the gun to my face and forces me to sign the contract. It’s right at the end of the movie, and I think that scene holds a special place for me because we were not sure about the scene that was written by Taylor Sheridan. It didn’t feel like it belonged in what we were trying to achieve between the characters. We wanted to change it a little bit. It was an idea that Benicio had. We were racking our brains as to how to finish this scene and this moment between the two characters. He always has so many crazy ideas, and he will have some absolute bangers in there. And he called me at about 11 o’clock the night before, and he goes, ‘I think I have it. What about this?’ And I said, ‘That is a great idea, because you’ve got this very idealistic FBI agent who’s pulled into this incoherent, amoral world. And she’s being forced to sign a contract that says everything they did was aboveboard, and that’s like a death to a character like that.’ We rehearsed that scene for two hours. Denis loved it, and then we all turned to [cinematographer] Roger Deakins: “Roger, what do you think?” And he gave his slow nod of approval, and then we shot it, and it was so.”

8. “A Quiet Place” (2018, John Krasinski) was Blunt’s first experience being directed by her husband. The memorable moment: giving birth in the bathtub as a killer monster hovers nearby, listening for any noise. “We shot that whole sequence from the water breaking in the bathtub in order, which I was grateful to John for. It took four days. We did two takes of that bathtub scene because he shot it mainly as a oner. It starts as the blood’s trickling out, and it comes up, and you see the creature, and then it goes into that scream, and then the fireworks go off, but yeah, it’s a wild scene. It’s really smart to have a baby in a silent world. Every woman I’ve spoken to about that scene, they go: ‘Oh my God, that scene made me cross my legs.” And I was: ‘Okay, all right.'”

9. “Oppenheimer” (2023, Christopher Nolan) offered Blunt a constrained role as Kitty, the recessive wife of the great physicist (Cillian Murphy). Blunt agreed that the scene that earned her the Oscar nomination was in the courtroom where she is badgered by the formidable Jason Clarke. “I knew that was the monster scene. When I read the script, I thought, ‘What an extraordinary scene, that you have this person staggering in, looking like a liability,’ and Chris had written that she almost chokes, and you think she’s going to blow it. When I talked to him about it after I read the script, I said, ‘What a reclamation that scene is of that extraordinary brain coming back to life.’ The brain that had gone crazy at the ironing board, probably meant for bigger things than being someone’s wife and someone’s mummy, and I had a great deal of empathy for her and a lot of women who went crazy at the ironing board. She owns Jason Clarke in a way, and you realize she could probably run circles around him. He played such a wonderful bully in that film, but we saw what Meryl [Streep] did with Miranda Priestley: There’s such power in quiet, great, great power and great dignity.”

10. “The Devil Wears Prada 2” (2026, David Frankel) allowed Blunt to indulge Charlton’s excesses. “We all had scenery stuck in our teeth on that one. It was so fun to go back to playing that lunatic. My favorite scene was the funeral scene where she comes in and rants about Dolce and Gabbana. It was such a ludicrous outfit to be wearing to a funeral. Anne Hathaway is the most unstoppable force. And what a wide range of roles she has access to. I feel this moment in her life. She’s in this full wingspan of being able to harness everything she can do and everything she has to offer, and I can’t believe she had the year she just did, and she was pregnant!”

“Disclosure Day” (2026, Steven Spielberg) leaned on Blunt to carry the sci-fi thriller. “The four-and a-half minute oner in the beginning when she arrives at the news station. I’ve seen what Steven Spielberg can do visually, his visual prowess is rather unparalleled. So to be in a oner that he conjures up on the day, that happened spontaneously — he was planning on covering it. And I said, ‘what would help me so much is if you could let me whirlwind out of control in one take from the moment I pull up, going into the makeup room, coming out speaking Korean, she’s in this incoherent tailspin, and then you see her disintegrate over the course of it. And she gets up there to deliver the weather, and she starts to speak in the alien language. Can we just try it as a oner, just for me to see where I’ve got to get to?’ And he watched me do it. And by the time I got up there to do the weather, my legs were shaking. I was out of breath, beside myself, and he loved it. And he goes, ‘We’re going to do it as a oner.’ And we were done by 2 pm. because he planned to shoot it all day. It was Steven in his element of going, ‘Oh, I see it’ and not only was he intentional about creating the environment for me to be able to do that so he didn’t overcover it, he saw a cinematic advantage.”

Blunt plays several characters in one. “All the stuff in the childhood home was deeply moving because that also dealt with that moment where the character goes from crisis to serenity and the ability to then deploy these powers rather than be puppeteered by them. So I loved that shape-shift in the character, like playing two people throughout the course of this film. And the other moment that felt so human to me was the panic attack in the box car after the train sequence, and she’s at max capacity, bubbling over, overwhelmed, and a few people, including myself on set, had experienced panic attacks, and that felt like a real reaction to someone who was utterly overwhelmed. That also felt so Spielbergian: no one’s a slick elite action hero in Steven’s films. Everyone’s afraid. Everyone, including Indiana Jones, everyone’s scared. That hand that’s shaking on the way to Omaha Beach, that is trauma. He can relate to your vulnerabilities. Everyone’s a bit over their head, and in a different action movie, me and Josh O’Connor would have dropped in the boxcar and gone, ‘Whoa, that was crazy.’ And instead, she has a panic attack. I got them a lot in my early twenties, and Steven’s not immune, neither is Josh. All of us have experienced that. That moment where he takes my hands and he puts them on the piano and he goes, ‘This is real. This is real. Feel this. I’m here. You’re here. We’re here.’ I’ve done that. So it just was like, ‘Oh my God!’ You get to sublimate what you’ve experienced into this creative art form sometimes. That’s the great gift often on movies.”

The languages were right in Blunt’s wheelhouse. She has always loved languages. She learned them two to three months before the start of the shoot. “I learned those scenes. The first thing I learned was the Russian and the Korean, because I wanted it to be spoken at such a velocity that it sounded as conversational as it does as me speaking to you right now, and she doesn’t know she’s speaking Russian,” she said. “She thinks she’s speaking English. You have someone who is white-knuckling their way through most of this film, and these forms of mind control are unconscious to her in the beginning, it’s compulsive.”

Next up: “Walk the Blue Fields” directed by John Crowley and co-starring Andrew Scott as another hot priest, Father Joe, presiding at a wedding. “It’s a short story that I bought the rights to about six years ago by Claire Keegan. If you’ve ever read any of her short stories, they’re like laser beams. They’re so wonderful. My sister Felicity is a book agent. She represents Claire, and she sent it to me. Story A is a wedding day, and story B is what led up to that wedding and why everything is starting to unravel on the wedding day. And it plays like a thriller,” she said. “She’s coming back to Ireland to try to build a relationship with her Irish father [Ciaran Hinds] after they’ve been estranged for years, and it’s a story about identity and religion and love. Andrew Scott has to be one of the most beautiful actors I’ve ever shared a scene with.”

And, of course, John Krasinski’s upcoming “Quiet Place 3,” which co-stars Jack O’Connell, Cillian Murphy, Jason Clarke and Noah Jupe, is shrouded in secrecy. “I don’t want to blow John’s cover here,” she said. And “Sicario 3” is also moving forward with the original cast, a script by James Bond writer Steven Knight and director Padraic McKinley.

#3329. Six Things You Should Do Now to Optimize Your Setup for GTA 6

You’re almost ready for Grand Theft Auto VI. You’ve preloaded the game on your console, you’ve taken the next month off work, and you’ve locked your phone in a Faraday cage and set it adrift at sea. You’re prepared to lock in, and you haven’t forgotten a thing…right? Well, just to make sure, here are the most important tips to optimize your setup before you fire up the most anticipated game of the decade.

GTA 6 is absurdly large. According to Rockstar, you’ll need up to 212GB of storage space. For high-end consoles like the PS5 Pro, that’s more than 10% of the available storage space, and close to half the space on the more budget-conscious Xbox Series S. There’s a good chance you’ll have to delete something to make room.

Alternatively, it’s pretty easy to add more storage (if you can afford it). External SSDs are probably the cheapest route, though you’ll want to make sure to use a high-speed USB cable to connect it. It’s even worth shopping around for alternate models of SSD. For example, at the time of writing, the popular 2TB WD_BLACK external drive was close to $200, but the exact same drive in pink was $132.

You can also directly upgrade the storage of your console with expansion drives. The Xbox Series X|S supports proprietary expansion cards, while the PS5 and PS5 Pro can accept most M.2 internal SSDs. These will generally be faster, since they plug directly into the console via higher-speed connections than a drive hooked up via USB.

Let’s face it: Half the fun of any sandbox game is the weird, unique stuff that happens to only you. So you’re probably going to be hitting that “record recent gameplay” button more often than usual. While you’re cleaning up your storage space (or adding more), make sure to account for all the video clips you might want to save.

File size of video clips depends on a lot of factors, but 4K recordings can generally take up to 0.5GB per minute of footage. You can cut that down by saving footage in 1080p instead, but either way you’ll want to leave a little extra space.

Game footage is also a pretty good place to look if you need to make room on your console and don’t want to delete any games. Be honest with yourself: You don’t need all those clips from Horizon Forbidden West you saved four years ago. Dive into the settings on your console and find the biggest media files you forgot you even had on there.

According to Rockstar, GTA 6 will be targeting 30fps across consoles at launch, which is pretty low as modern AAA games go. Part of the reason for that is all the processing power going to rendering a complex environment, but it also means you won’t need a fancy high frame rate TV or monitor any time soon to get the most out of it. Still, it couldn’t hurt to check a few settings on your display.

First, make sure you’re using a higher refresh rate than 30Hz. While the game is targeting 30fps, it is technically capable of more, so if your console can keep up, you don’t want to accidentally bottleneck your frames. This setting will vary by device, so check the manual that came with your screen.

Also, make sure you have HDR enabled on your hardware. There’s a good chance this is already turned on for your TV, but sometimes other devices can switch display modes if they only support SDR. The game will help you calibrate your HDR settings for GTA 6 specifically when you launch it, but only if it detects HDR compatibility in the first place.

If you’re planning to buy a console specifically for GTA 6, this might be one of those rare instances where a PS5 Pro really is worth the upgrade. According to Rockstar, certain features like ray-traced shadows will only be available on the Pro version of Sony’s console.

More importantly, the PS5 Pro version supports PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (or PSSR), which upscales lower-resolution images to get better detail and higher frame rates out of the same hardware. Given that GTA 6 is already starting at a meager target of 30fps on most consoles, anything that can give your frame rate a boost is probably going to feel like a welcome improvement over the baseline.

I’ll tell you a secret as someone who’s spent a lot of time testing different game controllers: Most of the time, you really don’t need an expensive “elite” controller. Most of the time. I don’t buy into the idea that a taller control stick is going to make you an esports athlete. It can be nice to have, but it’s not a game changer. What does matter is customizing your controls, especially for long gaming sessions.

The DualSense Edge wireless controller is a favorite of mine, mainly because of the rear paddles and adjustable triggers. The former lets you map any button to a rear lever that you can access with your fingers underneath the controller, which can often ease some of the wrist strain of awkward button combos. And the adjustable triggers let you activate the buttons with less motion, again reducing repetitive stress.

The Xbox Elite Series 2 controller has similar features for the Xbox, as well as custom caps for the D-pad. Both consoles’ versions of pro controllers are more expensive than the standard ones, but if you’re planning to game for many hours, it can be worth it to get a controller that’s more comfortable for you.

If you have an Xbox One, you don’t necessarily have to upgrade your console to play GTA 6, but you might want to take a look at your network. GTA 6 will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming on day one, and you’ll be able to stream the game to an Xbox One console (as long as you purchase Cloud playtime as well or get some with your Game Pass subscription). This is the only way to play on a console older than the current generation, so if you don’t want to shell out for new hardware, this might be your best bet.

Xbox recommends a minimum of a 20Mbps connection to run cloud gaming, but more is obviously better. If you can connect your console to a wired Ethernet connection, that would be better and provide more stability. If you can’t connect a cable, then at least make sure you’re well within range of your wifi router, and try to limit any other bandwidth-hogging applications on the network while you’re playing.

#3328. PlayStation Plus Officially Makes 10/10 2005 PS2 Masterpiece 100% Free

Fans of classic shooters won't want to miss this new addition to the PlayStation Plus catalog. The late 90s and early 2000s gave us classics like the Nintendo 64's GoldenEye 007 and Perfect Dark. These have remained some of the best shooters (and games, in general) of all time, according to many fans and critics.

I'm talking about TimeSplitters, the time-traveling first-person shooter that served as a spiritual successor to Perfect Dark and GoldenEye 007. The first TimeSplitters title was developed in 2000 by Free Radical Design, a team which was made up of developers who'd worked on both the other two titles. The studio was founded in 1999 by former Rare devs who left the larger studio while work was ongoing for Perfect Dark.

Free Radical Design brought their experience and ideas to the creation of TimeSplitters, which can be felt in everything from the overall feel of the game to its combat and storytelling. The first game was released as an exclusive PlayStation 2 launch title.

It introduced the titular TImeSplitters, odd beings that travel through time and alter human history. The game is told through the point of view of multiple characters between 1935 and 2035, similarly to the cult classic Eternal Darkness, which was released two years later. Throughout the years, the characters you follow set out to complete their own agendas, but are foiled at every turn by the interfering TimeSplitters.

The second game, released two years later, continued the story and freed the PlayStation exclusive, expanding it to the Xbox and GameCube. It dove deeper into the lore and set up several characters and a story that led into the third and most recent addition to the PlayStation Plus Premium games catalog: TimeSplitters: Future Perfect.

The 2005 TimeSplitters: Future Perfect was the third and final game in the TimeSplitters saga. This was by far the most story-rich of the three games, exploring the titular time-leaping creatures and their origins. The title also lets players interact with their own past and future selves, taking the idea of time-travel a step further.

The game continues right after the end of TimeSplitters 2, with space marine Sergeant Cortez crash-landing on Earth in the future. Cortez sets out to stop the TimeSplitters from interfering with the world and dooming it. And to do so, he has to travel back in time in order to save the future.

TimeSplitters: Future Perfect completes the trilogy and resolves a lot of the questions left unanswered by the previous two games. You could technically play the third game without the previous two. But since all three are available for free, it's worth at least checking out TimeSplitters 2 before Future Perfect, since the third game is a direct sequel to the previous title.

The trilogy arrived on modern consoles—the PS4 and PS5—when it was re-released in 2024 as PS2 Classics. The games now include some quality-of-life upgrades like faster loading times, trophies, and a rewind feature. Future Perfect also originally included online co-op for long-distance gaming, but this is no longer supported.

All three games feature arcade-style first-person combat, a map creator, a multiplayer "Arcade" mode, and the ability to play through the game in local co-op. They offer fans of classic shooters a chance to revisit the origin of the modern shooter through these timeless classics.

A fourth game was in development more recently, but unfortunately, we'll never get to see it: development was canceled in 2023 when Free Radical, then owned by Deep Silver, shut its doors for good. Luckily, the three existing games are still available to experience, and now you can do so for free thanks to the PlayStation classics PS Plus catalog.

TimeSplitters, TimeSplitters 2, and TimeSplitters: Future Perfect are all now available to play for free with a PlayStation Plus Premium subscription.

#3326. HBO's 8-Part Thriller Masterpiece Is Aging Like Fine Wine

Certain franchise TV shows suffer from longevity for a variety of reasons, but an eight-episode thriller on HBO is the complete opposite. The ever-increasing investment in shared universes has sometimes led to disappointing end products, especially those that rely far too much on tying to wider narratives or character arcs. For instance, several MCU TV shows have had this issue, be it Echo's reliance on characters from Netflix's Marvel shows or She-Hulk's attempts to explore the franchise in a meta way.

Still, there are others that age well. HBO, in particular, is a studio that has several examples of this; The recent Lanterns, despite the DC Universe's future now being in doubt, is one of HBO's best sci-fi shows and is a self-contained story that doesn't require wider viewing. This is just one example of HBO's ability to produce TV shows that work in their own right, despite being part of a wider universe. However, even Lanterns could age poorly, given James Gunn's recent exit from DC Studios.

Conversely, one HBO show that is aging like fine wine is an eight-part story that still exists within a wider continuity, but operates as a concise, well-written, utterly compelling thriller with its own narrative themes and weight. That show is The Penguin, 2024's spin-off of Matt Reeves' The Batman. The Penguin exists within Reeves' Batman Epic Crime Saga, but it works on its own, meaning it doesn't rely on The Batman, its upcoming sequel, or any other entries in the franchise.

This alone renders The Penguin a show that will age well, as it could be watched 10 years from now with no prior viewing and still work as an excellent, character-driven thriller. Beyond that, though, The Penguin will avoid the aforementioned issue with some shared universe entries, as it doesn't need the wider franchise to succeed. With all of the uncertainty surrounding DC at the moment, shows tied to the wider narrative like Lanterns or, in an even more extreme case, Peacemaker, may see lingering threads fizzle out. As its own entity, however, The Penguin will age well with or without the wider DC franchise.

The future of DC being so unsettled raises questions about The Batman - Part III, while Part II remains plagued with production issues. The latter recently paused production due to Matt Reeves' personal issues, with Steven Soderbergh taking over to finish filming. This indicates The Batman - Part II will still be released in February 2028, but the impending shake-up at DC could mean the planned third installment will not happen, especially with Reeves facing so many issues making the second movie.

When looking at The Penguin, it will not matter whether The Batman franchise continues after Part II. The tight, eight-episode narrative wraps everything up perfectly, with only the subtle hints and Easter eggs to the events of The Batman being woven into it effortlessly, without any need to know the context. Moreover, The Batman - Part II is not expected to feature the character of Oz Cobb all that extensively, meaning The Penguin will only continue to age well, no matter the fate of its wider franchise.

All of this just proves that The Penguin nailed how to be part of a shared universe, only as its own spin-off. As alluded to, some franchises fail to find this balance, with even some of Marvel's better-rated shows, like Ms. Marvel, being essential viewing before The Marvels or, presumably, the upcoming Avengers: Secret Wars. The Penguin, on the other hand, feels like its own thing. Yes, it has connections to The Batman, but the central character arcs and wider narrative are not directly impacted by the movie, nor does it set up any sequels with lingering plot threads.

The Penguin can still tie into future stories, should they so wish to be constructed as a sequel of sorts. Still, it remains the case that this will be a decision of different filmmakers, as opposed to The Penguin's creative team actively writing the show to tie it to future stories. Instead, The Penguin was constructed to be its own entity, with its own unique story, characters, and eight-episode narrative.

#3325. The Best Visual Effects in ‘Wildwood’ Are the Ones You Can’t See — Watch

There are all sorts of magic worlds waiting to be discovered in the stop-motion epic “Wildwood,” but it’s a credit to the film that one of them is Portland, Oregon. Laika Studio’s Head of CG Animation Benoit Dubuc was involved early and often in order to determine what would be shot practically by the stop-motion animation team and what CG effects would be used to achieve. Even in the most mundane and ordinary moments of the film question of either/or. It was one of how the collaboration between different kinds of animation would work.

“We mostly shoot two or three puppets at a time, so any time that there’s background characters, they’re gonna be digital,” Dubuc said during IndieWire’s Craft Roundtable on visual effects. He pointed out that when Baby Mac gets kidnapped by a murder of crows under the command of the dread sorceress Alexandra (Carey Mulligan), the amount of work to achieve that moment fully through stop-motion would mean they’d probably still be animating it. Related Stories From ‘Disclosure Day’ to ‘Devil Wears Prada’: Emily Blunt Breaks Down 10 of Her Greatest Movie Moments How Sound Design Helps ‘Minotaur’ Get Away with Murder

“We’ll often get [animators] to produce some practical work to lead the visual effects work. We built a crow puppet to spec. We didn’t animate it in the film, but it informed the visual effects work. We try to stay away from simulations as much as possible, knowing that what we’re chasing is something that feels handmade and something that is slightly imperfect,” Dubuc said.

That goes for individual characters and for the vibrant backgrounds of “Wildwood” alike. “The audience would think that we built sets the size of an airport hangar with a hundred thousand practical puppets running downhill. It’s not possible,” Dubuc said. The fact that it looks possible, in both the most intricate battle sequences and the ordinary chaos of biking past Powell’s Books, means that the VFX team has done its job. “ The portrayal of Portland that we were striving for is a beautiful, vibrant city,” Dubuc said.

Black Friday is usually a great time to grab a new e-reader, but the ongoing RAM crisis has made that a question mark this year: Amazon recently raised the prices of all its Kindles by around $50 and refreshed the entire lineup, which means your odds of grabbing one at a big discount are low. But you aren't totally out of luck: If you haven't noticed, micro-e-readers—I'm talking credit card-sized, with screens that measure around four inches—are all the rage in 2026, and right now, you can pick up one of them for around $55.

If you too can see the appeal of carrying all of your books with you on a device so small you'll forget it's even in your pocket, it's a great time to jump in: The recently released Xteink X4 Classic is currently 38% off for Black Friday, bringing it down to $54.87, a record-low price. Meanwhile, the smaller X3 is $55.72, or 19% off. Both are available in either "mist grey" or "space black." The discounts should last through the end of Cyber Monday on Nov. 30.

Xteink is a Chinese startup that shook up the e-reading world last year with the launch of the X4, a super bare-bones device that made up for its lack of features and usability with a cheap sub-$70 price point. Since then, a huge online community of fans has formed, sharing tips on Reddit and even coming together to crowdsource an alternate operating system that fixed a lot of early problems. Xteink quickly followed up the X4 with a slate of other devices, including the 3.7-inch X3 and the X4 Pro, which adds a front light and touchscreen (at the cost of screen clarity and two physical buttons).

The X4 Classic and the X3 improve on the original X4 with quality-of-life upgrades like a larger battery, relocated page-turn buttons, a real-time clock, and a tilt-to-turn-page feature. They're also lighter and thinner than the X4, though there is a trade-off involved: They drop the USB-C charging port in favor of magnetic pogo pins that require a separate adapter (included).

These upgrades also increased the cost: The X4 Classic typically retails for $89, $20 more than the discontinued X4 and only $10 less than the X4 Pro, while the X3 launched at $79. But right now, the X4 Classic is just under $55, or around 38% off, and the X3 is about a dollar more. Either is a great option for those who prioritize crisp, readable text above the conveniences of a built-in light or touchscreen, as those add extra layers between the inner screen and outer glass. It's also important to understand what you're getting into: These devices support only e-books without Digital Rights Management (DRM), which means you can't use it to read your existing library of Kindle books. On the plus side, there's no longer a need to worry about flashing new firmware if you don't want to, as the native version has been totally overhauled and is now one of your best options (though the new firmware, called "Licorice," isn't available on the X3 quite yet).

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

No. If you find the product you're looking for with a major discount right now, get it. It's not likely to drop any lower, but it could always run out of stock. Take advantage of price matching or guarantees instead of waiting. Remember, you can always return products later if you change your mind. For the majority of products, the deal from Black Friday will be the same one on Cyber Monday.

#3323. 8 Most Confusing Sci-Fi Books of All Time, Ranked

If it isn't mind-melting, it isn't sci-fi. Over the years, the science fiction genre has evolved beyond stories centered exclusively on science, often using scientific elements as a backdrop for deeply human experiences. However, sci-fi in its purest form puts science and its related fields at the forefront, exploring just how far humanity can push scientific boundaries. These ideas aren't always easy to grasp, and following the science behind it can be just as demanding as understanding the story itself.

Even the most dedicated sci-fi fans can struggle with meticulous prose, complex theories, and unconventional storytelling. Deciphering the themes is one thing, but making it through the entire book is a challenge in itself. From fragmented narratives that blur the line between reality and fiction to stories built around challenging mathematical reasoning, here are the most confusing sci-fi books of all time, ranked.

Set in the fictional American city of Bellona, Dhalgren follows a young man who arrives with no memories of himself, not even his name. Referred to as The Kid, he wanders through Bellona's streets, meets its eccentric residents, and gets involved with Lanya Colson, a woman living in a local commune. As he settles into this strange city, he begins experiencing bizarre events that blur the boundaries between time, identity, and reality.

Dhalgren's unusual literary style can take some getting used to. While Dhalgren isn't particularly difficult because of hard science or technical jargon, its fragmented, experimental prose can be confusing to follow. Readers are constantly thrown between incomplete thoughts, abstract observations, and sudden shifts in perspective. Much of the narration also follows a stream-of-consciousness style, making it hard to keep track of what's happening and differentiate between the Kid's mind and reality.

Set during the final days of World War II, Gravity's Rainbow follows American soldier Tyrone Slothrop, whose sexual encounters appear mysteriously connected to German V2 rocket strikes across London. When intelligence agencies discover this bizarre pattern, they begin monitoring him, pulling him into military conspiracies, psychological experiments, and secret Nazi research surrounding rocket technology.

Thomas Pynchon certainly doesn't skimp on characters, with the novel featuring hundreds of named individuals. Keeping track of who's who, figuring out which characters actually matter, and connecting their stories to the bigger picture can feel like homework. Still, Gravity's Rainbow has plenty of bizarre, hilarious moments to keep readers entertained, including Americans being forced to eat British candy. It's a wild ride, even when you have no idea what's going on.

Set across two different timelines, The Peripheral follows Flynne Fisher, a skilled gamer who witnesses a brutal murder while filling in for her brother on what she believes is a virtual-reality security job. Unbeknownst to her, the crime takes place in the distant future, where a London publicist named Wilf Netherton becomes entangled in a murder investigation that connects their two worlds through mysterious technological links.

If you enjoyed Netflix's Bodies, The Peripheral is an even bigger mind-bender. Besides juggling two seemingly unrelated timelines, the novel throws new characters and situations at readers without much explanation of who they are or why they matter. You're expected to figure out who's who while the plot keeps moving. William Gibson doesn't make things easier either, rarely stopping to explain what's going on.

Set on a dying Earth under a dimming red sun, The Book of the New Sun follows Severian, an apprentice torturer exiled from Nessus after showing mercy to a condemned prisoner. Armed with his executioner's sword, Terminus Est, he travels across a decaying world filled with ancient technology, strange creatures, and warring factions, slowly moving toward a destiny that could change humanity's future.

The confusing part starts with Gene Wolfe's writing style, which feels closer to 19th-century literature and is packed with obscure words that most readers won't recognize. Wolfe also describes futuristic technology using unfamiliar, old-fashioned terms. Even the appendices make it all the more confusing, presenting fictional translators' notes that claim the story was translated from a language that hasn't even come into existence yet.

Humanity's first encounter with extraterrestrial life doesn't exactly go as expected in Blindsight. Set in 2082, the novel follows five transhuman specialists sent aboard the spaceship Theseus to investigate a mysterious signal near the edge of the solar system. Their search leads them to Rorschach, a massive alien structure inhabited by creatures called Scramblers. Despite their intelligence, these beings show no signs of self-awareness, raising some pretty unsettling questions about life itself.

Peter Watts takes this strange discovery and turns it into a full-blown exploration of human consciousness. The novel gets particularly confusing when it starts challenging the very concept of consciousness, mixing complex neuroscience, evolutionary biology, and philosophical arguments into its alien encounters. The idea gets even harder to wrap your head around when the novel suggests that consciousness might actually hold humanity back.

Neal Stephenson's Anathem takes place on the planet Arbre, where scholars live in secluded monasteries called concents, dedicating their lives to science, philosophy, and mathematics. However, their untouched world is disrupted when an alien spacecraft appears in orbit. Fraa Erasmas, a young monk-in-training, joins his fellow scholars in investigating the mysterious visitors, only to discover that there's much more to their arrival than anyone expected.

The real brain workout comes from Stephenson's wild scientific ideas, which touch on consciousness, quantum physics, parallel universes, and alien civilizations. The novel also explores how mathematics might exist independently of the physical world and even shape reality. Between complicated theories, conflicting timelines, and multiple layers of existence, keeping track of what's actually happening can be a challenge.

Set in the 30th century, Diaspora imagines a future where humanity has moved far beyond its biological origins. Humans now share the world with artificial intelligences and digital minds living in simulated environments called "polises." When astronomers spot a cosmic disaster heading toward Earth, a group of physicists sets out to investigate.

It takes a serious amount of brainpower to keep up with Greg Egan's take on physics. Rather than sticking to established scientific theories, he introduces his own framework, called Kozuch Theory, to explain how particles work through some pretty unconventional ideas. The science gets increasingly difficult to wrap your head around as Egan introduces concepts that challenge everything readers know about how the universe works.

The Three-Body Problem opens during China's Cultural Revolution, when astrophysicist Ye Wenjie gets involved in a secret military project searching for extraterrestrial life. After receiving an unexpected message from an alien civilization on Trisolaris, she makes a decision that puts humanity’s future on the line. Centuries later, Earth discovers that an alien invasion is coming.

The science is already demanding enough, as Liu Cixin takes a classical physics concept and expands it into an extreme hypothesis. Imagine a planet caught between three suns, constantly shifting between extreme heat and freezing temperatures because of their unpredictable gravitational pull. The characters don't make things easier either. They're emotionally distant and often feel like vehicles for scientific discussions, with conversations that read more like lectures. Here's hoping the science and characters are easier to understand when the Netflix adaptation returns in January 2027.

#3320. Netflix's 6-Part Dystopian Series Is A Masterclass In Updating Classic Sci-Fi

While one of Netflix’s best dystopian sci-fi shows had a long and tricky road to the small screen, the investment was worth it in the end thanks to the show’s triumphant debut season. Sci-fi TV is currently enjoying a golden era in the 2020s. While the ‘90s had classics like The X-Files and Star Trek: The Next Generation, the advent of streaming services has opened up a whole new world of small-screen sci-fi storytelling.

On Apple TV alone, there is Invasion, Monarch: Legacy of Monsters, Foundation, Dark Matter, Severance, Murderbot, and the Colin Farrell vehicle Sugar, a high profile hit that doesn’t even reveal its sci-fi elements until an audacious plot twist midway through season 1. On Netflix, Stranger Things, Black Mirror, and 3 Body Problem have all expanded the possibilities of small-screen sci-fi’s scope and scale, while Hulu’s Margaret Atwood adaptation The Handmaid’s Tale managed to expand on the iconic novel's story without losing the show’s critical acclaim.

Not one to be outdone, Netflix offered viewers a dystopian adaptation of its own in early 2025, and this six-season season had a historically long and rocky road to the screen. Based on the classic 1957 comic book of the same name, The Eternaut is an Argentinian sci-fi show that follows a group of survivors navigating a sudden, catastrophic alien invasion of their home city of Buenos Aires.

Penned by Héctor Germán Oesterheld (HGO) and Francisco Solano López, the comic series El Eternauta was first published between 1957 and 1959. The comic follows a group of survivors in the aftermath of a deadly alien invasion, and the comic was remade in 1969 with a revision that made its political messaging more explicit. After HGO was disappeared by Argentina’s fascist government, the rights to his most influential work went to his widow.

There was a failed attempt to mount an animated adaptation of El Eternauta during HGO’s life, but only an expensive pilot of this proposed adaptation was ever produced. Despite plentiful interest in a potential movie adaptation, complex copyright issues and the author’s uncertainty about translating the story’s political allegories to an English-speaking, non-Argentinian context stalled any potential developments.

In the years that followed, the dystopian masterpiece The Eternaut was repeatedly almost adapted, only for various practicalities to stall its production. In 1995, a live-action miniseries was almost funded before it was abandoned, while, in 2007, The Headless Woman director Lucrecia Martel was hired to write a screenplay, only for producers to leave the project in limbo after over a year of development.

Finally, As Luck Would Have It director Álex de la Iglesia began working on an adaptation of The Eternaut in 2018 and, although this wasn’t the version viewers received from Netflix, its development kick-started the show that was finally released in 2025. Created by Pizza, biro, faso director Bruno Stagnaro, Netflix’s The Eternaut maintained de la Iglesia’s choice of leading man, Ricardo Darín, in role of Juan Salvo.

Perhaps emboldened by the critical success of HBO’s dystopian shows Station Eleven and The Last of Us, Netflix released The Eternaut to widespread critical acclaim in 2025. Although season 1 did depart from its source material with the addition of Ariel Staltari’s new character Omar, The Eternaut was still widely celebrated as a faithful and intelligent, but also enthralling and exciting adaptation of the seminal comic.

Now that HGO’s iconic comic has finally found its way to the screen, viewers of season 1 will be delighted to hear that the show will only go from strength to strength in its sophomore outing. Netflix renewed The Eternaut for a second season in May 2025, and the source material offers more answers to its many mysteries as its story continues.

#3319. AI Film ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ Deemed Ineligible by Academy for Best Animated Feature Oscar

“Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” an upcoming film from YouTuber Gossip Goblin that was made entirely with generated artificial intelligence, was deemed ineligible for the Best Animated Feature Oscar at the upcoming Academy Awards.

As IndieWire previously reported on “Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” which is the first fully AI movie to be released theatrically, the film had submitted for consideration and had planned FYC screenings alongside its theatrical release on December 4.

But the film was not included among the list of 38 animated films deemed eligible for this year’s Oscars that were announced Monday, November 23. IndieWire understands that the Academy’s Animation Branch Executive Committee determined “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” did not meet the Academy’s definition of an animated film under the rules for the 99th Awards. Related Stories The Best Visual Effects in ‘Wildwood’ Are the Ones You Can’t See — Watch From ‘Disclosure Day’ to ‘Devil Wears Prada’: Emily Blunt Breaks Down 10 of Her Greatest Movie Moments

Here’s the full rule as written that the Academy felt “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” did not satisfy:

An animated film is one in which characters or objects are given the illusion of life by having movement created for them, by any human means. While the crucial movement of a live-action motion picture is captured at speed, animation is the craft of human creation and manipulation of images to produce a performance from inanimate objects. At least 75 percent of the motion picture’s running time, without opening or end credits, must include animation of the primary subject or subjects. An animated feature has a running time of more than 40 minutes. Upon submission, filmmakers must provide information supporting how the motion picture qualifies as an animated film.

Edward Saatchi, a producer on “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” with Fable Studios, told IndieWire he and director Zack London (a.k.a. Gossip Goblin) plan to appeal the animation branch’s decision and cited the example of Richard Linklater’s rotoscoped film “Apollo 10 1/2,” which was originally deemed ineligible but saw the branch reverse its decision upon appeal. Saatchi said that the film, in addition to submitting for Best Animated Feature, also submitted in other categories such as Best Director, Adapted Screenplay, VFX, and Sound. But if the film doesn’t fall under the animation branch today, he believes eventually AI movies will inevitably find a place somewhere within Academy rules, even if it ends up being a theoretical “Best AI Movie” category.

“‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ is starting a big debate around where cinematic works of art made with AI fit. Is it time to consider a ‘Best AI Movie?’ Do these films fit best in the voice-actor led animation category? Is AI simply the new VFX? It’s going to take the whole industry time to figure it out,” Saatchi said. “With traditional garlanded directors like Matthieu Kassovitz, Alex Proyas, and Doug Liman making heavily-AI films, it’s going to be a good debate of how to categorize. We think Best Animated is simplest, but it may be the Academy decides ultimately that a Best AI movie category will make the most sense with these films where everything you’re seeing is generative.”

Of note, one of the films that did qualify for Best Animated Feature was “Coyote vs. Acme,” which is a hybrid animated and live-action film featuring the Looney Tunes alongside human actors in the real world. The Academy on Monday also announced the eligible features in the Best Documentary Feature race and the Best International Feature race.

As part of the Academy’s most recent rules changes from earlier this year, only roles credited in the film’s legal billing that are demonstrably performed by humans with their consent are eligible for acting categories, and screenplays must be human-authored to be eligible. That rule changed followed on guidelines from last year ahead of the 98th Oscars in which the Academy specified, “[Gen-AI] tools neither help nor harm the chances of achieving a nomination. The Academy and each branch will judge the achievement, taking into account the degree to which a human was at the heart of the creative authorship when choosing which movie to award.”

In the case of “Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” the film has a script written by London, and though all the characters in the film are generated with AI visually, it features real human actors doing the voice work for the characters. The film also features cameos of some real-life people playing parts resembling themselves, most notably the pop star Grimes. But the film has elaborate look books, visual reference points, and photo mashing that all went into the creation of these characters, something that clearly has human authorship and goes beyond a computer interpreting a single prompt.

Part of Gossip Goblin’s battle in legitimizing “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” is in showing there was a human team, between 30-35 people, working for years on the film’s creation. Gossip Goblin also recently released a behind-the-scenes documentary that showcases the film’s composer, its foley artist, its voice actors, and more detailing the human effort that went into the project.

Discussion over AI in Oscar eligible films came to a head after several movies in the 2024 Oscar race were reported to have included AI in their post-production editing process, including “A Complete Unknown,” “The Brutalist,” and “Emilia Pérez.” The examples were for traditional VFX, not for anything that enhanced or altered performances, but the Academy as a result now requires disclosure of AI if it is used in a film.

“Gods Don’t Give Gifts” begins its theatrical run on December 4, which will initially be an Oscar-qualifying run, and it will expand on January 22 alongside a rollout with the film’s international distributor AGC International.

#3317. Why Is the ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Trailer So… Gloomy? Internet Erupts Over Latest Look at Marvel Movie

There’s a storm brewing, chere, and it has nothing to do with the weird Gambit (Channing Tatum) and Herbie the Robot Dunkin Donuts ads that played like once a quarter during all the football games on Sunday.

The final trailer was released ahead of Marvel’s “Avengers: Doomsday,” the mega-Sentinel, crossover-tastic 165-minute Russo Brothers opus out on December 18. And the response hasn’t been great — in part because Cyclops says, “To me, my X-Men!” and there isn’t actually a Storm.

Way back in the salad days of 2012, Joss Whedon first did an “Assemble” shot that roved in a circle all of the original “Avengers” film, while an Alan Silvestri score bwaaamped the brassy “Avengers” theme. Say whatever you like about Whedon’s strengths and weaknesses when it comes to visual style, but the first time this happened, the shot’s continuous nature served a storytelling purpose. It was the cinematic way to finally bind these crazy kids together in superhero fellowship — through the timeless crucible of New York City getting shredded into CGI bits by alien-monster things. Related Stories AI Film ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ Deemed Ineligible by Academy for Best Animated Feature Oscar The Best Visual Effects in ‘Wildwood’ Are the Ones You Can’t See — Watch

But over the many, many Phases of the MCU, the Avengers Assemble shots have kept happening. And happening. And sure enough, the “Doomsday” trailer crescendos with a bunch of our heroes stuck in a gray-black wasteland void that looks like a glitched “Expedition 33” loading screen, with the camera straining to create that same sense of unity.

It doesn’t. At least not in the trailer. Which is why so much of the response to the finale “Doomsday” trailer has been focused on it.

As folks online have pointed out, Steve Rogers (Chris Evans) looks like he’s standing in entirely different lighting from the people closest to him. There’s no sense of texture or proximity that suggests anybody was placed against the same green screen together, let alone acting together (a problem that has been pointed out about the filmmaking process for “Doomsday” already).

No amount of money can make up for shooting for maximum flexibility — which so often can devolve into being indecisive — or for pursuing relentless revisions throughout the VFX pipeline. That is exactly what leads to shadowy, sloppily-framed environments like wherever the hell the Avengers are fighting Doctor Doom (Robert Downey Jr.) and his creations. And because the environment is so flattened and indistinct, only the barest hints of color survive. And really, only because Reed Richards (Pedro Pascal) is still wearing a coat from a different movie.

Now, what comes most naturally to Cyclops is shooting an optic blast from his eyes, and what comes most naturally to us is posting negative takes online. The trailer takes that shot out of context for nostalgia’s sake; its dramatic purpose within the film itself might be more complicated, or the setup for a twist in three different timelines’ worth of Avengers’ fortunes. But when it comes to all the cinematic crimes of artless visuals, repetitive plots, and overbearing lore that have contributed to superhero fatigue? The “Avengers: Doomsday” trailer doesn’t seem to be beating the charges.

If you're shopping for an iPad this holiday season, you might be a bit intimidated by Apple's price tags. The iPad mini starts at $599; the base iPad Air is $749; and the entry-level iPad Pro is a whopping $1,199. Most of Apple's iPad line certainly lives up to its expensive reputation.

That's where the iPad A16 comes in. This is Apple's least expensive tablet, with an MSRP of $449. But despite being Apple's "budget" option, the iPad A16 shouldn't be ignored by customers looking for the best all-around device. In fact, it's really the best iPad for most people, which is why I named it the best tablet gift of 2026. What's more, retailers are giving the iPad A16 a $50 discount ahead of Black Friday, bringing the entry-level price down to $399.

The iPad A16 isn't Apple's best iPad (that would be the iPad Pro). It doesn't have the best display, the best camera, or the best processor. But it doesn't need those things: This iPad has a display, camera, and processor that are good enough for most use cases, without unnecessarily driving up the price. Simply put, it's one of the best tablets you can buy right now.

The iPad A16 has a large, 11-inch (technically 10.86 inches, according to Apple's fine print) IPS display with a brightness of 500 nits. As the name implies, it has Apple's A16 chip, the same processor as the iPhone 14 Pro and iPhone 15. That chip is about four years old at this point, and while that means it won't be as fast as Apple's newer SoCs, it still holds its own with iOS 27. It comes with two cameras: One 12MP wide camera on the back, with support for 4K video recording, and a 12MP Center Stage camera on the front.

Apple says this iPad can run for 10 hours while browsing the internet on wifi or watching video. You charge the tablet with USB-C, which supports data transfer up to USB 2.0 (which nets you 480Mb/s transfer speeds). It also comes with other perks you might expect from Apple's more "pro" tablets. You can connect the iPad to an external display, up to 4K resolution at 60Hz. It also supports two Apple Pencil models: The USB-C Apple Pencil and the first-gen Apple Pencil.

The only real consideration here is storage: This model comes with 128GB of storage, which can run out fast. It's particularly usable for users who rely on cloud storage or mostly stream their entertainment. But if your giftee plans to store photos, videos, or music on their iPad, it's worth considering upgrading. The $50 discount applies to most storage models, as well as the cellular iPad options, except for the 512GB models: The wifi-only model has a smaller discount, while the cellular option has a $100 discount.

Sure, the iPad A16 doesn't have the fastest processor, an OLED display, support for newer accessories, or Apple's sharpest cameras. But all of the specs it does have are enough to run the things you need on iPadOS. If someone on your list is looking for an iPad for web browsing, streaming, messaging, and light gaming—and they don't need something for professional work—this device is likely more than enough iPad for them.
