If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

#3315. Jon Bernthal’s 100-Minute Taylor Sheridan Thriller Is Officially Cut From Netflix

If you’ve binged Taylor Sheridan’s TV universe twice over, it’s time to check out one of his movie projects that will be leaving Netflix on December 1, making November 30 your last chance to watch. Those Who Wish Me Dead is a 2021 action thriller starring Angelina Jolie and Jon Bernthal as characters who face the worst of nature and humanity during one wild fight for survival. It features all that’s good about the Yellowstone creator’s storytelling, combined with two stars who know how to make you feel every step of their journey.

The Oscar-winning star plays Hannah Faber, a smokejumper (wildland firefighter) in the Montana wilderness who is haunted by a past failure that cost lives. Now living in isolation, her simple routine is shattered when she encounters Connor (Finn Little), a young man who witnesses a murder and now has the killers on his tail. Hannah must use all of her experience to navigate a forest which is being ravaged by a wildfire, in order to evade capture and confront the demons of her past.

It is the third film to be directed by Sheridan, who also co-wrote the script, and has been compared to cult ‘90s survival thrillers like Cliffhanger and The River Wild, where nature becomes as foreboding as the villains. Hannah and Connor’s every turn is blocked by a new life-or-death challenge, with the emotional stakes being raised constantly. It’s an entertaining story of redemption, elevated by the traits that made Sheridan a TV mogul.

Sheridan has shown strength as a director of mid-budget dramas and thrillers intended for adult audiences.

Taylor Sheridan had already scored big with Yellowstone at the time of the film’s release, starting down a path that would see him become synonymous with big stars, big ranches, and even bigger plot twists. Those Who Wish Me Dead has a different setting, but there’s so much in the story that is typical of what Sheridan does best. His signature themes of blue-collar heroics, the burden of responsibility, and frontier morality are all present, as are low-key protagonists who are reluctantly drawn back into a world that forces them to deal with the past.

He delivers action free of the fantasy trappings of genre cinema. You won’t find any special powers or enchanted weapons here, just the will to survive and the force of ordinary people pushed to the limit. Sheridan would write more celebrated movies, such as the crime thriller Hell or High Water and the Sicario films, but if you’re a completist of his work, then this is a cinematic adventure his fans won’t regret seeking out.

Since his breakthrough on the TV show The Walking Dead, Bernthal has specialized in gritty, working-class characters who have more depth than their gruff exteriors suggest. Whether it’s the vigilante fury of The Punisher, the calculating criminality of his role in Baby Driver, or his striking appearance in The Odyssey, he is someone who can bring a lot of impact no matter how high he is on the call sheet.

Those Who Wish Me Dead is no exception, as he holds his own with one of Hollywood’s biggest stars. He plays Ethan Sawyer, a sheriff’s deputy who becomes part of the chase and an ally to Hannah. In many ways, he is a classic Taylor Sheridan hero – a quiet man who does the right thing and gets the job done in order to save innocent lives. He is a direct counterpoint to the villains, in that he is a thoroughly decent man who puts himself in danger to do the right thing. It’s not a huge role in the movie, but it gives an extra human element to a set-piece-heavy movie.

Those Who Wish Me Dead didn’t find the audience it deserved upon release, arriving as the world was still recovering from the 2020 pandemic and people were still reluctant to return to theaters. However, given Sheridan’s status only seems to go from strength to strength, people who want to see even more from him will find everything they love about his TV work in 100 action-packed minutes.

That said, there are plenty of Star Trek stories to enjoy throughout the decades. The series has been around for so long that countless creatives have taken cracks at it, some of whom are better at navigating deep space than others. But if you're a fan of the Kelvin Timeline, you're in luck, as Star Trek: Divergent Timeline is bringing them back with a recent release.

In case you haven't been following Star Trek, the Kelvin Timeline was introduced in 2009's film simply titled Star Trek, directed by J.J. Abrams and starring Chris Pine as James T. Kirk.

In essence, in the year 2387, the Romulan Nero travels back to 2233 and destroys the USS Kelvin, along with First Officer George Kirk. This splits the timeline, creating the alternate universe many refer to as the "Kelvin Timeline." It's garnered a mixed reception since its original release (especially in terms of its sequel, Into Darkness), but it still has fans, and it's part of Star Trek's decades-long history.

That timeline is now making it into Magic: The Gathering, as shared by Wizards of the Coast officially:

Experience 60 years of Klingons, Vulcans, Tamarians, and more with Magic: The Gathering® | Star Trek™! Magic's latest set puts the stories and characters that have captivated generations front and center, celebrating the legacy and future of the Star Trek franchise with Booster Fun treatments like borderless scene cards. Each scene card is part of a larger, multi-card piece that depicts a corner of the Star Trek universe, whether that's an iconic episode or an especially chaotic moment on the bridge. Here are all the scenes you can find in this set!

Multiple crew members have made it onto the set, topped off by a release called Divergent Timeline, which reunites the film trilogy crew in scene cards. So here's what we're getting with Divergent Timeline:

JB Casacop's scene aboard the Enterprise features Kirk, Spock, Uhura, and more, but they look a tad different here! This is the Kelvin timeline, depicted in 2009's Star Trek and other films. You'll also find these incarnations of the crew on the set's Stardates cards.

In other words, we're getting Captain Kirk, as well as Spock, Uhura, Chekov and McCoy, Scotty, and Sulu, as they appear in their Kelvin Timeline forms in the feature films. They bear the likenesses of the films, in line with the rest of the sets.

The other big scene card addition includes Enterprise-Q, depicting the chaos of this particular episode when Q meddled with the Enterprise. Depicted by ALexandaar Gering, it gives us a close look at the Next Generation crew, including the iconic Jean-Luc Picard. Even if Star Trek is rudderless in the years to come, it's had plenty of celebrations so far that are worth remembering.

#3309. If You Loved 'Phony,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Our relationships are foundational to our lives—our sense of safety and how we understand the world around us. When someone close to us suddenly, imperceptibly shifts, it can be unsettling, especially because you can’t be sure what’s changed or why. Those are the waters where Hulu’s Phony swims, delivering a perfectly pitched dramedy about a teenager (Sam Nivola) who emerges from a brief coma convinced that his mother (a pitch-perfect Connie Britton) has been replaced with a double. If you loved the series (and similar shows) and you’re looking for more intriguing stories about doubles and impostors close to home, you should definitely watch Goodnight Mommy.

Goodnight Mommy definitely leans into the psychological horror aspect of an impostor mother much, much harder than Phony, but it’s just a deeper dive into the show’s darker implications (and, fair warning, this movie is dark).

A woman identified only as Mother returns from having cosmetic surgery with her face totally enveloped in bandages, and her twin sons observe strange differences in her behavior that convince them she isn’t their real mother—she appears to ignore one of her sons completely, and disciplines them much more harshly than before. The boys also find clues that bolster their fears, including a photograph showing their mother posing with a woman dressed identically to her.

The boys’ attempts to force her to confess rapidly descend into a kind of madness, ultimately leading them to tie her to the bed in an effort to force her to admit she’s not their real mother. It all leads to a reveal as affecting as Phony’s ultimate explanation (albeit a lot more grim and violent). The film goes way harder than the series, but if you were totally into the premise, this is the more horrifying version you’ll want to see. The original film is German; there was a 2022 remake starring Naomi Watts, and while it's pretty good, the original is the right choice. Stream Goodnight Mommy on Kanopy or Plex, or rent it on Prime Video.

Looking for more impostor stories that dig into the psychological and emotional impact of suspecting someone has been replaced? Here are a few more movies that dig into the concept.

The Hole in the Ground offers an inversion: A mother who becomes convinced that her son has been replaced by an impostor. Firmly in the supernatural horror genre, the story still plays the same game with the viewer: Is Sarah (Seána Kerslake) crazy, or has her son, Chris (James Quinn Markey), been replaced by a creature living in the woods near their home? It’s got the same disturbing energy as Sarah struggles with how much her son’s changed behavior is her own psychological projection and how much is clear evidence that he’s no longer the same person—or, possibly, even the same species. Stream The Hole in the Ground on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

Taking a slightly more literary approach (it’s based on a novella by Fyodor Dostoyevsky), The Double explores what happens if you find yourself replaced by a doppelgänger. Simon (Jesse Eisenberg) is a nonentity—ignored at work, lonely, and silently longing for the girl living across the street, Hannah (Mia Wasikowska). One day, a new employee named James appears at Simon’s job—and James looks exactly like Simon. But James is assertive, confident, and charming, sending Simon into a spiral. As the two versions slide into a battle for dominance, Simon finds himself turning to increasingly deranged moves to rid himself of the new and improved version of himself. If you loved the psychological implications that Phony explores, check out The Double. Stream The Double on Kanopy, Hoopla, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

On one level, Denis Villeneuve’s 2013 film is about a college professor named Adam (Jake Gyllenhaal) who discovers an actor named Anthony who looks exactly like him (also played by Gyllenhaal). When he tracks his double down, their lives merge in messy ways, ending in tragedy and one of the most striking (and confusing) final shots in cinema history. On another level, Enemy is a deft trick, exploring someone’s subconscious using dream logic and misdirection. If the best part about Phony was the disorienting sense that a secret just under the surface will explain everything, Enemy is the perfect choice. Stream Enemy on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re looking for a deeper, crazier, and more terrifying story about doubles, Andrzej Żuławski’s 1981 film is a terrific choice. Inspired in part by his own feelings in the wake of a painful divorce, the story follows Mark (Sam Neil), a spy who returns to West Berlin at the height of the Cold War only to find out his wife, Anna (Isabelle Adjani), has been having an affair and wants a divorce. But Anna’s behavior becomes increasingly strange, and then Mark meets their son’s teacher, Helen, who looks just like Anna. And that’s before Anna kind of ... grows a replacement Mark from a tentacled creature kept in her bathroom (and that’s just the beginning of how weird this movie gets), resulting in two doubles. How much of the film is meant literally and how much simply represents the trauma of romantic betrayal and divorce is up to you, but Possession will definitely leave a mark. Stream Possession on Shudder, Kanopy, or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Obsession looks at the Doppelgänger Effect from a different perspective. Cliff Robertson plays Michael Courtland, a wealthy businessman whose wife (Geneviève Bujold) and young daughter, Amy (Wanda Blackman), are kidnapped in 1959. When he follows police advice against delivering the ransom, both appear to be killed in an explosion. Courtland spends the next 16 years hating himself, until he encounters a young woman, Sandra (also Bujold), who looks almost exactly like his late wife. He works to make Sandra look as much like his wife as possible, and eventually proposes—but then Sandra is kidnapped in precisely the same way as his wife and daughter sixteen years before. This all leads to a head-spinning series of reveals and a twist that echoes the Hitchcock classic Vertigo. Rent Obsession on Prime Video.

#3308. Apple TV’s Masterpiece Spy Thriller Series With 4 Seasons On The Way Delivers A Masterclass In Tension

Apple TV is the home of many high-profile shows, including a spy thriller series that defies streaming rules in multiple ways, such as by having four confirmed seasons on the way, and it is a show that delivers a masterclass in tension for a few reasons. Apple TV has become the go-to for those searching for good production values and consistency in the age of streaming.

Apple TV tends to give shows the necessary time to develop, find their footing, and conclude their stories. In addition to that, it is the perfect streaming service for viewers who are looking for engaging, high-stakes, intense series. Multi-season projects that fit that bill include Severance, Silo, For All Mankind, and more, with not all of them being part of Apple TV's excellent sci-fi catalog.

Slow Horses, a spy thriller series, is certainly part of that group, and Apple TV recently confirmed how it might trust the gritty series more than any other project on its library of shows. After all, while Slow Horses season 6 recently concluded, the show is confirmed to return for at least four more seasons, up to season 10, and its delivery of a masterclass in tension is key to that.

Slow Horses has released six seasons so far on Apple TV, all of them consisting of just six episodes. This plays into how the show is so intense, as the spy thriller series is all plot, no filler, yet it packs quite a bit of much-needed character development without impacting the show's pacing. Another factor that ups the tension in this espionage story is the fact that nobody is safe, as both major characters and long-running supporting players have died over the course of Slow Horses' six seasons. Fans are left worrying about the fates of their favorites the whole time.

Another added layer of tension for the series comes from the fact that the agents of Slough House, while capable, are not near-perfect spies like James Bond. These are fallible characters who are known to make mistakes and misjudge situations, having to find ways to overcome the many challenges that arise along the way as they stumble upon major conspiracies. This both makes the show an exciting watch, but also a nerve-wracking espionage thriller. Finally, there is also the fact that Gary Oldman, one of the best actors alive, lights up the screen when Jackson Lamb drops the slacker act and means business.

Slow Horses has another four seasons on the way, but fans of the spy thriller series only have a good clue of what might happen in seasons 7 and 8. After all, the show is based on Mick Herron's series of novels, and there are currently only two more books left to be adapted, Bad Actors and Clown Town. A clear plot point set to be picked up and elevate the tension next season is the reveal of what will happen to Jack Lowden's River Cartwright, who collapsed at the end of season 6 and looked like he was about to die.

Season 7 should feature the team at Slough House hunting a mole inside the British government, a trope known to always add tension related to the character(s) being investigated and even within those leading the investigation. When it comes to season 8, a clash between Jackson Lamb and Diana Taverner should shake things up in a major way, continuing to make the thriller a show you never know exactly what to expect, and that is why Slow Horses delivers a masterclass in tension.

#3306. 'SilverFin's Full-Cast Audiobook Is an Immersive Look at the Boy Who Would Be Bond | Review

There’s officially a new James Bond on the big screen in the shape of Robert Pattinson, which means there’s a whole new 007 to spend the next few years speculating about. There’s also a new Bond to listen to right now, and he’s still a schoolboy. The fun of Big Finish’s SilverFin is hearing how much of the iconic spy is already there at thirteen, although it's fair to say the production is in absolutely no rush to introduce us to him.

In fact, it spends nearly ten minutes with two children, Alfie and Jeannie, on a fishing trip that will initially have you thinking, "where's the Bond boy?" However, Joe Kraemer’s score and Benji Clifford’s sound design are so striking that they give the loch just enough time to go from peaceful to ominous. Then there's an attack, and then something attacks, the new theme kicks in, and suddenly it sounds like Bond.

Isaac Rouse (The Crown) plays James in the full-cast audio adaptation of SilverFin, the first novel in Charlie Higson’s Young Bond series, produced by Big Finish and Ian Fleming Publications. Higson takes Bond back to the 1930s, when he’s a new boy at Eton. Instead of global annihilation, his biggest problem here is a bully with a rich father. Imagine. Then James goes to Scotland for the holidays, the children’s disappearance becomes his first real mystery, and it's not the bully that's the big problem; it's the rich daddy.

The remainder of the cast includes Charlotte McBurney as Wilder Lawless, Charlie Higson as Michael Merriot, Tim McInnerny as Max Bond, Miranda Raison as Charmian Bond, Miriam Margolyes as Cleek MacSawney, William Hope as Lord Randolph Hellebore, Christopher Nathan as George Hellebore, Paterson Joseph as Dr. Perseus Friend, Harry Marcus as Red Kelly, Lucy Fleming as Madame Ouspenskaya, Timothy Bentinck as Sergeant White, and Penelope Rawlins as Alfie Kelly.

Spanning 8 hours across 16 episodes, the adaptation has been helmed by writer and director Barnaby Edwards, and he wisely makes the decision to give James time to settle into both worlds. After all, there's an entire school sporting competition to get through, and at one point Uncle Max explains how a Rolls-Royce engine works in frankly ridiculous detail. The scene has every right to be boring, and yet, it’s fascinating, partly because Max takes such pleasure in explaining it and partly because James perks up once he realizes how many little explosions it takes to make a car go. That’s SilverFin at its best. It gives its characters time to enjoy one another’s company, which makes it hurt all the more when things go horribly wrong.

Now, Rouse is a hard sell as a 13-year-old boy, and even more so when the story flashes back to an even younger James. Yet, by the end of the Hellebore Cup, you cannot imagine anyone else doing the role. The things that pop out instantly are the charm, that basically obnoxious and undeserved confidence he has at that age, and the way he's still figuring out how far a witty line can get him.

Rishi Manuel’s Pritpal Nandra gives the Eton episodes their warmth. He explains the school to James and the listener in one go, in a moment that actually feels very "Basil Exposition," if you want to feel extra Bond-meta. Their teasing feels like two boys actually becoming friends, and there’s room for another episode of that before the Hellebore Cup takes over. After two episodes of George Hellebore being an absolute Malfoy of a boy, hearing James overtake him is wildly satisfying. Then George has to face his father, and suddenly third place feels like the worst thing that could have happened to him.

Perhaps the heart of the Scottish scenes is when James and his Uncle Max go fishing, something you wouldn't think could be that compelling in an audio drama — yet, it is. McInnerny is just great here, and he brings that same easy charm and warmth to the scene where Max tells James about working as a spy during the war, as well as how he got the limp he came home with. Miranda Raison’s Aunt Charmian makes it easy to see why coming back to this family matters to James, especially after the surprisingly affecting flashbacks to his parents.

Red Kelly’s return is a delight, and Wilder Lawless makes such an immediate impression that it’s a shame she takes more than three hours to turn up. And then there’s Meatpacker Moran, a name that deserves to go down in history, whom Stuart Milligan makes unexpectedly good company. The first half’s finale spends most of its time following him, James, and Red around the outside of Castle Hellebore. Clifford’s sound design makes the grounds easy to picture, so there’s time to appreciate the sheer scale of the place and how much trouble the boys will be in once they go inside.

William Hope makes Lord Randolph Hellebore vile from the moment he opens his mouth, and Miriam Margolyes makes his gamekeeper frightening enough to carry a scene on her own. Even in that company, Paterson Joseph is something else as Doctor Perseus Friend. He talks to George about eugenics and mass death like they've just caught up for coffee in Cafe Nervosa in Seattle. Later, he manages to make the simple prospect of watching someone eat sound deeply sinister. A plan to create super-soldiers using eels sounds gloriously daft on paper, but Joseph makes it disturbing by playing Friend as a man who’s found an excuse to do exactly what he wants to do.

The laboratory episodes spend a long time explaining what Hellebore is doing, and by the later chapters a few of Kraemer’s cues have become a little too familiar. “The Future of Warfare” still lands hard enough to make a break between episodes feel welcome. Edwards gives away very little about what happened to Alfie and Jeannie. Those first ten minutes on the loch do a lot of the work. By the time James and George start smashing up the laboratory in “Hellfire,” it’s a punch-the-air moment. George’s change of heart happens quickly, but Christopher Nathan has been letting the fear slip through his arrogance since Eton.

And then there’s Uncle Max. The series gives plenty of reason to suspect he’ll die, and his letter is still an absolute gut punch. He’s reminding James how to start the car one moment and telling him how much those last few days together meant to him the next. Then Charmian says, “How lucky we are,” even as she’s grieving him. It’s a lovely way to end their time in Scotland.

SilverFin is an enjoyable, impressively atmospheric start for Big Finish’s Young Bond, but its eight-hour runtime gives the uneven pacing plenty of room to show. The school adventures and quieter family scenes build an appealing world around James, but lengthy laboratory explanations slow the story just when it should be gathering momentum. The irony is that, in reviewing this audio adaptation, the strongest praise goes to the performances, direction, and sound design, while the biggest frustrations lie with a story that’s been around for two decades and is showing its creaks. However, Isaac Rouse’s charm, a strong supporting cast, and Benji Clifford’s vivid soundscape do a lot of the heavy lifting, while the emotional finale delivers a proper gut punch, rounding off a promising debut for Big Finish.

Superb performances and atmospheric audio production make SilverFin an engaging Young Bond debut, though the decades-old story shows its weaknesses through uneven pacing and lengthy exposition.

#3305. This Apple Watch Is a Lifehacker 'Gift of the Year' Award Winner, and It's $50 Off Ahead of Black Friday

Apple has three main Apple Watch "lines." There's the flagship, currently the Series 12, which represents Apple's mainstream wearable. For athletes and users who think they'll put their watches through some extreme scenarios, there's the Ultra line, currently the Apple Watch Ultra 4. And while both the Series 12 and Ultra 4 are excellent devices in their own right, they can be pretty pricey (particularly the Ultra). That's why the third category, the SE, is actually best for most people, and Lifehacker's choice for best smartwatch gift of the year. Better yet, the third-generation SE is currently $50 off ahead of Black Friday, perfect for most people asking for an Apple Watch this year.

The SE 3 does just about everything you'd expect an Apple Watch to do. It, of course, has a heart rate sensor to keep tabs on your pulse, including high and low heart rate alerts; the ability to track dozens of different workouts and exercise types (including swimming, thanks to the device's water resistance); a sleep tracker with daily analyses available in the Health app; notification forwarding to check in on your alerts without opening your iPhone; and the ability to send and receive text messages.

It comes in two sizes (40mm and 44mm) depending on how large or small you prefer your watch. No matter which model you get, the watch comes with the S10 chip, Apple's last-generation watch processor. While it isn't as fast as the current S11 chip, the S10 is more than capable of running watchOS 27. Apple says the SE 3 can run for up to 18 hours on a single charge, and up to 32 hours in Low Power Mode, with fast charging from 0% to 80% in 45 minutes.

The majority of the features missing from the SE 3 aren't essential. Apple's other watches have things like bigger, brighter displays, additional health tracking tools like hypertension alerts and an ECG sensor, longer battery life, and Audio Intelligence—the latter of which might be a benefit to miss, depending on who you are.

If your giftee wants or needs any of those additional features, Series 12 or Ultra 4 might be a better choice. But for anyone who wants the essential Apple Watch experience, the SE 3 is simply the best-value watch Apple sells right now—especially at this discount. Right now, the watch starts at $199 for the 40mm watch, or $229 for the 44mm. You can also save on the cellular versions of these watches: $249 for the cellular 40mm watch, and $279 for the cellular 44mm model.

#3302. Why Black Friday and Cyber Monday Are Bad Days to Impulse Buy Electronics

Black Friday sales officially start Friday, November 28, and run through Cyber Monday, November 30, 2026, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews and comparisons before it's over.

It's Cyber Monday, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews and comparisons before the sales are over.

Sales are accurate at the time of publication, but prices and inventory are always subject to change.

Not every Black Friday or Cyber Monday deal is as sweet as it seems. With electronics and tech in particular, you could be buying last year's model that has actually been on sale since the summer—and was maybe a better price a few months ago. Here’s how to avoid impulse buying a misleading Black Friday “deal” and make sure you’re getting the best bang for your buck.

When you see products like food, clothes, or home goods with a big "Black Friday" or "Cyber Monday" tag slapped on them, it's probably safe to take advantage of that deal. Chances are it's the same exact product you'd find on other days of the year. The same can’t be said for a TV, laptop, and other tech deals, where the product itself is constantly being upgraded.

Because tech is always evolving, and retailers want to move inventory before new models come out, electronics are especially susceptible to a practice known as "price anchoring." That's when retailers mark up prices in the weeks leading up to Black Friday, before "slashing" those prices back down, giving the appearance of a deal that isn't really a deal at all. Still, when you see that marked-up number, aka the "price anchor," you might get tricked into thinking you're saving money when you're not. There's also the false sense of urgency that gets created. It's second nature to assume that anything labeled "deal" won’t last long—even when this so-called deal price has actually been going on since the summer.

Price anchoring isn't even unique to Black Friday. The nonprofit Consumers’ Checkbook tracked prices at 25 major retailers over 33 weeks in 2022 and found that more than half the items tracked were offered at false discounts every week or almost every week. Less common, but also worth noting, is a known practice of "derivative" or retailer-exclusive models produced specifically for the holiday shopping season. These versions often feature cheaper components, fewer features, or lower specifications than their regular counterparts. A 55-inch TV from a reputable brand might look identical to the year-round model, but it could have a lower refresh rate, inferior panel technology, or fewer HDMI ports.

In the same vein, that "amazing deal" on a laptop might come with last year's processor, or a smartphone that's about to be replaced. The issue isn't that the tech is an older model, but again, it's that it probably has been at this low a price, or lower, since the summer. Alternatively, some deeply discounted electronics are refurbished units or open-box returns that have been repackaged. Again, while this isn't necessarily a bad thing, impulse buyers may not fully realize what they're buying.

The key phrasing here is impulse buying. Events like Black Friday are psychologically engineered to trigger impulse purchases. Limited-time offers, countdown clocks, and "while supplies last" warnings create artificial urgency. When you're caught up in the moment, it's easy to convince yourself you need a new tablet, smartwatch, or gaming console, even if you hadn't considered buying one before.

To avoid a low-key scam, do your research. The easiest way to tell that you’re getting the correct product is by checking the model or serial number. And with online shopping, finding and double-checking those numbers is quick and easy. In addition, don't just compare prices—compare specs. Look at processor speeds, RAM, storage capacity, screen resolution, refresh rates, and connectivity options. A $300 laptop isn't a deal if a slightly more expensive model offers significantly better performance that will last longer.

If you do see a deal that catches your eye, it could pay to wait. Cyber Monday, post-Christmas sales, and even January clearances often feature electronics deals that rival or beat Black Friday prices, all without the famous chaos and pressure. Then again, you risk more “out-of-stock” results if you wait, so the risk is up to you, depending on the popularity of the item you’re eyeing (and how badly you want it).

The bottom line: Don’t fall victim to a falsely advertised lower-quality product, and do a little research to find actually good deals ahead of time.

The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. #3301. 5 Classic Books Better Than 'Moby-Dick'

At any given moment, Scott Simone has at least three books jockeying for his attention. He’ll never turn down a campus novel with a literary bent, nor will he hesitate to add yet another mystery to his Leaning Tower of Pisa-inspired to-be-read pile — which is built upon the bedrocks of too many short story collections, how-are-these-real true crime books, and classics waiting to be cracked open again. Topics that have him ripping through pages the fastest include closed-circle murders, unhappy professors, life-questioning philosophical deep dives, so long as they feature sharp sentences, a dark sense of humor, and at least a little malice.

He’s spent so much time in book shops over the years he is, to his wife’s chagrin, continuing to build a library that doesn’t quite respect the dimensions of the apartment meant to contain it.

It's hard to describe Moby-Dick. On the surface, it's a simple story of revenge, about a ship captain hunting the whale that took his leg. But the novel comes in waves. There are chapters about whale anatomy and the whaling industry. There's an entire chapter devoted to the color white. These chapters, at times, drown the whole whale hunting business until it once again bobs its head above it all. Yet all that diving and resurfacing is what made Moby Dick such uncharted territory. Herman Melville hooks you with the promise of adventure, but it's the examination of obsession, of fate, and of man's relationship with nature that continues reeling you in. It's an attempt to understand and to make sense of the world, and it reads part adventure, part encyclopedia, part philosophical argument. And somehow it all works.

That's what the greatest novels manage to do. They use a simple story — about a man, about a family, about one small part of the world — as the basis to explore so much more. They make us care about people we might otherwise despise, or they find tragedy in the ridiculous. They don't need to be so obviously about absolutely everything as Melville was. Some manage an extraordinary amount with very little. Some sprawl across generations, taking us so far from where we began that it's difficult to believe we're still reading the same book. So, sure, Moby-Dick deserves its place among the greatest novels ever written. But it's hardly the only one to make an improbable story into something extraordinary; and a few have managed to do it even better.

Don Quixote has become something of a punch line. A sort of shorthand for anyone undertaking an obviously outlandish pursuit. It’s about an aging man who reads one too many stories about knights. He decides he ought to become one himself and heads off to fight giants that turn out to be windmills. It's all a little ridiculous. But while Miguel de Cervantes' deluded knight is farcical, he has a way of exposing some truths. Yes, he's hopelessly out of touch with reality; but, he still believes in honor and justice, and takes it upon himself to defend anyone who needs protection.

Then there's Sancho Panza. A grand promise of an island to govern sends him trotting alongside Don Quixote. We're to think he's the sensible one despite that. After all, he knows that windmills aren't giants. Yet he follows Don Quixote from one absurd adventure to the next. He argues with him, sure, but he also loves to indulge Don Quixote. He even has the tendency to get caught up in all the nonsense goings-on himself. As the whole thing unfolds, it becomes harder and harder to pinpoint who the actual fool is. Because it's the people who humiliate Don Quixote that have a much uglier view of the world, and we're not talking about his tendency to see castles where everyone sees inns. Like Melville's Ahab, he's a man possessed by an idea, unwilling to accept anything that contradicts it. But where Ahab's obsession leaves death and destruction in its wake, Don Quixote's produces something altogether more complicated.

Rodion Raskolnikov has a theory: the usual rules of morality don't apply to certain men. They're just a bit too special. Napoleon didn't get where he did by worrying about all the people who died along the way. And Raskolnikov, a penniless former student living in St. Petersburg, decides he might belong to that exclusive club. So he decides to test his little theory and murders an elderly pawnbroker, reasoning that her money could be put to better use. Then he murders her sister, too.

But the murders take up little of Crime and Punishment. The real story is about Raskolnikov trying to get on with his life afterward. He's feverish and he's paranoid. He's insufferable to the few people who still give a damn about him. He panics after perfectly innocent conversations. Every encounter with Porfiry Petrovich, the magistrate investigating the murders, is fraught with tension; not only the pitter and the patter between the two, but internally as he contemplates whether he's about to be arrested or merely imagining things. Raskolnikov, like Melville's Ahab, has convinced himself he's somehow above the rest of humanity. But unlike Ahab's obsession dragging an entire ship toward disaster, it's Raskolnikov dragging himself, and only himself, into demise.

Middlemarch sounds like a hard sell. Nearly 800 pages about the goings-on in a provincial English town. People marry the wrong people. They borrow money. They gossip, and they meddle in one another's affairs. There's not exactly a whale to chase. But there is Dorothea Brooke, who's desperate to do something with her life. She convinces herself she can help Edward Casaubon, an older scholar, produce some great intellectual work. And so she marries him. There's just one little issue to contend with: Casaubon isn't nearly as brilliant as she imagines.

What makes Middlemarch engrossing is how decisions tend to become someone else's problem. A marriage made with the best intentions turns miserable. A few unpaid bills threaten to derail a promising career. And a bit of gossip, passed from one drawing room to another, can do more damage than anyone intended. Nobody is entirely innocent in all this, though few are outright villains. Even the most infuriating characters have their reasons for behaving as they do, and we get to see how they came by them. George Eliot gives us an entire town of people pursuing their own ideas of happiness, often at the expense of someone else's. Melville sends Ahab halfway around the world to examine the forces that govern human lives; Eliot hardly needs to leave the confines of a small English town.

Britain makes more detective television than any country has any business making, and somehow almost all of it is good. Here is the one you belong in, what it says about you, and the case for it being the best of the four.

You want the tea, the gossip and the vicar behaving oddly. Midsomer is a county where the scenery is beautiful, the fete is on Saturday and the murder rate is roughly that of a small war, and absolutely nobody involved thinks this is strange.

You feel other people's grief as if it were handed to you personally. Broadchurch is less a whodunnit than a study of what a small town does to itself when it finds out that the answer was always going to be somebody everybody already knew.

You go through things rather than around them. John Luther is the best detective in London and a liability to everybody who works with him, and the show is completely honest that those two facts are the same fact.

You say the thing and you do not dress it up. Vera Stanhope turns up in a hat and a mac, is rude to almost everybody, and is the only person in the room prepared to ask the question that the family has been waiting years for somebody to ask.

Germinal takes us underground. Deep underground, into the coal mines of northern France. Émile Zola introduces us to Étienne Lantier, who finds work at Le Voreux, a mine that's been swallowing generations of workers. Take the Maheu family. Nearly everyone works in the mines, yet there's hardly enough money to put food on the table. They spend their days risking their lives. They come home exhausted, get up the next day to dig. Rinse, repeat. All the while, the mine owners live a comfortable existence. So when the company makes an already miserable existence even harder, Étienne helps organize a strike.

But refusing to work means no food. As the strike drags on, the cupboards empty. Families who barely had enough to begin with now have nothing. Solidarity amongst the miners fractures. Some want to hold out. Others are desperate to get back to work. People who've spent their lives working alongside one another are turning against each other. There's anger and there’s violence. That's what makes Germinal so devastating. Zola gives us an entire community whose lives are dictated by the work that's slowly killing them. Like Melville, he's interested in man's struggle against forces much bigger than himself. But while Ahab drags his crew halfway around the world to confront the source of his misery, Zola's miners have to descend into theirs every morning.

Good luck keeping track of the Buendía family in One Hundred Years of Solitude. The foliage that the various José Arcadios and Aurelianos alone occupy on the family tree is astounding. And that's before getting into all the strange things happening around them. An outbreak of insomnia leaves people forgetting the names of everyday objects, so they start sticking labels on everything. A young woman floats off to heaven while folding bedsheets. The dead occasionally stop by for a visit. And nobody seems particularly bothered by any of it. In Gabriel García Márquez's world, the impossible is just another part of everyday life.

But the names aren't the only things that keep repeating. Over seven generations, the Buendías fall into the same traps as their parents and grandparents. They pursue doomed romances and they nurse old grudges. They throw themselves into grand ambitions that inevitably come to very little. And their hometown of Macondo experiences its own troubles. There are civil wars. There are political upheavals. There's the arrival of a foreign banana company. When striking workers are massacred, the authorities insist it never happened. And before long, almost everyone seems to believe them. Where Melville uses the pursuit of a single whale to examine mankind's place in the world, García Márquez gives us a century of births, deaths, wars, and family squabbles to explore how history gets repeated, distorted, and sometimes forgotten altogether.

#3299. GTA 6 Boss Gives Official Update On GTA 7

GTA 6 was such a monumentally anticipated release that everything dealing with it was under a microscope. This was the case for several other GTA games before it, once GTA 3 brought even more fame to the series. But with GTA 6, and expectations that it would be one of the biggest entertainment releases in any sector, it made sense there would be even more scrutiny.

That's ultimately part of the reason why Rockstar (under the ownership of Take-Two) decided to delay the game multiple times. Since everyone in the world would be watching when it came out, it needed a level of polish that many AAA games don't get anymore.

So imagine our surprise when GTA 7 was already mentioned, less than a week after the release of GTA 6. Speaking to Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick, TBPN got an unexpected response regarding GTA 7 [via X].

Talking to Zelnick, when asked if "GTA 7 would be a live version of the entire world," Zelnick had this to say in response:

I can't help myself. We at Take-Two just went live with GTA 6 on November 19, wait let me check my watch, it's still November 19, and we're talking about GTA 7...I mean guys, really? I don't know, my father-in-law had a line whenever...he had many great business achievements...and if you ever said anything nice, he'd say those are yesterday's headlines.

“Once you get through several hundred hours of the most incredible fun you’ve ever had, ask the question again," he also noted. While it sounds rough on paper, Zelnick took the response in stride and talked about the achievements of GTA 6.

Once again, GTA 6 has entered the collective consciousness, and it's pretty much all the entertainment industry is talking about right now. There are so many moving parts in GTA 6; it's wild, especially when it comes to the Easter Eggs, secrets, and detailed recreations of South Florida's infrastructure.

Having played through the entire game, it's a true testament to how much money Rockstar is willing to throw at their game budgets. We saw this with most mainline GTA games, but Red Dead Redemption 2 also tested the limits of what AAA games could offer. With its expansive and dynamic open world, it whisked players back to a bygone era.

But with GTA 6, it's much different. The team had to recreate a modern aesthetic but also give it its own unique spin, which I think they succeeded at. After all, the world of GTA is slightly askew compared to ours, with alternate acronyms for organizations and a lot more nuances.

GTA 7 might be over a decade away at this point, but people will be talking about GTA 6 for that long, if not longer. That's definitely going to be the case whenever Rockstar gets to the next iteration of GTA Online, which is bound to happen at some point, along with the inevitable PC port.

#3298. Zane Lowe shares Apple Music Radio audience numbers, recalls ‘crickets’ in the early days

In a new interview with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, Apple Music’s Zane Lowe discussed the early days of Apple Music Radio and revealed just how many people tune in each month. Here are the details.

Apple is rarely terribly specific about how many people use its services, including how many tune in to its radio stations.

In 2019, for instance, Eddy Cue said Beats 1 (now Apple Music 1) had ‘tens of millions of listeners,’ but Apple has rarely provided more specific figures since.

Apple Music’s Zane Lowe, however, has now offered a more concrete figure, revealing that the service reaches over 50 million unique listeners every month:

We were never, you know, delusional enough to assume we were going to get a huge audience overnight. We’d have to build it like anyone else would have to build anything. But we’ve just got to a point in our 11 years on where we now, overall, reach over 50 million unique listeners a month, which is a really large number for us, and it’s growing exponentially and really fast.

The revelation came in a wide-ranging interview published today with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, where Lowe discussed Apple Music Radio’s early struggles, its approach to supporting emerging artists, and why human curation remains central to the service.

When discussing the early days at Apple Music, Lowe recalled:

When we started the radio here, I didn’t have access or opportunity with a lot of the artists that I built relationships with from the BBC because we were unproven. And I came over here thinking, “Well, I’ve got Jimmy Iovine over here, and I’ve got Apple over here and I feel unstoppable, and who’s not going to want to come and launch this thing with us?” But it was kind of crickets… As upsetting as that was at the time, two good things came out of it. Number one, it snapped me back into the reality force field of building something from scratch. And number two, it made us focus really clearly and in a big way on new and emerging artists.

He also mentioned some of the first artists Apple Music Radio supported, including Billie Eilish with “Ocean Eyes,” Khalid with American Teen, and Bryson Tiller with his first song.

At the time, Lowe noted, these artists were just getting started, and supporting emerging talent became a defining part of Apple Music Radio’s approach, one that continues to this day:

The really cool number is on our radio network. We played — this year alone — over 6,500 individual artists, which is not a commercial radio model. [Other radio networks’] playlists are very small, and the amount of plays is very great. Our playlist is gigantic. We play a lot of different artists, and over half of those 6,500 artists we’ve played in one year are new or emerging. So, think about 3,300 artists, roughly, getting played, who may be on their first song, their first EP, their first album…It’s proof of concept. It’s great.

Still on the subject of the early days at Apple Music, Lowe said “it was very clear [from the start] that that was very important to everybody who was responsible for bringing Apple Music to life,” adding that “serving artists and the artistic community in a way that is of most value and of most service” still drives “a lot of the decision-making” at the platform.

When the conversation turned to Apple Music’s recent rebranding, which introduced a new logo physically created using sound waves from a composition by Fred again.., Lowe said he couldn’t speak to the decisions behind it, but stressed the human element and the creative process that went into it:

We could have created that in a way that could utilize all of the tech available. We could type that into a prompt. But at the end of the day, seeing how it’s made is so much more additionally inspiring than just seeing it. It speaks to, I think, what we try to do here, which is, we love the process of what we do, and the result is a byproduct of getting to do it and loving to do it.

The issue of algorithms also came up when Lowe discussed Apple Music’s approach to music discovery, with the executive emphasizing the importance of human curation over automated recommendations:

Well, we don’t want to say that too loudly, because someone could be like, “Wait a minute, we could cut costs here? Man, how did we not think of that!” Look, I mean, jokes aside, we’ve been incredibly fortunate, and I’ve been incredibly fortunate to take that step from the BBC into a company and to work with people that value exactly what it is you’re describing: this idea of place and this experience of sharing things with each other, and how meaningful it is when someone shares a record with you and it comes with context. It’s a gift…

One of Amazon’s biggest sales of the year, Black Friday and Cyber Monday, is set to start Nov. 27, but many early deals are already rolling in. If you sign up for an Amazon Prime account to take advantage of the sale but decide you don’t want to pay for an ongoing membership, you’ll need to cancel your subscription before the end of your free trial.

You can cancel your Prime subscription via web browser by first logging into your Amazon account. Amazon has a Cancel Your Prime Membership button on its support page to launch the process, or you can follow the steps detailed on Amazon's page:

Hover over the Accounts & Lists menu on the top-right of the window, then select the Prime Membership option.

Then tap the End Your Amazon Prime Membership button and finally click the Cancel Your Prime Membership orange button.

Follow the on-screen instructions to cancel your Prime subscription.

Note that Amazon requires a bunch of clicks to finalize your cancellation, giving you lots of “opportunities” to change your mind.

Open the Amazon Shopping app on your mobile device.

Click the three horizontal lines on the bottom right.

On the top bar, slide all the way to the end and select Help.

Then tap the End Your Amazon Prime Membership button and finally click the Cancel Your Prime Membership orange button.

Follow the on-screen instructions to cancel your Prime subscription.

As mentioned, closing your account will immediately end your access. Amazon also offers you the option to pause your benefits and billing temporarily instead of canceling them completely. Either way, your Amazon account is still active—you simply won’t have Prime benefits.

Finally, if you have other subscriptions connected to your Prime account, those will end when your billing is up. And if you signed up for Prime through the Android mobile shopping app or the Prime Video Android app, you’ll have to go through Google Subscription to manage your membership.

#3292. The 8 Best Tom Clancy Books, Ranked

Tom Clancy was one of the most successful writers of his era, with over 100 million books sold worldwide. He's also one with a very particular recipe: his stories are usually geopolitical thrillers packed with military hardware, intelligence operations, political maneuvering, and uncomfortably plausible international crises.

Submarines, nuclear weapons, special forces, and international diplomacy are the key ingredients, all rendered with obsessive attention to detail. However, the best of the author's books combine all that with high-tension plotting and characters we actually care about. Here are some of the finest, ranked.

“The difference between fiction and reality? Fiction has to make sense.” Rather than depending primarily upon battlefield action, this one leans harder into pure espionage, building tension around information. At the center is CARDINAL, a highly placed American intelligence asset inside the Soviet Union who is becoming increasingly vulnerable. Jack Ryan becomes deeply involved in the attempt to protect CARDINAL's secrecy while Soviet intelligence officers work to uncover the leak.

Clancy's detailed understanding of intelligence procedure is a big part of what makes the book work. Thanks to his research and detail, a compromised communication or suspicious pattern of behavior can be every bit as dangerous as a gunfight. Refreshingly, The Cardinal of the Kremlin also gives its Soviet characters motives and internal conflicts rather than treating the Cold War as a simple contest between interchangeable villains and heroes.

"Ryan had learned long before that people did not think clearly when they were afraid.” Patriot Games gets unusually personal. In it, Ryan is visiting London with his family when he stumbles into an attempted kidnapping involving members of the royal family. His instinctive intervention saves lives, but puts him directly in the path of a violent splinter group. Soon, Ryan is trying to protect his wife and daughter after his actions make his family a target.

Clancy builds this into a classic story of a good man up against dastardly foes, anchored by a protagonist with a moral code. The early sections also spend time letting us get to know Ryan's family and understand the bond between them, which makes sure the emotional stakes hit hard later. The plot is also handled briskly, keeping the pages flying by the whole way through.

“The only way to prevent war is to make sure that everyone understands what war means.” The Sum of All Fears gets unsettlingly plausible with its take on nuclear risks. Here, neither superpower actually wants an atomic showdown, but circumstances make them believe the other does. The plot kicks into gear after a missing Israeli nuclear weapon turns up just as peace talks seem poised to deliver a breakthrough. For Jack Ryan, now CIA deputy director, the timing could hardly be worse.

Relations between Washington and Moscow are deteriorating, and a Palestinian terrorist group sees the bomb as a way to set the two superpowers against each other. In other words, this setup takes recognizable geopolitical tensions and pushes them to the brink of World War III. However, Clancy's signature recipe of technical detail and outsize plotting ensures that the final product is still a fun thriller.

“The end does not justify the means. There are no ends, only means.” Clear and Present Danger places Ryan in conflict not only with America's enemies but with decisions being made inside his own government. After Colombian drug traffickers murder an American official and his family, powerful figures within the administration authorize a covert campaign against the cartels, and even Ryan himself is kept out of the loop.

American light infantry teams are secretly inserted into Colombia, where they begin targeting the infrastructure supporting the drug trade. Domingo "Ding" Chavez and John Clark (a character sometimes described as "Ryan's dark side") play major roles in the operation​​​​​​, making this a great Ryan/Clark crossover episode. That setup also allows Clancy to explore the moral complications of covert warfare while still delivering the military and intelligence detail his readers expect.

“Safety is something that happens between your ears, not something you hold in your hands.” Speaking of John Clark, the character finally takes center stage in Rainbow Six, which shifts attention away from Jack Ryan's political ascent and toward international counterterrorism. Clark commands Rainbow, a newly created multinational unit composed of elite operators. Soon, the team is up against a group of extremists plotting biological terrorism on a staggering scale, motivated by an ideology that regards humanity as expendable.

At 740 pages, Rainbow Six is a substantial thriller even by Clancy’s standards. However, some of the characters could still use more depth even with all that screen time, and the villains’ scheme sometimes sounds like something out of a second-tier Bond adventure. That said, the sheer number of gripping action sequences makes up for a lot, and the book spawned a video game franchise for a reason.

“John Kelly had known death before.” This gem is the original story for John Clark (aka John Kelly), and it's noticeably darker and more personal than most of Clancy's geopolitical epics. Essentially, it explains how a regular Navy SEAL is forged into the CIA’s deadliest black-ops agent. Set during the Vietnam War, the novel cuts between two missions. In one, Clark hunts down the drug dealers who killed his girlfriend.

In the other, he joins a secret operation to bring home American prisoners of war held in Vietnam. Taken together, these storylines make for what might be Clancy's strongest character portrait. Clark’s grief and moral convictions dictate the course of the story, and his doubts give him a depth that few of the author’s other protagonists enjoy. Clancy himself described the book as an inquiry into what justice means and how it should be carried out.

“Wars are begun by frightened men.” This is one of the very few Clancy books not set in the Ryanverse, but it's still a banger. Here, a Soviet fuel crisis sets the stage for a surprise invasion of Western Europe as Moscow tries to secure its oil supply. The attack draws NATO and the Warsaw Pact into an all-out war fought across land, sea, and air, but purely with conventional weapons. No nukes involved.

The book swaps out larger-than-life heroes for a multi-front look at how a Third World War might actually look. Indeed, we see the conflict from numerous perspectives: frontline tank commanders, frigate captains, fighter pilots, Kremlin strategists, and more. Submarines stalk one another beneath the Atlantic, aircraft battle for control of European skies, NATO forces attempt to hold back Soviet armor, and Iceland becomes strategically vital to control of the North Atlantic.

“Listen, I don't have to know why. I have to know what.” The Hunt for Red October introduced the world to Jack Ryan and put Clancy on the literary map, eventually becoming a killer movie, too. At the start of the book, Soviet submarine commander Marko Ramius takes the technologically advanced Red October to sea and appears to be heading toward the United States. The Americans need to determine whether he's preparing to attack them or attempting to defect. That uncertainty drives almost the entire novel.

Ryan becomes convinced that Ramius intends to hand the submarine over to the US, but he has to persuade his bosses of that while both American and Soviet forces search for Red October. From here, we get a depiction of submarine warfare that's rigorously detailed and yet still incredibly suspenseful. It mostly involves people listening, calculating, waiting, and trying to infer an opponent's intentions from incomplete information.

#3291. 62-Episode Prime Video Sci-Fi Series Only Gets Better With Age

Time is as cruel to sci-fi television as it is to humans. As more time goes by, it becomes hard not to notice how sci-fi shows that were once considered masterpieces are slowly decaying into tomorrow's relics. Good sci-fi storytelling alone remains timeless. However, from a visual and legacy standpoint, many TV shows of our time struggle to sustain what they started.

Fortunately, Prime Video's The Expanse is a rare exception.

Perhaps in a decade, even the visuals from The Expanse will start feeling dated. The CGI from earlier seasons already seems a little rough around the edges. Yet, overall, The Expanse can still stand well against some of the biggest big-screen productions. The reason being that its visual language emphasized grounded physics and industrial grit instead of extreme photorealism.

When it comes to The Expanse's themes, it feels more relevant than ever. Its portrayal of manufactured class divides, information war, and humanity's unchecked ambition reflects real concerns surrounding today's world. Beyond its themes and visuals, however, there is another aspect that ensures the Prime Video sci-fi show ages like George Clooney.

Way too many sci-fi shows have landed in the ever-growing graveyard of the streaming era's cancelations. This has happened to a point where many viewers have even given up on getting too invested in shows. After all, one can never know when the proverbial plug will be pulled.

The Expanse, too, almost became a victim of the same trend. Despite earning immense acclaim after landing on Syfy, it was canceled after just three seasons. History could have repeated itself. The Expanse could have become another forgotten sci-fi series that fell short of reaching its full potential.

However, this is when fan-campaigning and Amazon eventually saved the day.

More often than not, fan campaigns go unnoticed. When the economics stop making sense, streaming services and networks care little about fan campaigns from cult audiences. In The Expanse's case, though, fans did everything from flying a place over Amazon Studios to launching a miniature Rocinante into near-space.

As a result, The Expanse was saved by Amazon, and Jeff Bezos himself announced its return. He said (via Forbes),

"I just got word that The Expanse is saved. The show is extraordinary, and these guys are unbelievably talented.”

While Prime Video, too, could not eventually sustain the show's run beyond season 6, it is hard not to be grateful that The Expanse got to last so long. Some of the best aspects of the series emerge after season 3, which shows how it would not have been half as good if Prime Video had not given it a second chance.

Unlike many canceled sci-fi shows, The Expanse has a reliable 6-season arc with a solid legacy. It continues to age so well because it got the opportunity to reach its full potential.

Lined up with the same team as The Expanse, Prime Video is adapting Daniel Abraham and Ty Franck's The Captive's War book series. Naren Shankar of The Expanse fame is returning as the showrunner, while director Breck Eisner is also set to helm the series. Reports suggest that even Daniel Abraham and Ty Franck​​​​ are actively involved in the series' writers' room.

With so much going in The Captive's War's favor, it is hard not to hope that it will get the same treatment as The Expanse. Unlike The Expanse, The Captive's War only consists of a trilogy of books. Owing to this, if its creators adapt only one book per season, the show could wrap its run in just three seasons.

However, given how unpredictable streaming cancellations have become, one can only pray that it will last long enough to cover its entire source material. Given the strength of its production team and source material, though, The Captive's War could have a strong three-to-four season run before concluding its story.

If all goes well, the upcoming Prime Video sci-fi series could also match The Expanse's legacy and maybe even pave the way for its return after season 6.

The Expanse is a sci-fi series set in the distant future where humanity has spread out across the solar system, but the alliances between the three most potent governing bodies have reached a state of cold war. A mixed-up crew finds themselves at the center of a dangerous intergalactic conspiracy that threatens to bring war to the colonized worlds.

Whether you want a full-featured fitness smartwatch or a more recovery-focused tracker, here are the discounts you can find right now, including on brands like Apple, Oura, Garmin, and more.

The Oura Ring 5 is at its lowest ever price: $299 for black and silver, $399 for all other colors. These are the lowest prices ever for these rings, which usually go for $399 and $499, respectively. For an even cheaper deal, the older Oura Ring 4 is $249—a full $100 off its list price of $349. If you opt for "stealth" (matte black), the price is $279; for gold, it's $286.61, down from $399. I also wouldn't normally recommend Whoop Life, since its ECG readings and blood pressure estimates aren't really worth the extra $100+. Right now, I'm seeing it for as low as $329, down from the list price of $399. (And if you're stuck deciding between an Apple Watch and a Fitbit, Beth breaks it all down in her comparison of the two watches.)

The CMF Watch 3 Pro is Nothing's latest smartwatch, and it incorporates AI features powered by ChatGPT; you can currently pick it up at a major discount. Originally $99, you can get the CMF Watch 3 Pro for $55. This is the lowest price this smartwatch has been.

If you're looking specifically for a sporty, outdoors watch, Garmin sets the standard. (You could definitely call me something of a Garmin enthusiast.) Here are the best Black Friday deals on Garmin watches that I've seen so far:

The 44mm Garmin Instinct 3 is 249.99 (down from $449.99). The 1.2-inch color AMOLED display makes the screen more readable in bright daylight conditions, and battery life is best-in-class—a must for those going off-grid.

The Garmin Fēnix 8 in titanium with a gray band is $749.99 (down from $999.99). While this is last year's model, it's a perfectly solid option if you don't specifically need the titanium case or the latest mapping engine in the latest Fenix 9 Pro.

The Garmin Forerunner 265 is $299.99 (down from $449.99). Although it isn't the latest and greatest anymore, this is still a fan favorite among Garmin users. It's a step above entry-level options, with dual-band GPS, power meter compatibility, and advanced analytics (like training status).

These aren't the only sales you'll see on fitness watches and trackers during the big shopping holiday; the following brands have announced they'll be launching more deals on Nov. 19:

Additionally, though the sale has ended, the Google Pixel Watch 5 was recently marked down by $100; I'll be keeping an eye on this device to see if that particular deal comes back once Black Friday officially arrives.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

The best thing you can do is compare the prices with other retailers that have Black Friday sales. If that seems like too much work, you can just follow our Black Friday coverage (we're already doing all the searching and vetting for you). Some other tips are making sure you're not being sold an older or cheaper version and always reading reviews.

For most people, the Apple Watch SE 3 at $199 is a good starting point, covering everyday fitness tracking, notifications, and essential health features without the higher price of the Series 12. If you want more advanced health monitoring and a more premium smartwatch experience, the Series 12 at $329 is worth considering.

Yes, Garmin is one of the best brands when it comes to rugged sports watches and fitness trackers. The Forerunner line especially, is a go-to pick for accurate and reliable GPS tracking for runners.

#3284. The Hunger Games Meets The Walking Dead In This 40-Episode Sci-Fi Thriller Series

On paper, The Hunger Games and The Walking Dead are two distinct franchises. But picture a dystopian world where the apocalypse is not ruled by zombies but by monstrous humans themselves. Even the games they play among themselves to increase their class divides are more political and terrifying. There lies the premise of a compelling 40-episode sci-fi thriller.

Loosely based on the French graphic novel Le Transperceneige and Bong Joon Ho's movie of the same name, Snowpiercer has a distinct post-apocalyptic setup. Some shows, like The Walking Dead, are open world survival thrillers. Others, like Silo, unfold in underground bunkers. Snowpiercer primarily takes place in a titular train that endlessly circles Earth.

Finding shelter in a constantly moving train does not sound too bad when the planet outside is frozen beyond repair. In Snowpiercer's world, however, the man-made divides and horrors inside the train are far more disturbing than the thought of freezing to death. Owing to this, it seems fair to compare Snowpiercer with both The Hunger Games and The Walking Dead.

Panem, in The Hunger Games, weaponizes spectacle and controlled scarcity to exploit the lower classes. They quietly aggravate the existing divides between oppressed districts while ensuring the Capitol remains safe and sound. A similar system can be noticed in Snowpiercer. Just like Panem's districts in The Hunger Games are numbered based on economics, humanity is divided through a train's cars in Snowpiercer.

While the elite accommodate the front cars of the trains and enjoy every luxury, the ones at the back rot in inhumane conditions. Much like President Snow in The Hunger Games, the train's creator, Wilford, also has a cult-like following where he is almost treated like an overarching deity. Similar to Jennifer Lawrence's Katniss Everdeen, Snowpiercer also finds its reluctant rebel in Andre Layton.

He emerges from the depths of the lower classes but, like Katniss, realizes that overthrowing a tyrant is far easier than leading a deeply divided population without becoming a tyrant yourself.

Similar to the characters in The Walking Dead, the ones in Snowpiecer, too, gradually experience moral erosion in their post-apocalyptic world. Alliances keep shifting, and, instead of uniting against one common evil, the people get lost in their own petty conflicts and selfish desire to survive. Despite these overlaps, though, Snowpiercer finds its distinct voice through its detective noir drama.

Overall, Bong Joon Ho's Snowpiercer is an absolute masterpiece. The show does not even come close to being as gripping and intense as the award-winning film. However, the series still makes good use of its long runtime to expand the world-building from the movie. While the movie quickly moves from one car to another, the show carefully reveals how everything from water supply to food production works.

Instead of jumping from one action set piece to another, the show paces itself and introduces gripping mysteries to keep viewers hooked. The movie is star-studded, with Chris Evans, Tilda Swinton, Ed Harris, Song Kang-ho, Jamie Bell, and Octavia Spencer serving as its leads. Even the show, however, boasts memorable performances from Jennifer Connelly, Daveed Diggs, Rowan Blanchard, and Sean Bean.

All in all, the Snowpiercer show never comes off as a forced extension of the original movie. It also does not try too hard to draw any connections to the film, which helps it etch its own solid identity like The Hunger Games and The Walking Dead.

Snowpiercer is set aboard a perpetually moving train that carries the last survivors of humanity after Earth is frozen into an uninhabitable wasteland. As passengers remain divided by a rigid class system, former detective Andre Layton is drawn into a murder investigation that exposes growing unrest and ignites a struggle over who should control the future of the train.

#3283. Forget 'Slow Horses,' This Sci-Fi Thriller Is Gary Oldman’s Greatest Role

If you only know Gary Oldman as the lethargic Jackson Lamb in TV hit Slow Horses, it may shock you to know that much of his career was spent bringing to life characters who were high energy, operatic, and filled every moment of screentime with their voice. There’s no greater example of this than The Fifth Element, Luc Besson’s 1997 sci-fi thriller that became an instant classic thanks to its unique vision of the future and memorable performances. As Jean-Baptiste Emanuel Zorg, a flamboyant industrialist working for the film’s evil forces, he becomes larger-than-life in the best way possible. And with the film charting among Tubi's top 10 most-watched films, now's the perfect time to revisit.

Set in the 23rd century, the film stars Bruce Willis as Korben Dallas, a New York City taxi driver and former special forces operative who is stunned when a mysterious woman named Leeloo (Milla Jovovich) falls into his cab. He learns that Leeloo is the key to fighting a great evil that is making its way toward Earth, and uniting her with stones representing the four classical elements is the only way to save humanity. With the government, as well as crazed mercenary Zorg (Oldman), on their tail, Dallas must do everything he can to save Leeloo, and become the hero he was always meant to be.

In a summer that featured dinosaurs (Jurassic Park: The Lost World), aliens (Men in Black), and kick-ass presidents (Air Force One), the French filmmaker's whimsical sci-fi tale stood out amongst traditional Hollywood fare to create a worldwide hit that retained the record for admissions in France for over a decade. The film's impact was largely due to its unique look, which captivated audiences regardless of whether they knew of Besson or understood the film's concept. Those visuals were the product of Besson collaborating with equally imaginative co-creators.

'Slow Horses' Season 5 premieres September 24 on Apple TV+.

Having made his first American-set movie with Léon: The Professional, Besson would go on to develop a story he first created when he was just 16 years old. To match his unique story, filled with prophecy, philosophy, and unknown cultures, he hired artists who would make the visuals unlike anything previously seen on the big screen. For the production design, he recruited French comic creators Jean Giraud and Jean-Claude Mézières to envision 23rd century New York City, where classic iconography met eye-popping futurism. This was symbolized by Korben Dallas’ flying yellow taxi cab, and skyscrapers that seemed to have no beginning or end.

The groundbreaking costumes, such as Leeloo’s orange suspender ensemble and the wild leopard print chic of radio host Ruby Rhod (Chris Tucker), were designed by celebrated fashion guru Jean Paul Gaultier and gave every character their own unique style. Besson already knew how to tell a compelling action story, having built his name on movies such as La Femme Nikita and Subway. By bringing in these iconoclastic artists, he would make every frame look like a comic book come to life, giving both the sci-fi and action genres a new perspective.

The counter to Willis’ sardonic, laid-back hero is Oldman’s Zorg, a character who doesn’t have a drop of subtlety in his blood stream. Elaborately dressed and prone to violent tantrums, Oldman plays Zorg with a manic intensity that borders on cartoonish. Parading around his premises like an emperor, he tries to dominate everyone he comes across, betraying his cowardice only when presented with an opponent he truly can’t overcome. The emotions are right on the surface, reflecting the actor’s previous collaboration with Besson in Léon: The Professional, where he played the corrupt, abusive, and unhinged police officer Norman Stansfield.

In a film where the effects could easily dominate proceedings, Oldman's magnetic presence becomes one of the film’s highlights. As well as giving a human face to the threat Dallas faces, he also provides a villain that feels right at home in the gaudy excess of the future that Besson brings us. A vain capitalist who is used to everything going his way, there is something in his portrayal of a powerful man with deep-seated insecurities that will resonate with today’s society as much as it did in 1997.

The mark of a great actor is the ability to tell a story in multiple ways, and Gary Oldman has made a career of sidestepping expectations. Jean-Baptiste Emanuel Zorg could not be further away from Jackson Lamb, and yet both characters showcase the commitment and ability of a star who can find a way to become part of whatever world he finds himself in. If you’ve just finished the latest season of the Apple TV hit and can’t wait for the next, check out this cult classic to see just how far your favorite spy’s range can stretch.

#3280. Gavin Newsom Blasted By Mother of Murdered 8-Year-Old After Commuting Death Row Sentences

Gavin Newsom was raked over the coals by the mother of a murdered 8-year-old and several other family members of victims after he commuted the sentences of all of California's death row inmates.

Here's the deal ... earlier this month, Governor Newsom commuted all 548 death row inmates -- changing their punishment from death to life in prison.

President Donald Trump, looking to shame the governor for his choice, hosted family members of several victims at an event Monday ... at which he called out Newsom for standing with "the murderers and the child slayers."

The prez then handed off the mic to Sandy Friend ... whose 8-year-old son Michael Lyons was sexually assaulted, tortured and killed by Robert Boyd Rhoades in 1996.

Rhoades was sentenced to death, but it was never carried out ... and the commutation means he will now serve a life sentence instead.

At the podium, Sally spoke directly to Newsom ... saying, "Face me, Governor Newsom. Tell me Michael’s life doesn’t matter. Michael deserved a governor who would stand with the victims, honor their justice, and respect the will of the people.”

Other victims -- including the family of a slain police detective and the father of 12-year-old Polly Klaas, who was strangled to death in 1996 -- also ripped into the governor.

It's worth noting ... the last time a California inmate was executed was 2006 -- though California voters chose not to abolish it at least twice since then.

In a statement to the New York Post, Governor Newsom said, "To the families standing with him today: your grief is real. Every person on California’s former death row will die in prison. Not one walks out. Donald Trump’s criminals walk out.”

In line with the company’s design language, these headphones feature transparent elements and bold, geometric detailing that make them stand out from typical matte-black pairs.
