#3275. Major privacy breaches reported in Muse AI – company responds [U]

This includes again accessing end-to-end encrypted messaging without permission, and sharing what may be the bank balances of another Muse user …

Siri AI was not the only AI app to launch back in September; Meta’s Muse AI app was launched the same month, with the company describing it as “your personal AI agent that gets things done across every part of life.”

Muse initially launched as an iPhone app, with Mac and iPad apps following shortly afterwards. It immediately moved to the top of the US App Store charts, overtaking ChatGPT. It quickly exceeded 5 million downloads following a major advertising push by Meta, and that number has since doubled.

Security researcher Patrick Wardle also discovered a zero-day vulnerability that could allow an attacker to hijack dictated prompts, directing them instead to their own server.

I said at the time that I would absolutely not be one of the millions of people using the app, and the wisdom of that decision has now been underlined by a fresh report.

Reuters now reports Meta employees discussing further breaches. This includes another example of accessing encrypted messages without permission.

The report says this appears to have been done by capturing push notifications. However, this was what the app claimed had happened in the earlier case, and it turned out not to be true. The AI Now Institute was able to replicate the problem of Muse accessing Signal messages without permission.

Another employee reported receiving unsolicited bank balances that they say appeared to be those of another Muse user.

Muse had randomly added an extra message to its regular chats about fishing-related weather and tide information, saying: “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”

“I have never shared my bank account with Muse and never discussed any banking topic with Muse. I’m afraid it’s sending other’s bank info to me,” the staffer wrote in his post.

Meta told Reuters that these were “isolated incidents” and suggested that the bank balances may have been AI hallucinations rather than leaked information. Update: Meta has now told us that the balances were definitely hallucinations.

"AI Agent" = Malware. There are an expanding number of "I told it not to do that" cases.

The instructions (prompt) you give the agent are a tiny fraction of the total prompt context the agent uses, and Meta/Grok/etc. is not going to let you see that context. Agents harvesting your data (ex. see full disk access) and sending it to the mothership is just another revenue/training stream. Even if you are paying you are still the product.

Meta has taken issue with the messaging claims. It says that access to either notifications or messaging must be explicitly granted.

With Android, users have the option to grant apps notification access, which allows apps to see notifications as they’re received. This is something users need to opt in to and is not specific to Muse. With Mac, to allow Muse to work on your behalf, you not only need to click allow for accessibility and screen recording, but after that it takes you to a settings screen where you once again need to confirm and turn this on.

The company also implies that the experience of employees may relate to internal versions of Muse.

Employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.

I can only repeat my previous take on Muse: Nope.

#3273. Mary J. Blige’s ‘Real Love’ Did Not Infringe on ‘Impeach the President,’ Appeals Court Rules

A federal appeals court on Monday upheld a lower court ruling that Mary J. Blige’s 1992 hip-hop soul anthem “Real Love” did not infringe the copyright of the funk classic “Impeach the President.”

In a 10-page ruling from the Second Circuit Court of Appeals, the justices found that the 2024 lawsuit filed by Tuff City Records against Universal Music Publishing failed to state a viable claim. The ruling found that the two songs “are not substantially similar as a matter of law.”

“The works as a whole are distinct,” the ruling obtained by Rolling Stone reads. “The songs differ in their lyrics, melody, genre, subject matter, and overall sound.”

The Honey Drippers released “Impeach the President” in 1973, and it quickly became a Nixon-era protest anthem with a distinctive drum break that would become widely sampled by artists including Janet Jackson, J. Cole, and Doja Cat.

When Tuff City sued Universal over “Real Love” in 2024, it was the latest in a decades-long history of copyright litigation targeting some of the biggest names in hip-hop. The New York-based independent label brought claims over allegedly unauthorized samples of “Impeach the President” in songs by LL Cool J and EPMD in 1991 and later pursued litigation involving Run DMC, Kanye West, and the Beastie Boys.

In filing its appeal, Tuff City argued that the lower court used an incorrect legal standard to compare “Real Love” with “Impeach the President.” The appellate court disagreed.

“While ‘Impeach the President’ and ‘Real Love’ share certain percussive elements, other elements are notably different, such as open versus closed hi-hats and distinct snare and kick drum rhythms,” the ruling states. “The songs’ ‘total concept and overall feel’ reinforce the conclusion that the works at issue are not substantially similar.”

Agreeing with the district court, the ruling found that “Impeach the President” is a protest song that “fits squarely within the soul/funk genre,” whereas “Real Love” is a “hip-hop soul song about heartbreak, not politics.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

“‘Impeach the President’ is sung by a male group, incorporates a call-and-response technique, and features horns and guitars,” the opinion read, adding that by contrast, “Real Love” is sung by a woman and “is driven by piano and percussion.” The three-judge panel stated, “Considering both the alleged percussive overlap and the works as a whole, we conclude that the district court properly dismissed [the] claim of copyright infringement of the musical composition.”

Hillel I. Parness, a lawyer for Tuff City, said the company was “very disappointed” by Monday’s ruling and “will be seeking further judicial review.” He described “Impeach the President” as one of the “most widely- and consistently-sampled songs from the classic hip-hop era” and warned that the decision could have far-reaching implications for the genre. Trending Stories Watch Taylor Swift Surprise Brenda Lee With ‘Rockin’ Around the Christmas Tree’ Honor Previously Unseen Footage of Led Zeppelin at Madison Square Garden Surfaces After 49 Years Bob Seger and the Silver Bullet Band Bassist Chris Campbell Dead at 78 Billy Ray Cyrus Shares Snapshots From Miley’s Wedding: 'Beautiful' to See Family 'United by Love'

“Allowing Universal publishing’s refusal to pay for its undisputed sampling to stand would upend decades of law, and decades of industry practice, all designed around ensuring that creators and owners are paid for the use of samples, even if the samples themselves are then reconfigured,” Parness said in a statement to Rolling Stone.

Lawyers for Universal did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

#3271. Canva introduces new controls to hide generative AI features

In light of growing pushback from users who want more control over how AI is integrated into their apps (if at all), Canva is introducing new settings that let them hide generative AI features and see less AI-generated content. Here are the details.

Canva today announced new controls that will let Free and Pro users choose whether to see generative AI features across the app, as well as how much AI-generated content appears in search results and in recommendations for templates and design elements.

The company notes that both controls are available at no additional cost and can be turned on or off at any time.

According to Canva, “the future of creativity isn’t a choice between AI and no AI.” For this reason, it is introducing the following controls:

The company says that, while it knows that there is an ongoing debate between users with opposing views on whether AI has a place in creative work, it thinks “both views are valid”:

“It’s not our place to tell anyone how to create, so today we’re launching two new controls that put that decision firmly with our community […].”

Importantly, the company noted that select features that use AI without generating new content will remain available even when generative AI features are turned off:

“Some of Canva’s everyday editing tools use AI to make simple tasks faster, without generating anything new. Background Remover, one of Canva’s most popular tools, lifts a subject cleanly out of a photo in a single click, and Magic Grab lets creators select an object in an image and move it somewhere else in the design. Both remain available when the generative AI switch is off, because they work only with what’s already in a design.”

Canva added that these tools also won’t add an AI label to a design’s metadata, since that label is reserved for AI-generated content.

As for the company’s design content library, Canva said that while “a small portion of the library is AI-generated content made by Canva, including some abstract backgrounds and illustrated graphics,” its community has told it “they want an easier way to find design assets made by real people, so the content control reduces the number of AI-generated templates and elements that appear in search results and recommendations.”

With today’s announcement, Canva is essentially expanding on the AI permissions already available to administrators of Business, Enterprise, Teams, and Education accounts, which let organizations control how their teams use AI.

#3267. OLED iMac plans may be cancelled by Apple for two reasons

Apple is considering abandoning plans to launch an OLED iMac, according to a new supply chain report. The news comes just weeks after the first OLED Mac was launched in the form of the new touchscreen MacBook Pro.

The company is said to be holding discussions with display partner Samsung about either delaying the planned launch or abandoning it altogether, with two reasons cited …

1. The size. 24” is undesirable at the prices they ask.

2. No target display mode. Making the display unusable with multiple computers or after you’ve upgraded to a new model of Mac.

Adding OLED doesn’t solve either of these, and raising the price obviously doesn’t solve it.

At the same time, there’s an important distinction between commercial viability and margins. Apple is concerned with the latter, not the former.

An OLED iMac would be a commercially viable product at current prices, but it might not have the 30 to 40 % hardware profit margins they desire. Adding OLED would raise Apples costs, without adding more sales (due to 1 and 2) to offset that slightly lower but (still industry leading) profit margin.

Apple’s journey into OLED screens began with the Apple Watch while other products were still using IPS LCD. The company subsequently switched to OLED for some iPhones and iPads before a long-awaited launch of the first OLED MacBook Pro back in October.

It was expected that the company would gradually transition to OLED across the full range of Macs over time. However, this process was expected to take a number of years, with the iMac not likely to join the party until 2029 or 2030.

The Elec today reports that the move may be delayed even further or even abandoned altogether, for two reasons: cost and demand.

The company is said to be discussing a potential delay or cancellation of the project with Samsung Display. High OLED panel costs and weak sales of existing OLED-equipped products are believed to be factors behind the reconsideration […]

The biggest factor behind the review is cost. The iMac sells in smaller volumes than smartphones or laptops, making it difficult to maintain competitive pricing if expensive OLED panels are adopted. Weak sales of the OLED iPad Pro are also believed to have influenced the decision.

The report suggests that incoming CEO John Ternus has been reviewing the commercial viability of upgrading more products to OLED. As further evidence, the report says Apple has sent quotation requests to LCD suppliers for an iMac screen to be launched in around 2029.

#3263. Bob Seger and the Silver Bullet Band Bassist Chris Campbell Dead at 78

Bob Seger and the Silver Bullet Band bassist Chris Campbell, who joined forces with Seger in 1969 and remained a core member of the band through Seger’s farewell tour in 2019 — playing on timeless hits like “Turn the Page,” “Night Moves,” “Rock and Roll Never Forgets,” “Still the Same,” “Hollywood Nights,” and “Against the Wind” — died on Sunday. He was 78.

Campbell’s wife, Courtney, confirmed his death with Rolling Stone, adding that Campbell died of natural causes.

“I’m grieving the loss of my long-time friend and Silver Bullet bandmate, Chris Campbell…..RIP,” Silver Bullet Band vocalist Shaun Murphy wrote. “Prayers and condolences to his wonderful wife, Courtney Campbell, and his three beautiful daughters!! I am forever grateful for all the cherished memories I have.”

Campbell grew up in Plymouth, Michigan, and was a regular on the Detroit club scene that gave rise to the MC5, the Stooges, and the Amboy Dukes. “You were playing to smaller crowds and things were more intimate,” he told the Observer & Eccentric in 1987. “There weren’t any barriers in front of the stage with six-foot security guards.”

Just one year after the Bob Seger System scored a nationwide hit with “Ramblin’ Gamblin’ Man” in 1968, Campbell was offered a spot in the band. “I was hired in what I thought was a temporary job as bass player because Dan Honaker had just broken his wrist about a week before the Mongrel tour [in a motorcycle accident],” he told Rolling Stone in 2011. “I had a week to prepare. I had to learn this album frontwards and backwards.”

Honaker’s bad luck turned out to be the opportunity of a lifetime for Campbell because of what transpired not long after the Bob Seger System dissolved. “Bob called me…I think it was ’71, ’72,” Campbell told Rolling Stone. “He said, ‘I’m thinking of putting a band together.’ I said to him, ‘That’s kind of bizarre, I have a keyboard player and a drummer.’ He goes, ‘I got a guitarist, Drew Abbott.’ That was the start of the Silver Bullet Band.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

The early years of the Silver Bullet Band were a brutal grind, memorialized in the lyrics of 1972’s “Turn the Page,” but everything changed once the concert LP Live Bullet took off in 1976. The follow-up LP, Night Moves, turned Seger into one of the biggest names in rock.

Unlike similar groups like Bruce Springsteen’s E Street Band and Neil Young’s Crazy Horse, membership in the Silver Bullet Band was somewhat fluid, and studio musicians often backed Seger on albums. This arrangement didn’t suit Abbott, who quit the group in 1983 and never returned. But Campbell, background singers Shaun Murphy and Laura Creamer, and saxophonist Alto Reed were lifers. Grand Funk Railroad keyboardist Craig Frost also became a key component of the group for decades.

For Campbell, it wasn’t always an easy ride. “We have all [thought about leaving] at one time or another,” he told the Observer & Eccentric in 1987. “It would be an out-and-out lie to say we haven’t. You get tired, and it’s terrible on relationships.”

The job got easier after the tour for Seger’s 1995 LP It’s a Mystery wrapped, and the group went off the road for more than a decade. “Bob works at his own pace,” Campbell told Rolling Stone in 2011. “I can go out and do something else. It’s the way it’s always been since 1969. I wouldn’t know any other way. This is my life, and I’m very happy with it. I have wonderful kids and a good life, and we’re all friends. We’re all very fortunate. There’s no animosity and no fighting. Bob is our rock, our patriarch. We all look up to him. He’s so easy to work with. He’s a wonderful man, just as a human being.” Related Content John Christ, Original Danzig Guitarist on ‘Mother’ and More, Dead at 61 Richard Sterban, Oak Ridge Boys’ Bass Singer, Dead at 83 Anthony Clark, Stand-Up Comic and 'Yes, Dear' Star, Dead at 62 Stacy Keach, ‘Mike Hammer’ and ‘Fat City’ Star, Dead at 85

Bob Seger and the Silver Bullet Band launched a farewell tour in 2018 that wrapped up in 2019 at the Wells Fargo Center in Philadelphia. They became just about the only act in rock history to say farewell and truly mean it. Trending Stories Watch Taylor Swift Surprise Brenda Lee With ‘Rockin’ Around the Christmas Tree’ Honor Previously Unseen Footage of Led Zeppelin at Madison Square Garden Surfaces After 49 Years Bob Seger and the Silver Bullet Band Bassist Chris Campbell Dead at 78 Billy Ray Cyrus Shares Snapshots From Miley’s Wedding: 'Beautiful' to See Family 'United by Love'

Two years after the tour wrapped, Campbell filed a lawsuit against Seger and longtime manager Punch Andrews over alleged unpaid royalties from albums and tours. “Bob Seger and Punch Andrews have loyally supported our friend for 45-plus years,” they said in a statement. (Campbell ultimately lost his recording-royalty claims.)

Campbell kept a low public profile after the farewell tour. But in 2011, he told Rolling Stone why he enjoyed the latter-day tours so much. “We’re kind of old-school,” he said. “We aren’t glitzy. You don’t see any flash pots going off up there. We just do things the way we do. We aren’t really concerned about press agents and all that. We just play. And the older we get, the more fun we have. When you get older, you don’t take it as seriously as you once did when you were younger. If you can’t have fun at our age, don’t do it.”

#3260. This Note-Taking Pebble Ring Is so Simple, and I Love It

Pebble’s $75 ring, the Index 01, has one job: It lets you record voice memos. That seems like it would be underwhelming, and the idea was ridiculed by some of Pebble’s fans when the product was first announced. But I’ve been wearing it for a few weeks, and folks: I love it.

In this era where every tech product is trying to also be every other tech product, I appreciate the Index’s simplicity. This is a ring with no heart rate sensors or even charging pins, just a microphone, a button to activate it, and a light to let you know that it’s working. The audio is processed on your device; no need to send anything to the cloud.

To buy the Index 01 ring, you get yourself a sizing kit (either buy one for $10 or 3D print it yourself), order the ring, and pair it with the Pebble app on your phone. I use an iPhone rather than an Android, which means I can’t use certain features like setting timed reminders or connecting to Beeper, but it’s still an incredibly useful little device. The Index has no charger, since it uses a disposable battery that Pebble estimates will last about two years.

The simplest way to use the Index is to wear it on your index finger (hence the name, get it?) and press the button with your thumb. Speak a quick note while holding the button in, and the ring will flash to let you know it got the message. A moment later, you’ll get a notification saying that it added (whatever you said) to your “Notes to self” note.

To take this further, you can create different notes and ask the ring to add what you say to a specific note. You can also double-click the button to ask a question. The answer will appear in the notification you get on your phone or watch a moment later. (The ring does not speak to you.)

All the notes you leave yourself appear as plain text in the Pebble app, fully editable. If you tap on each one, you can see a timestamp from when you left the note, and you can replay the voice recording if the transcription doesn’t make sense. (Why is there a “pencil sharp pepper” on my packing list? Ohh, that’s a pencil sharpener.) You can also add notes by typing them, which I find useful when starting a to-do list or a packing list.

It’s incredible how useful a simple timestamped note can be. I used to do something similar with my “notes to self” chat in Signal, but the Index makes it even easier since I won’t get distracted by opening my phone. For example, I make a note on the Index whenever I take a medication, so that tomorrow morning I will be able to check whether I already took, say, a long-acting allergy pill. (You do not want to accidentally double up on those.)

There’s one thing that, for years, I wished for a simple tool to help me do. It’s trivial, which makes it extra frustrating that I have not been able to find a good solution. I would simply like to note when I leave for a road trip, and when I start and end each stop. This way I can tell how long the driving took as a portion of the whole trip, and how long my stops tend to be so I can plan them better next time.

You’d think this would be easy, but every existing tool drove me nuts in a different way. Stopwatches only store a single number, so I can’t break down how long each stop was—and if I miss a button press, I’m screwed. Sending myself a Signal text is probably my best option, but if I’ve just parked my car after three hours of driving, the second I pick up my phone I’m going to see all the notifications that arrived while I was on the road, and I’ll forget to actually send that text.

But this is exactly what the Index does well. I don’t even need to open my phone or look at my watch. Pressing the button with my thumb means I can do this one-handed without having a microphone always listening. (It’s also a great way to jot down the random things I think of while driving.)

The Index worked perfectly for my travel log, and I even used it for a workout after I got to my hotel room that night. I’d do 10 pushups, then tell the ring “add 10 pushups to my workout.” I’d do 20 crunches, and add that as well. I left the workout note open on my phone and could glance over and see what I had already done, since my messages got added to the note as I went.

I didn’t need a workout app for any of this, or a special-purpose travel app. I can just leave myself a dang note, and the note-taking app can remember when I left the note and, if I choose, play back exactly how I said it. It’s gloriously simple. Good job, Pebble.

#3258. UK court rules Apple can share the top secret order everyone already knew

The Investigatory Powers Tribunal – essentially a British court that deals with complaints about state surveillance – has ruled that Apple is allowed to reveal a secret order it received from the UK government.

Apple had already found a clever way to alert British customers to the classified order without breaking the law, but it can now confirm what we all already knew, and talk openly about the issue …

In 2025, the British government ordered Apple to create a backdoor to allow access by security services and law enforcement. Even worse, the order was issued under legislation that prohibits companies from revealing that they have received this demand.

This would have meant that British customers who enabled ADP would think that their data was safe when in fact it wasn’t. As we’ve said many times before, any backdoor created for use by the good guys is vulnerable to discovery and exploitation by the bad guys.

“Apple can no longer offer Advanced Data Protection (ADP) in the United Kingdom to new users and current UK users will eventually need to disable this security feature. ADP protects iCloud data with end-to-end encryption, which means the data can only be decrypted by the user who owns it, and only on their trusted devices. We are gravely disappointed that the protections provided by ADP will not be available to our customers in the UK […] As we have said many times before, we have never built a backdoor or master key to any of our products or services and we never will.”

Tell me you’ve been ordered to create a backdoor to ADP without telling me you’ve been ordered to create a backdoor to ADP …

The UK government must admit that it issued a secret order to Apple to allow it access to encrypted customer data, a court has ruled […] The Home Office has “not established that it would be damaging to national security” to reveal that Apple had received a “technical capability notice” (TCN), the tribunal said. The ruling means that […] “much” of Apple and the non-profits’ legal challenge can now take place in open court.

One of the great ironies is that most people had never heard of ADP until the government effectively made it headline news in the tech press three years after it launched – a classic example of the Streisand Effect.

This ruling is a win both for transparency and commonsense. To be clear, the actual requirement for a backdoor remains in place, but this can now be challenged in open court.

#3256. Gemini Notebook's New Interactive Site Builder Is Much More Useful Than I Expected

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

Gemini Notebook, Google's AI tool for study and research, already lets you do a lot with your notes: You can turn them into flashcard quizzes, interactive podcasts, video explainers, mind maps, and infographics, as well as interrogating the sources you've collected through AI-powered prompts and responses. Now there's something new. You can also build interactive websites from your notebooks.

That might not immediately seem like the most obvious fit, turning your research notes into a mass of HTML code. But it gives you another way to look at your material and to get insights from it. Here's how it works, what you could potentially do with it, and how impressively it worked when I put it to the test on some early 20th-century Irish literature.

Website building is rolling out now for Gemini Notebook's web app for all users, and is "coming soon" to the mobile app.  You won't see a website option in the Studio panel alongside Audio Overview, Reports, Quiz, and the rest; instead, you type something along the lines of "make me a website" in the prompt box.

To make a website, you need sources, so I set Gemini Notebook to collect information about James Joyce's 1914 collection of short stories, Dubliners. As I studied Dubliners many years ago (I highly recommend it), I was hoping I'd spot any AI errors and hallucinations, and be able to properly assess the quality of Gemini Notebook's analysis.

With a suitable amount of information absorbed into the AI brain, I got Gemini Notebook to make me a website. Google doesn't give too much official guidance here, but says you should add "a description of what you want to build for work or study," so if you have a particular style or angle in mind, include it.

Here was my prompt: "Build a website using all the sources and information collected so far. Make it an interactive guide to the individual stories in Dubliners, as well as the overarching themes and context. I want to use it as a study aid to explore different aspects of the story collection."

The finished website pops up in the Studio panel, and in my case it took around five minutes to put something together from 26 different sources. Click on the website, and it opens in a new window—you can use it from there, open it in a separate tab, or download the code to your computer.

I was honestly impressed by how much Gemini Notebook managed to pack into a single website: I got plot summaries, analysis, critical context, and some of the main themes and motifs outlined. There was an interactive quiz at the bottom of the page to test my knowledge, and even a graphic I could click through to reveal different elements of how the stories fit together.

Everything was well laid out and functional, albeit with the standard "sheen" you get from anything made by AI (which tends to always pick the same colors and fonts). I wouldn't have necessarily thought that I needed a website if I was still studying Dubliners today, but I can definitely see how it would have helped.

For something like my project, a website really works well as a study aid, since it offers a different way of interrogating the information. You can already do that in the main chat, and with tools such as the audio and video overviews, but this is different. It's a bit like having a mini-Wikipedia focused just on whatever you're researching.

The interactive elements that are included—so in my example, I could click from story to story, and theme to theme, within the same page—make a site more engaging than a standard report document and a static wall of text, and should help the information stick if you're trying to study it.

I can also see how this might be useful for sharing data with others. Maybe you need to analyze monthly report figures, or you want to chart how your organization has developed a product over time—perhaps an interactive website will relay that information in a more compelling way than a slide deck or PDF.

Maybe you have a notebook stuffed with details of a big family vacation. Putting together a website through Gemini Notebook would give your family a hub that they could use to easily check up on the details of the trip—where you're going and when, what you'll see there, what they need to pack, and so on. Another idea might be a family tree, if you have ancestry data and sources packed together in a notebook. Putting together a website would be a great way to visualize it, and, again, it's something you could share with relatives. If there were updates to the data you've collected, you could generate a new website.

Bear in mind that you can do a lot with your prompt. My website turned out the way it did because that's what I asked for, and if you need more interactivity or specific types of sections, then you can ask. Based on my follow-up prompts, you can also specify colors and certain layout choices, though it's not quite a full-scale website builder.

It looks like these sites are single-page creations, though they do have interactive elements and sections that change as you click around. It might be better to think of them as mini apps rather than sites. As of yet, there's no built-in option for publishing a site online or sharing it with others, so you need to download the HTML and do that manually.

#3255. The Best Magnesium Supplements and What to Look For, According to an Expert

Magnesium is one of the most popular supplements on the market thanks to wide-ranging potential benefits like better sleep, stress reduction, and improved digestion. Much of this popularity has been driven by social media, including the viral #SleepyGirlMocktail trend. Plus, a slew of A-listers from Taylor Swift to Scarlett Johansson to Lenny Kravitz have also talked about taking magnesium to relax.

So what is magnesium? Like most supplements, it’s a mineral used by our body’s cells to function. It helps turn food into energy, strengthen bones, and support normal heart rhythm. Another key function of magnesium is sleep regulation, since the mineral helps calm muscles and the nervous system and regulate sleep-related hormones. That means taking magnesium may help consumers get better natural sleep instead of being sedated.

There are several types of magnesium supplements, and each binds magnesium to a different molecule, affecting absorption and how the supplement is used. “Magnesium citrate, chloride, lactate, and aspartate generally have better bioavailability than magnesium oxide because they are more soluble and more readily absorbed,” Dr. Martina Ambardjieva, MD, Ph.D., urologist, and medical expert at Invigor Medical, tells Rolling Stone. “Magnesium glycinate also tends to be well tolerated.”

Studies show that magnesium citrate may support digestion and bowel regularity, chloride muscle and nerve function, lactate energy production, aspartate muscle function and energy, and glycinate relaxation, sleep, and stress management. According to Ambardjieva, the recommended total daily magnesium intake is approximately 310 to 320 milligrams daily for women and 400 to 420 milligrams for men, including food sources.

In order to choose the right magnesium supplement for your health and lifestyle, Ambardjieva recommends checking the amount of elemental magnesium (the actual weight of the magnesium in the supplement) and avoiding unnecessarily high doses. The best magnesium supplements also have third-party testing, such as USP or NSF verification.

If you’re looking to try magnesium for yourself, pick up one of the supplements below.

Pros: High dose, can be mixed with waterCons: May cause bathroom urges

Thorne Magnesium Citrate delivers 250 mg of highly absorbable magnesium in a convenient citrus-berry powder that can be mixed with water, ideal for those who don’t feel comfortable swallowing pills. Although a powder, it’s not recommended to take it before bed, like other powders in the #SleepyGirlMocktail trend, as magnesium citrate is a type of laxative. On the other hand, it supports muscle and cardiovascular health, promotes regular digestion, and helps maintain urinary mineral balance, with NSF certification.

Pros: Approved by over 32,000 Amazon customersCons: Reviewers say there is an aftertaste

BioEmblem’s Triple Complex provides 300 mg per serving from glycinate, malate, and citrate. The three types of magnesium here promote bone health and muscle support, and the brand is third-party tested and NSF- and Labdoor-certified. However, it does not clearly distinguish how much of the 300 mg is elemental magnesium. Still, it’s proven to be a popular option among customers, with over 32,000 reviews and a 4.6-star rating on Amazon.

Pros: Dual-amino-acid chelate formula for better absorption, powder form, great for relaxationCons: Flavor might not be for everyone

Unlike the other options on this list, this one from Viactiv uses magnesium lysinate glycinate, a dual-amino-acid chelate. In plain English, this is meant to improve absorption and digestive tolerability of the magnesium, which is a common side effect that people report. It’s a powder, which is great for mixing with water or shakes, and comes in a stevia-sweetened peach flavor.

Pros: Supports bone, heart, nerve, and immune health in oneCons: The dose is higher than what is doctor-recommended for adults

Vitalitown’s Magnesium Complex provides four forms: glycinate, citrate, taurate, and malate. The product is NSF certified and third-party tested. At 500 mg per serving, its dose is relatively high compared with typical daily magnesium needs, making dose awareness important. As Dr. Ambardjieva tells us, there isn’t one ideal supplemental dose for everyone, so guidance from your physician about the right dose is recommended.

Pros: Targets fatigue, muscle issues, and constipationCons: Lower mgs than what is doctor-recommended for an adult to take daily

Double Wood’s Magnesium Chloride provides 120 mg of elemental magnesium per serving and includes chloride, which Ambardjieva identified as generally well absorbed. In addition to promoting sleep and supporting muscle and nerve function, studies show that magnesium chloride is a good option for when your body is already deficient. According to the doctor, magnesium deficiency may cause fatigue, weakness, nausea, muscle cramps, tingling, and, in severe cases, seizures or irregular heart rhythms. Double Wood Supplements is also described as third-party tested for purity, potency, microbes, and heavy metals.

Pros: Gentle on the stomachCons: Must take three large capsules to reach the recommended dose for an adult

Nature Made Magnesium Glycinate provides 300 mg per three capsules and clearly identifies the amount of magnesium provided. Although Ambardjieva says there is less comparative evidence showing that magnesium glycinate is clearly superior to other well-absorbed forms, research shows that magnesium glycinate is a stomach-friendly supplement, unlike magnesium oxide, and may reduce stress and muscle tension, among other benefits. The product is also USP verified, addressing the recommendation to look for independent quality testing.

Pros: Lactose-free and absorbs quickly into the bloodstream Cons: Customers say the pill size is quite large compared to other magnesium capsules

Swanson Magnesium Lactate provides 84 mg of elemental magnesium per capsule and is among the forms Ambardjieva identified as generally well absorbed due to its high bioavailability. Research suggests that magnesium lactate causes fewer digestive side effects than some other forms of magnesium, and may support healthy blood pressure and normal cell function. Swanson also says its finished supplements undergo independent third-party laboratory testing for purity and potency.

Pros: Vegan ingredients and the best magnesium supplement for athletesCons: The glass jar makes it susceptible to breaking, according to some reviewers

Bluebonnet Magnesium Aspartate provides 400 mg daily as magnesium aspartate, a form Ambardjieva identified as generally well absorbed. The brand’s supplements undergo rigorous testing for authenticity, purity, and potency, although it does not specifically mention USP or NSF verification. Scientists found that magnesium aspartate helps with proper muscle contraction and is a popular magnesium form for athletes.

Pros: A vegan and kosher supplement that targets multiple health issuesCons: Only 60 tablets per jar, so long-term users may need to reorder more often

New Chapter Magnesium Bisglycinate Complex contains glycinate and provides 325 mg. It includes chelated bisglycinate, which supports high absorption, along with sea-sourced and fermented magnesium forms. New Chapter says it puts its supplements through third-party testing and validation, and this particular product is 100 percent vegan and kosher, making it suitable for those with dietary restrictions.

There isn’t a single magnesium dose that’s right for everyone, and more isn’t necessarily better. According to Ambardjieva, the recommended daily intake for adults is about 310 to 320 milligrams for women and 400 to 420 milligrams for men, including magnesium from both food and supplements. How much you may need from a supplement depends on your diet and individual health needs. When comparing products, look for the amount of elemental magnesium on the label rather than simply the total amount of the magnesium compound.

Taking too much supplemental magnesium can cause diarrhea, nausea, and abdominal cramping, while extremely high magnesium levels can lead to more serious problems, including effects on the heart and kidneys. People with a documented deficiency or those advised to supplement by a healthcare professional are the clearest candidates. If you’re unsure whether you need magnesium or which form and dose are appropriate, talk with a healthcare professional.

Magnesium supplements are generally well tolerated when taken appropriately, but higher amounts can cause digestive side effects, including nausea, diarrhea, or abdominal discomfort. The risk of side effects can also vary depending on the form of magnesium.

Because magnesium supplements can also interact with some medications, people taking prescription drugs or managing a medical condition should check with a healthcare professional before supplementing.

We first interviewed Ambardjieva about magnesium, including which forms may be better absorbed, research-backed benefits, appropriate doses, deficiency symptoms, potential risks, and what consumers should look for in a quality supplement. We then researched available products and evaluated them based on magnesium form, elemental magnesium per serving, ingredient transparency, and serving size. We prioritized products containing forms discussed by the doctor and considered options for different preferences, including vegan, kosher, capsule, and powder formulations.

We also considered tolerability, since some forms and higher doses of magnesium may cause digestive side effects. We did not rely solely on marketing claims, popularity, or customer reviews when making our selections, and third-party testing was a priority for every product. Our picks reflect a combination of evidence, product quality, safety, and practical considerations rather than one-size-fits-all recommendations.

Sophie Dunne is an e-commerce writer at Penske Media Corporation, writing across Rolling Stone, Billboard, The Hollywood Reporter, WWD, and Footwear News. Originally from Ireland and based in Los Angeles, she previously worked at Static Media as a writer and editor, covering entertainment, lifestyle, fashion, and travel. Her bylines have appeared in Women’s Health, The List, Women.com, Islands, Grunge, WebMD, and more. Before beginning her writing career in 2019, Sophie lived in Dubai for four years working as an Emirates cabin crew member. Having traveled to 71 countries with the airline, she began writing for an LA-based publication as a travel writer during her final year. Sophie has a degree in Humanities from Carlow College, St. Patrick’s (now South East Technological University) in her native Ireland. She studied English, history, philosophy, and psychology. Sophie mostly reports on entertainment merchandise and celebrity brand partnerships.

#3254. iOS 27.3 beta can cause HomeView issues, Apple confirms

Apple’s new HomeView just launched last Friday, but some early adopters reported issues with Siri AI in their first days of use. Apple shipped fixes in HomeView 27.2.1 yesterday, but it also confirmed the iOS 27.3 beta is responsible for some of the problems.

Yesterday Apple released its first post-launch software update for HomeView, less than a week after the product debuted.

Per the company’s official release notes, HomeView 27.2.1 focuses on bug fixes, including a fix for the following issue:

Pairing with an iPhone or iPad running the iOS or iPadOS 27.3 beta may cause Siri requests to fail

It’s unknown how many reports of Siri issues on HomeView can be attributed to the iOS 27.3 beta. However, it wouldn’t surprise me if many of the reports were from beta users. That’s in part because early HomeView reviewers didn’t seem to have the same problems.

With HomeView 27.2.1 now available, those problems should hopefully be taken care of. However, if you’re on the iOS 27.3 beta, there’s a new issue you’ll need to deal with temporarily.

As discovered by pdfu, if you try to make a Personal Content request on an iPhone running iOS 27.3, Siri in HomeView 27.2.1 now says: “I can’t help with that because your personal device is on newer software.”

If you’re on iOS 27.3, Siri on HomeView can’t use your iPhone for personal context, likely until December.HomeView won’t send Siri requests to an iPhone on newer software. Without a HomeView update, your only option is iOS 27.2.x.On-device requests like timers still work. https://t.co/8UbRs7z496

It’s understandable that issues might arise from having iOS and HomeView software that’s out of sync. Unfortunately though, there’s no beta software available for HomeView at the moment.

That means unless Apple releases a beta soon, users might have to wait until the public launch of HomeView 27.3 in December to get Personal Content features back.

How has Siri AI been working for you on HomeView? Let us know in the comments.

#3253. ‘Hooters: The Movie’ Sets Owen Patrick Joyner, Kyle Clark & Audrey Trullinger

EXCLUSIVE: Hooters: The Movie is officially open for business, meaning cameras are rolling in the Tampa Bay, Florida area with Owen Patrick Joyner, Kyle Clark and Audrey Trullinger starring in the origin story of the chicken wing chain.

Pic follows lifelong friends Ted and Lenny (Joyner and Clark) who unexpectedly build a restaurant empire. What begins as a spontaneous road trip to Clearwater Beach in pursuit of Diane (Trullinger), a young woman Ted first spots in a spring break commercial, turns into an adventure neither friend could have anticipated with Diane becoming the very first Hooters Girl. Tampa Bay is where the first Hooters restaurant opened in 1983. Related Stories News 'Hooters: The Movie' In The Works About Chicken-Wing Eatery's Origins News 'Only Murders In The Building' Returning To New York For Likely Season 7

Joining the ensemble are Carmen Electra (Baywatch, Scary Movie), David Koechner (Anchorman), WWE Superstar and former Hooters Girl Liv Morgan, Tanner Novlan (The Bold and the Beautiful), Louie Lombardi (Oppenheimer), Caitlin Serros (Night Visions), and Ava Allan (Young Sheldon, BUSTED). The film also features current Hooters Girls actress Gwynn Ali, Kiana Mahabir, the 2025 Hooters Calendar Cover Girl, and Kenzie Davis, winner of the Miss Hooters International 2026 pageant. Watch on Deadline

Casting was led by Lisa London and Catherine Stroud of London/Stroud Casting.

“There’s a whole lot more to the story than orange shorts and chicken wings,” said Marsha Droste, EP of Hooters: The Movie and leader of the Hooters Girl Alumnae community. “From the beginning, it was important to us that the women who helped build this brand had a voice in telling its story. Former Hooters Girls have shared their experiences, humor and memories to help shape the screenplay and bring authenticity to the characters. I’m especially proud that both current and former Hooters Girls are appearing in the film.”

“Even just a few days into production, the energy on set has been incredible,” said the pic’s director Jon Rosenbaum. “There’s so much personality in this story, from two friends stumbling into something much bigger than themselves to the people who helped make Hooters what it is today. We’re having a lot of fun bringing these characters and their stories to life, and I think audiences will have just as much fun watching it.”

Hooters: The Movie is also produced by Ed Droste, Chuck Melcher, Bill Williams, Elayne Schmidt, and Michael E. Brown.

Joyner (Final Destination: Bloodlines) is repped by Prototype Talent Agency, Protege Entertainment and Myman Greenspan Fox etc; Clark (Crew Girl, Riverdale) is repped by Nuance Talent Management, Linden Entertainment and Yorn Levine Barnes etc; and Trullinger (Law & Order: Special Victims Unit) is repped by Gersh, Authentic Talent and Literary Management, and Felker McGinnis & Ryan.
